text:
By WILL WEISSERT and REBECCA SANTANA, Associated Press

WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump said Thursday that he is once more trying to limit the number of people who are born in the country who can become American citizens, in a sign that even after his first attempt at limiting birthright citizenship was rejected by the Supreme Court, he’s ready to try again.

The president said he was signing two executive actions on immigration, including one limiting the number of people eligible for U.S. citizenship after being born in the United States, while another focused on stopping people from coming to the U.S. to give birth.

The written executive order released later Thursday was narrower in scope than the previous one shot down by the Supreme Court and appeared to focus on restricting automatic citizenship to specific categories of people, including children born to adults with connections to foreign embassies or organizations as well as anyone considered an “alien enemy” of the United States.

It also aimed to restrict birthright citizenship to anyone whose parents “engaged in fraudulent activity to obtain citizenship.”

A second order seeks to curb what Trump called “birth tourism” by increasing restrictions on visitors to the U.S. who want to obtain visas to give birth while in the country.

It was not immediately clear how successful the president’s most recent attempt to restrict birthright citizenship would be. Trump said he thought his latest actions would be constitutional and his drive to reopen the question reflected the administration’s zeal to restrict who gets to become an American.

“I thought we were going to win it at the Supreme Court. Unfortunately, we had a bad decision, very unfair decision. Our country suffers because of it and we’re ending it a different way,” Trump said.

The Migration Policy Institute noted in a 2026 article that it’s already considered fraud and grounds to restrict a visa if someone seeks a visa specifically to come to the U.S. and obtain citizenship for a child. Previous administrations have also sought to prosecute so-called “birth tourism” schemes that helped women hide their pregnancies while traveling to the United States to give birth.

Birthright citizenship has become a key rallying point in the president’s second term anti-immigration agenda, with the president and supporters arguing it makes the country a magnet for immigration and that American citizenship should be reserved for those who truly value it, as opposed to just being given to anyone born here.

But immigration advocates and many legal experts say that the Constitution is clear in outlining who is considered a citizen. They’ve also argued that birthright citizenship is a benefit to the U.S. by giving everyone an equal stake in the country’s future and that restricting who can become a citizen would create a second-class of people in America.

The Trump administration has painted birth tourism as a widespread problem. There’s no official estimate of how many births can be considered “birth tourism” births, but an estimated 26,000 might fall into that category out of the roughly 3.5 million births in the U.S. every year, MPI wrote in its 2026 article.

In June, the Supreme Court rejected Trump’s previous efforts to declare that children born to people in the U.S. illegally or temporarily aren’t American citizens, and upheld a broad conception of birthright citizenship.

The American Civil Liberties Union predicted that Trump’s second attempt would also be rejected.

“The Supreme Court already decided this issue: Birthright citizenship is guaranteed by the Constitution. No additional executive order can change the meaning of the Constitution. Any executive order that tries to rewrite birthright citizenship will meet the same fate as the last one,” said Cody Wofsy, deputy director of the ACLU’s Immigrants’ Rights Project, in a statement Thursday.

On Trump’s first day in office of his second term, he signed an executive order aimed at ending birthright citizenship, which allows anyone born in the United States to automatically become an American citizen.

Trump’s administration was immediately sued by opponents who said the executive order went against the 14th Amendment, adopted after the Civil War, which makes anyone born in the country a citizen, with very limited exceptions.

The executive order was blocked by several lower courts and never took effect.

In June, the Supreme Court struck down Trump’s order by a 6-3 vote. But the vote was too close for many immigration advocates and legal observers who felt the legal question of birthright citizenship was a long-settled issue.

When it came to the legal question of whether birthright citizenship was protected by the Constitution, the vote was even narrower. Only five justices said it was enshrined in the Constitution, while Justice Brett Kavanaugh rejected the executive order, but did so specifically on the grounds that federal law conveys birthright citizenship.

Santana reported from Sacramento.

title: ICE is now tracking nearly 54000 immigrants via ankle monitors - The Guardian
description:

text:
The US is tracking nearly 54,000 immigrants through GPS-enabled ankle monitors as part of a US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) electronic surveillance program, according to private prison corporation The Geo Group. Early last year, just 17,000 immigrants were wearing the devices..

The Geo Group owns BI Inc, the company that runs ICE’s intensive supervision appearance program (ISAP), and reported the numbers in its earnings call on Thursday.

The overall number of immigrants enrolled in the surveillance program remained flat at about 184,000. Geo Group executives said that a large number of participants were shifted from less intensive forms of surveillance, such as phone check-ins, to ankle monitors.

The shift to ankle monitors, which the company pitches as a “high-security level of monitoring”, has increased revenues for Geo Group . Ankle monitors cost ICE more than most of the other surveillance technologies administered by BI Inc. The company charges ICE a little more than $2 a day per monitor, while the SmartLink app – a facial recognition and location tracking smart phone app – costs about $0.96 for each immigrant enrolled, according to publicly available ICE statistics. At last count, more than 127,000 immigrants are required to check in using SmartLink.

“If this trend continues, the technology and case management mix shift will continue to increase revenues and earnings generated under the ISAP contract even if overall participation counts remain relatively stable,” said George Zoley, Geo Group chairman and CEO, on an earnings call on Thursday.

ICE directed agents in June 2025 to move more immigrants enrolled in ISAP to the ankle monitor program, according to a memo obtained by the Washington Post.

In a new class action lawsuit filed against ICE in June, immigration advocacy groups allege this “ankle monitors for all” policy “imposes continuous, real-time GPS monitoring without individualized justifications”. Individuals are being subjected to constant surveillance “without meaningful review, explanation, or opportunity to challenge these conditions”, the statement announcing the lawsuit read. That includes pregnant women, who the Guardian first reported were being fitted with smart watches.

“ICE has offered no justification for their ‘ankle monitors for all’ policy, but it serves their interest in making daily life harder for immigrants, while also increasing profits for their friends in the private prison industry,” said Evan Benz, managing attorney at the Amica Center for Immigrant Rights, in a statement announcing the lawsuit.

The Guardian has reached out to the Department of Homeland Security.

Anticipating an increase in reliance on ankle monitors, Geo Group began investing in building out its inventory of the GPS devices at the start of 2025. At the time, the company said it was investing $16m into manufacturing enough ankle monitors to “be in a position to scale up the federal government’s utilization of ISAP by several hundreds of thousands to upwards of several millions of participants as required”.

While the company’s predictions of an increase in the use of ankle monitors to track immigrants has started to pan out, investors on Thursday expressed concern about the lack of growth in overall numbers of immigrants being monitored through ISAP. Previously, Geo Group executives said they expected the Trump administration’s immigration agenda would result in a surge in the number of immigrants monitored through ISAP, allowing them to surpass the previous peak of 370,000 under the Biden administration. The company said they thought there would be enough demand from the US government to expand the surveillance program to monitor more than 400,000 immigrants.

Without going into specifics, Zoley said he was optimistic that recent shifts in policy could increase the number of people who “would be subject to immigration enforcement … So at a later point, maybe next year, we could see ISAP increase dramatically.” The Trump administration has most recently revoked Temporary Protected Status for Haitians, potentially subjecting hundreds of thousands of people in the US to detention or deportation.

Company executives have said in the past that they expect the numbers of immigrants enrolled in ISAP to grow once the government runs out of capacity in detention centers.

ISAP was first introduced as an alternative to detention and has been operated by BI Inc since 2004. The program relies on several forms of monitoring in addition to the GPS-ankle monitors, including smart watches that provide real-time location tracking, and a smart phone app.

text:
On Aug. 5, 2026, the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia confirmed that its prior order staying the termination of Haiti’s Temporary Protected Status (TPS) designation is no longer in effect following action by the U.S. Supreme Court and the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit. As a result, the court-ordered injunction that had temporarily prevented the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) from implementing its termination of Haiti TPS has been lifted. TPS beneficiaries can no longer rely on the District Court’s stay as a basis for continued protection from the termination.

However, the underlying lawsuit has not been dismissed, as the court has to rule on the core constitutional issue concerning equal protection. The District Court has directed the parties to submit a proposed schedule for further proceedings.

In November 2025, former DHS Secretary Kristi Noem announced the termination of Haiti’s TPS designation. The termination was published in the Federal Register (90 Fed. Reg 54733 (Nov. 28, 2025)) and would have ended TPS protections for Haitian beneficiaries. A group of plaintiffs challenged the termination in federal court, arguing that the decision was unlawful and seeking to prevent DHS from implementing it while the litigation proceeded.

In February 2026, the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia issued an order staying the effective date of DHS’s termination of Haiti TPS pending judicial review. This injunction preserved TPS protections for affected nationals of Haiti while the court considered the merits of the challenge. The injunction temporarily delayed the termination and allowed Haitian TPS holders to maintain their status and corresponding employment authorization during the litigation.

On June 25, 2026, the U.S. Supreme Court ordered the TPS terminations effective July 27, 2026, and remanded to the lower court to lift the stay. Mullin v. Doe, No. 25-1083. Following receipt of the D.C. Circuit’s mandate on Aug. 4, 2026, the District Court expressly stated that its prior order staying the effective date of DHS’s Haiti TPS termination “is no longer in effect.”

What This Means

Haitian TPS beneficiaries and employers should:

Closely monitor DHS announcements regarding implementation of the termination.

Review the validity of employment authorization as well as any related government guidance.

Evaluate whether Haiti TPS recipients may qualify for another immigration benefit or status.

Consult immigration counsel regarding individualized options and compliance obligations.

While the District Court’s injunction has been lifted, the case remains active, anticipating further litigation. Haitian TPS beneficiaries and employers should continue to monitor developments closely for additional court rulings, DHS guidance, or other administrative actions which may affect the timeline.

text:
WASHINGTON D.C. – Today, U.S. Customs and Border Protection Office of Field Operations unveiled the “OFO Strategy 2026-2030,” a new roadmap that outlines how OFO will continue to safeguard U.S. travel, trade, and agriculture, directly protecting our national and economic security.

As CBP’s largest component, OFO manages the security and movement of people and goods through our nation's ports of entry. The OFO Strategy focuses on four key goals to ensure continued mission excellence:

National Security: Leverage intelligence-based targeting, analytics, planning, and partnerships to fortify OFO’s security and enforcement posture.

Economic Security: Modernize processes and tools that evolve with industry to secure and fortify lawful trade and travel.

Integration: Promote a unified operating environment that drives continuous process improvement and optimizes systems to strengthen security.

Workforce Cultivation: Develop, equip, and empower employees in order to retain and attract a mission-focused workforce.

“To support our key priority of strengthening security and enforcing laws, this strategy will guide our expansion of technology innovation that not only benefits CBP but also our law enforcement partners, the traveling public and our trade and travel industry partners,” said Executive Assistant Commissioner Diane J. Sabatino, Office of Field Operations. “With increased funding, we have the opportunity to ensure our workforce has the tools and resources they need to enforce U.S. law and secure the flow of travel and cargo while mitigating threats before they reach U.S. borders.”

Overall, the strategy outlines key opportunities for OFO to optimize its processes by integrating advanced analytics using artificial intelligence and emerging technologies, modernizing physical infrastructure and technology at ports of entry, promoting informed travel and trade through heightened public and industry awareness, and equipping the workforce with reliable tools, technology, and training.

OFO’s mission is inherently complex, requiring the enforcement of hundreds of customs, immigration, agriculture, and trade laws on behalf of numerous federal agencies. Our critical operations face persistent, dynamic, and increasing threats, including the growing influence of transnational criminal organizations, the proliferation of illicit drugs like fentanyl, the dangers of human smuggling, and the economic and safety risks posed by illegal and fraudulent trade activities.

In Fiscal Year 2025 alone, OFO processed approximately 380 million travelers and $3.6 trillion in import cargo. During the same period, OFO officers seized over 504,000 pounds of illicit drugs, including fentanyl and methamphetamine, conducted 2,700 weapons and ammunition seizure events, and intercepted 1.7 million prohibited plant and animal products, preventing over 100,000 harmful pests from entering the United States.

The OFO Strategy 2026-2030 will guide OFO’s continued trade and travel operations, serving as a unified response to the complex and evolving challenges that threaten our borders and national interests.

text:
SALT LAKE CITY — Local immigrant advocates are taking aim at another aspect of the ongoing immigration crackdown — regular flights in and out of Salt Lake City International Airport by charter air companies hauling immigrant detainees.

The fights, in the general aviation area of the airport, have been occurring since at least April, advocates say, and they gathered Thursday in the main terminal to picket and call attention to them. A handful of demonstrators holding protest signs were on hand as of late Thursday morning in a designated free speech area adjacent to the baggage claim area at the airport.

"I think most people aren't aware what is going on out here every Monday and Thursday," said Carolyn Jenkins, one of the demonstrators, referencing the typical days flights hauling immigrants out of Salt Lake City occur.

Clare Coonan, who was also demonstrating, thinks the Immigration and Customs Enforcement flights — occurring all around the country — are another example of what she sees as overly heavy-handed action against the immigrant population.

"We want to stop the ICE flights and we want to stop the abuse that ICE is doing in the name of our government," she said.

Some immigrant detainees face regular movement within the United States from detention center to detention center, she said, and she charges that the intent is to deliberately separate them from family members, their communities and their legal representation.

"So out of this airport, twice a week, we are trafficking people, not because we want to keep our nation safe, but because we want to make it harder for those people to have constitutional due process rights," Coonan said.

The U.S. Department of Homeland Security noted attacks ICE agents and other DHS partners have faced in declining to provide specifics about detainee flights. Immigrant advocates around the country have tapped into public information about flight activity in determining when and where immigrant detainees and those facing deportation are going, within the country and to destinations abroad.

"Attacks and demonization of ICE and our partners is wrong. ICE officers are now facing a 1,300% increase in assaults against them. For operational security purposes, we are not going to confirm what airports our deportation flights are operating out of," the agency said in a statement to KSL.

Since at least April, the general aviation area of Salt Lake City International Airport has served as a stopping point for chartered flights hauling immigrant detainees, according to TJ Young, who has been tracking the air activity since July. She's witnessed, from afar, shackled detainees boarding airplanes operated by companies she and other local advocates identify as Global Crossing, Air Wisconsin and Eastern Air Express.

Representatives from the three companies didn't immediately respond to queries seeking comment.

Jenkins also witnessed detainees boarding one of the flights, shackled at the hands and ankles. The general aviation area of the airport, served by two fixed-base operations, sits east of the main commercial terminals and services charter flights and private air travelers.

"I guess they're held in hangars until the flight lands and then they're put into vans and they park near the airplane they're going to be riding in. And then the ICE officers put them into shackles and they are led upstairs (into airplanes)," Jenkins said. "It's upsetting."

Young has also witnessed the boarding of detainees and posted pictures of them on social media. In response, friends and family members of some of the detainees, on seeing her posts, have reached out to her, recognizing someone they know and worried about where they are.

Destinations of flights from Salt Lake City include Tacoma, Washington; Bakersfield, California; and El Paso, Texas, according to the organizers of Thursday's demonstration. In July alone, they say, 386 immigrants were hauled out of the airport on flights leaving Salt Lake City.

Participants in Thursday's demonstration included representatives from numerous immigrant advocacy groups that have formed in response to the crackdown on illegal immigration under President Donald Trump. They were assigned to a relatively quiet section of the terminal near baggage carousel 9, but Coonan said at least some in the airport were taking note of their presence.

"I'm watching people and they're clocking that we're here with our signs. They're reading the signs," she said.

The immigration crackdown has been a focus of sharp debate, with immigrant advocates charging that most detainees don't have violent criminal records. The Trump administration warns that immigrants in the country illegally sap public resources and pose a danger to the U.S. communities where they live.

Read more:

"Our brave law enforcement officers put their lives on the line to arrest pedophiles, rapists, murderers, drug traffickers and gang members," reads the DHS statement. "Nearly 70% of ICE arrests are of illegal aliens charged or convicted of a crime in the U.S. This statistic doesn't even count human rights abuses, wanted foreign fugitives, terrorists, and gang members who lack a rap sheet in the U.S."

Over the past decade, more than 80 state and local jurisdictions across 28 states have established and invested in legal representation programs.

text:
FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE

CONTACT: media@vera.org

WASHINGTON, DC — Today, Senator Adam Schiff (CA) reintroduced the Fairness to Freedom Act—landmark legislation that would establish a right to legal representation for anyone facing deportation. This legislation is crucial as the Trump administration continues to gut the constitutional right to due process by subjecting communities to increased immigration enforcement, “mega master” hearings, and inhumane and indefinite detention, as well as stripping pathways to legal residency.

But the solution is clear, and it works. Access to a lawyer remains the biggest factor determining whether someone can exercise their legal rights and secure lawful status. A recent study by the Vera Institute of Justice found that people facing deportation with legal representation were 4.7 times more likely to be granted relief than people without representation. Across the country, local governments and elected officials are increasingly recognizing that legal representation works. Over the past decade, more than 80 state and local jurisdictions across 28 states have established and invested in legal representation programs. And since 2025, state and local investments in deportation defense have nearly doubled, climbing from approximately $260 million to more than $500 million nationwide.

The stakes have never been higher. As hundreds of thousands of Temporary Protected Status holders are stripped of their status and thousands of immigrant children are at risk of losing representation after the administration’s termination of the Unaccompanied Children’s Program, the need for universal legal representation and deportation defense is more urgent than ever. Ensuring legal representation for every adult and child isn’t just good policy—it’s a promise that no one should have to fight for their freedom alone. This reintroduction includes language to remove barriers to obtaining counsel by removing the wet signature requirement for DHS forms.

“President Trump’s cruel immigration agenda has caused unimaginable, long-lasting harm in our communities, leading to unlawful deportations that have torn thousands of families apart. Having access to legal counsel during immigration proceedings is essential to fair outcomes, yet beyond the reach of many. Our nation has been shaped for the better by the extraordinary contributions of immigrants, and I’m leading this bill to ensure that families have a fighting chance to present their cases and achieve fair results in the courts,” said Senator Adam Schiff.

“For years, I have proudly led the Fairness to Freedom Act in the House because I believe due process should never depend on a person’s ability to afford an attorney. Today, as the Trump Administration escalates attacks on immigrant communities and undermines fundamental legal protections, that mission has never been more urgent,” said Congresswoman Norma Torres. “I’m grateful to Senator Schiff for introducing this critical legislation in the Senate. Together, we are making it clear that no one should face detention or deportation alone simply because they cannot afford legal representation. Justice should not be reserved for those who can pay for it.”

“Immigrants are being pushed through complex legal proceedings without legal representation, forced to navigate a confusing system alone as they fight for their freedom, their futures, and, for many, the chance to keep their families together,” said Senator Cory Booker. “This legislation helps ensure that no one has to face that system alone by providing the legal support they need to receive a fair hearing.”

“No one should be deprived of the fundamental right to due process, basic fairness, and human dignity in our immigration system. It’s time to make commonsense reforms,” said Senator Kirsten Gillibrand. “The Fairness to Freedom Act would ensure every person subject to immigration proceedings is guaranteed legal representation, leading to a more equitable and transparent system that gives immigrants a fair chance.”

“Everyone deserves access to legal representation during the immigration process, and no one should be denied legal counsel because of their inability to pay,” said Senator Alex Padilla. “As the Trump Administration continues its assault on due process and targets vulnerable communities, we must ensure immigrant communities understand their rights and have access to strong legal counsel. Our bill would help ensure that no one is forced to navigate our complex immigration system alone, protecting the dignity and fundamental fairness at the heart of our justice system.”

“People facing criminal charges in this country have the right to a lawyer, but immigrants facing deportation often do not,” said Congressman Robert Garcia. “As ICE raids under the Trump Administration threaten people’s constitutional rights, guaranteeing access to legal counsel is more important than ever. I’m proud to support this bill to protect due process.”

Shayna Kessler, director of the Advancing Universal Representation initiative at the Vera Institute of Justice and co-leader of the Fairness to Freedom campaign, said, “The Fairness to Freedom Act is an urgently needed piece of legislation to establish a right to federally funded legal representation for anyone facing deportation. This is about due process, keeping families together, protecting vulnerable children, and ensuring people have their fair day in court at a time when the Trump administration has trampled those rights and values. No one should be denied the opportunity to defend their freedom simply because they cannot afford an attorney. We proudly champion this bill and call on Congress to follow the lead of Senator Adam Schiff and Representative Norma Torres to pass the Fairness to Freedom Act.”

Nicole Melaku, executive director of the National Partnership for New Americans and co-leader of the Fairness to Freedom campaign, said, “Our families and communities are under attack by the federal government, and it’s time we give adults and children facing deportation the most effective support they need: a lawyer by their side. Since day one of his second term, President Trump has widened the dragnet of who is at risk, greased the wheels of the deportation pipeline, and deepened the due process crisis in our immigration courts. In a system that grows more punitive by the day, access to a lawyer is one of the strongest shields against wrongful detention, family separation, and deportation. As the Fairness to Freedom campaign, we are proud to stand with Senator Adam Schiff and Representative Norma Torres to champion the bicameral Fairness to Freedom Act—a bill that will establish the right to universal representation for people facing deportation. We urge every member of Congress who believes in due process, accountability, and dignity to join us.”

Trump's obsession with undermining birthright citizenship is more than a decade old

The executive orders signed on Thursday by Donald Trump, in which he tries, again, to undermine the guarantee of birthright citizenship enshrined in the US constitution reaffirmed by the supreme court just five weeks ago, is part of an obsessive campaign he has waged for more than a decade.

At a Republican presidential primary campaign event in Orlando, Florida in November 2015, Trump hinted that he had a plan to end what he called the scourge of “anchor babies”, a derogatory term for children of undocumented immigrants born in the United States as citizens.

“You can’t come into the country- you’re illegal, you come down, you sit down, you have your baby, and we take care of the baby for the next 85 years!” Trump said. “Everybody says, ‘Well, you need a constitutional amendment; it’ll take 15 years; it’ll never happen’. You don’t, you don’t. You need a simple act of Congress. You might not even need that.”

If elected, Trump promised the crowd at a resort near Disney World, “the anchor baby, birthright citizenship, it’s over, not going to happen.”

Three years later, as president, Trump said in a televised interview with Jonathan Swan just before the 2018 midterms that he planned to issue an executive order to instruct federal agencies that children born in the United States to non-citizens were not entitled to US citizenship at birth.

“It was always told to me that you needed a constitutional amendment. Guess what? You don’t,” Trump told Swan in an interview excerpt posted online on 30 October 2018. “You can definitely do it with an act of Congress,” Trump added, incorrectly, “but now they’re saying I can do it just with an executive order.”

As Swan reported at the time, Trump’s claim that he could undo the birthright citizenship guaranteed by the 14th Amendment to the constitution was a minority view among legal scholars, but was supported by a then-obscure figure: John Eastman, who had argued for decades that the amendment granting citizenship to “All persons born or naturalized in the United States, and subject to the jurisdiction thereof,” should be read to exclude the children of people who are not US citizens when their child is born.

Eastman later claimed in a 2020 Newsweek op-ed that Kamala Harris was ineligible for the vice-presidency because she had no right to US citizenship at birth, since she was born in Oakland, California in 1964 to non-citizen parents who were, “subject to the jurisdiction” of their native lands of India and Jamaica.

In the 2018 interview, Trump called birthright citizenship “ridiculous,” and falsely asserted that the US is “the only country in the world where a person comes in and has a baby, and the baby is essentially a citizen.” In fact, at least 30 nations grant citizenship this way. He also claimed that an executive order was in the process of being drafted.

Although that order did not materialize until the start of Trump’s second term, his obsession with casting doubt on the citizenship of children born in the US to foreign parents has had a clearly political element from the start.

After all, Trump’s original rise to political prominence was tied to his false claim that Barack Obama, born to an American mother and a Kenyan father in Honolulu, just two years after Hawaii became a state, might have been born outside the US.

Then, after Joe Biden picked Harris as his running mate in 2020, Trump repeatedly refused to confirm that she was eligible for an elected office open only to “a natural born Citizen.”

Instead, Trump called the question Eastman raised about Harris’s citizenship at birth in his Newsweek op-ed “very serious” and a potential “problem” for her. He also praised Eastman as “a very highly qualified, very talented lawyer” and called him “brilliant”.

Eastman, who went on to devise the fake electors scheme designed to keep Trump in office after he lost the 2020 election, and gave an inflammatory speech before the Capitol riot on January 6 2021, was finally disbarred by the California supreme court in April, based on “clear and convincing evidence that he advanced false claims about the 2020 presidential election to mislead courts, public officials, and the American public.”

The two new executive orders on birthright citizenship signed by Donald Trump on Thursday, just five weeks ago after the US supreme court struck down his previous order denying citizenship to the children of non-citizens, attempt to limit in two ways a right that has been enshrined in the constitution since the 14th amendment was ratified in 1868.

The second order seeks to deny citizenship to the children of certain categories of non-citizens.

The order excludes children born to any non-citizen parent in the following categories:

an alien enemy, “defined to include any member of a designated Foreign Terrorist Organization … or Specially Designated Global Terrorist”;

foreign government employees, including: ambassadors; other embassy or consulate employees who are nationals of that foreign country; anyone employed by a foreign government in an official capacity;

employees of international organizations that possess international-organization immunity;

people “engaged in a commercial transaction to purchase or access birthright citizenship”.

The children of foreign ambassadors have long been excluded from birthright citizenship.

Somewhat redundantly, the second order also denies citizenship to the children of non-citizens “born in a territory or territorial waters of the United States where citizenship is not conferred by Federal statute”.

Trump gives wildly inaccurate account of 14th amendment to explain new orders restricting birthright citizenship

Speaking in the Oval Office earlier on Thursday, Donald Trump gave a wildly inaccurate account of the nature and timing of the 14th amendment to the US constitution, which enshrined the principle of birthright citizenship, as he sought to justify two new executive orders attempting to deny citizenship to a wider pool of children born on US soil to non-citizens.

As he discussed the orders, “Continuing to Protect the Meaning and Value of American Citizenship” and “Ending Birth Tourism”, Trump called the supreme court’s decision to strike down his previous attempt to deny birthright citizenship through executive action “a very, very unfortunate decision.”

“So we’re, making adjustments because it’s very unfair,” the president said. “This was meant for the babies of slaves. It was right after – one week or two weeks after – the Civil war ended.”

In fact, General Robert E Lee surrendered the largest of the Confederate forces on 9 April 1865 at Appomattox Court House in Virginia. More than a year later, the 14th amendment was passed by Congress on 13 June 1866, and ratified on 9 July 9 1868.

Trump’s assertion that the framers of the amendment only intended it to apply to the children of former slaves was roundly rejected by the supreme court, not this year but in 1898, when the justices ruled 6-2 that Wong Kim Ark, who was born in San Francisco to parents who were both Chinese citizens, was a US citizen by birth.

Despite that well-known precedent, which was discussed at length during the recent supreme court deliberations over Trump’s first attempt to deny birthright citizenship to the children of non-citizens, the president’s adviser, Stephen Miller, insisted that Trump was right.

“As the president mentioned, the 14th amendment was passed exclusively in the aftermath of the Civil War to to ensure that the children of slaves would be citizens. It had no other meaning and purpose outside of that,” Miller said.

“They’ve taken birthright citizenship and they’ve made a joke out of it,” Trump added. “And we’re actually the only country, of size, I think just about the only country period, that does birthright citizenship.”

That too is wildly inaccurate. Thirty-two other countries, most in the western hemisphere, have birthright citizenship laws that are similar to US law, according to the Pew Research Center. About 50 more countries have more limited versions of birthright citizenship.

text:
On Aug. 5, 2026, the U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts denied plaintiffs’ request to stay USCIS’s implementation of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act’s (H.R. 1) limits on TPS-based employment authorization documents (EADs), while granting limited relief related to the new Annual Asylum Fee (AAF). Venezuelan Association of Massachusetts et al. v. U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services et al., No. 1:26-cv-13038.

TPS EAD Cap Remains in Effect

The plaintiffs challenged several USCIS actions implementing H.R. 1, including the July 2025 Federal Register notice establishing the one-year TPS EAD cap, the March 2026 USCIS website update applying that cap to previously issued 540-day automatic extensions, and related provisions of the April 2026 Interim Final Rule.

The court rejected each of the plaintiffs’ challenges to the TPS EAD cap. It held that USCIS was not required to engage in notice-and-comment rulemaking because the agency was implementing Congress’ statutory directive in H.R. 1. The court also concluded that applying the one-year cap to previously issued 540-day automatic EAD extensions for TPS beneficiaries from El Salvador, Sudan, and Ukraine was not impermissibly retroactive.

Finally, the court acknowledged that the new statutory framework could result in gaps in employment authorization, but it held that the possibility of such gaps did not render the Cap Policy unlawful. The court noted that USCIS could issue one-year automatic extensions to avoid gaps and that any future failure to comply with the TPS statute’s requirement that employment authorization remain effective throughout the TPS designation “may result in independent liability,” but such liability would be “independent of the mere implementation of the Cap Policy as required by H.R. 1.”

Court Stays Portions of Annual Asylum Fee Rule

The court granted a nationwide stay under the Administrative Procedure Act (APA) with respect to the April 2026 IFR provisions authorizing USCIS to reject pending asylum applications and initiate removal proceedings for failure to pay the Annual Asylum Fee. The court found those consequences were not required by H.R. 1 and likely violated the APA’s notice-and-comment requirements.

Employer Takeaways

The August 5 decision supersedes the court’s temporary July 21 administrative stay. As a result, employers should continue to follow current USCIS guidance regarding TPS-based EAD automatic extensions and Form I-9 reverification. The temporary relief preserving previously extended TPS EAD expiration dates is no longer in effect, although the litigation remains pending on the merits.

text:
Donald Trump signed two executive orders on Thursday to restrict eligibility for birthright citizenship and ban “birth tourism”, just over a month after the US supreme court rejected his first attempt to curtail the guarantee of birthright citizenship enshrined in the constitution.

“We had a very unfortunate decision in the supreme court concerning birthright,” Trump said in the Oval Office. “It was close, but a very, very unfortunate decision. So we’re making adjustments because it’s very unfair.”

The orders signed on Thursday seek to expand the definitions ​of children the White House deems ineligible ⁠for birthright ​citizenship and also ​seek to ban “birth ​tourism”, which the president claimed on Thursday is practiced by “hundreds of thousands” of people. They are expected to be challenged in court.

“They’ve taken birthright citizenship and they’ve made a joke out of it,” Trump told reporters. “People are building businesses around it. That’s not the way it’s supposed ‌to work. It’s a disgrace. They’re buying their way in, and we’re not going to let it happen.”

According to the Migration Policy Institute, the highest census-based estimate “puts birth tourism at 22,000 to 26,000 babies born annually on US soil, although government data show just 9,600 births to mothers with foreign addresses in 2024”.

That is less than 1% of all the babies born in the United States each year.

Trump has long sought to dismantle the principle of birthright citizenship, making it a top priority of his second-term immigration crackdown, but has thus far been unsuccessful.

On 30 June, his effort to deny automatic citizenship to children born to parents in the United States illegally or on temporary visas suffered a setback when the supreme court upheld the constitutional guarantee of birthright citizenship, affirming that nearly all people born on US soil are American citizens.

In an apparent attempt to circumvent that ruling, the president’s first order seeks to expand the definition of who would not qualify for automatic US citizenship.

Historical exceptions to the citizenship clause of the 14th amendment have included children born in the US to foreign sovereigns and diplomats; children of occupying foreign forces; children born on foreign ships; and children of Native Americans.

Stephen Miller, the White House deputy chief of staff and chief architect of Trump’s anti-immigration agenda, said the order aims to deny birthright citizenship to others, including children of members of “foreign terrorist organizations” as well as “large categories of people who lobby and act on behalf of foreign governments”, though it is unclear who would fall into the latter category.

The move “ensures that large numbers of people who [would] wrongly be getting birthright citizenship will no longer be eligible for those benefits”, Miller said.

The order also seeks to expand the exception of children born to foreign ambassadors to include more foreign government employees. It also refers to people born in “a territory or territorial waters of the United States where citizenship is not conferred by federal statute” as ineligible. At the moment, that only includes American Samoa.

It also aimed to restrict birthright citizenship to anyone whose parents “engaged in fraudulent activity to obtain citizenship”.

Trump’s second order seeks to increase restrictions on visitors to the US who want to obtain visas to give birth while in the country by targeting “birth tourism operators [who] use deceptive advertisements and inducements to entice foreign nationals to travel to the United States for the purpose of giving birth on American soil”.

The order goes on to say that “participants in birth tourism schemes abuse [temporary non-immigrant visa categories] to establish a permanent foothold in the United States by securing the advantage of citizenship for their children and then potentially for themselves”.

Travelling to the United States under the guise of tourism while actually intending to give birth so the child automatically obtains citizenship constitutes visa fraud and is already illegal, and it is unclear exactly how Trump’s new orders will build on what is already law.

Colombia Sees Increased Work Visa Delays and Heightened Scrutiny

Employers sponsoring foreign nationals in Colombia may experience longer processing times and greater uncertainty as immigration authorities increase scrutiny of work visa applications. While no formal legislative or regulatory changes have been announced, recent adjudication trends suggest a more discretionary review process ahead of the country’s presidential transition on August 7, 2026.

Reports indicate that work visa processing is increasingly exceeding the statutory 30-day adjudication period, with many applicants experiencing delays of several additional weeks. Authorities have also been exercising broader discretion by declaring some applications inadmissible or treating them as withdrawn, even where applicants believe they have submitted complete documentation.

In addition, visa required foreign nationals have reportedly been instructed to refile under different visa categories than those originally selected. These developments may result in additional costs, longer processing times, and delayed employment start dates.

The heightened review comes as Colombia prepares for a change in government, a period that often brings operational and administrative shifts. Employers should anticipate that visa processing practices may remain fluid while the new administration establishes its immigration policies.

Impact: Although no formal policy changes have been announced, employers should anticpate longer visa processing times and increased documentation requests when hiring foreign talent in Colombia. Starting the immigration process early and building additional time into onboarding plans may help minimize disruptions while adjudication practices continue to evolve.

USCIS Extends Somalia TPS Work Authorization Through August 10

U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services has announced another short-term extension of employment authorization for certain Temporary Protected Status beneficiaries from Somalia. Eligible Employment Authorization Documents issued under Somalia’s TPS designation will now remain valid through August 10, 2026, providing continued work authorization while related litigation remains pending.

The extension applies to TPS- related EADs with original expiration dates of March 17, 2023, September 17, 2024, and March 17, 2026. USCIS stated that the extension is automatic and is intended to maintain employment authorization while litigation involving Somalia’s TPS designation continues.

The agency continues to issue these brief extensions following the U.S. Supreme Court’s June 2026 decision permitting the Department of Homeland Security to proceed with terminating certain TPS designations. USCIS also remains subject to a federal district court order concerning automatic EAD extensions for certain TPS beneficiaries who timely filed renewal applications before October 30, 2025.

USCIS has emphasized that additional guidance may be issued as court proceedings continue and the legal status of Somalia’s TPS designation evolves.

Impact: The latest extension provides continued, short-term work authorization for eligible Somalia TPS beneficiaries while the underlying litigation continues. Employers should continue monitoring USCIS announcements and review employment authorization records regularly, as additional court decisions or agency action could result in further changes.

USCIS Extends Burma TPS Work Authorization Through August 7

U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services has announced another short-term extension of employment authorization for certain Temporary Protected Status beneficiaries from Burma (Myanmar). Eligible Employment Authorization Documents issued under Burma’s TPS designation will now remain valid through August 7, 2026, extending the previous automatic validity period that had been set to expire on August 3.

The extension applies automatically to TPS-related EADs with original expiration dates of November 25, 2022, May 25, 2024, and November 25, 2025. USCIS stated that the extension is intended to preserve employment authorization while litigation over the termination of Burma’s TPS designation continues.

The agency continues to issue these brief extensions following the U.S. Supreme Court’s June 2026 decision allowing the Department of Homeland Security to proceed with terminating certain TPS designations. USCIS also remains subject to a federal district court order concerning automatic EAD extensions for certain TPS beneficiaries who timely filed renewal applications before October 30, 2025.

USCIS has indicated that these extensions are temporary and that additional guidance may be issued as the underlying litigation progresses.

title: 'The Bird-Watchers' of Memphis: tracking ICE flights and documenting detainees in shackles
description:
That’s what she and her group of just under ten like-minded individuals call themselves — The Bird-Watchers — as they go about tracking ICE flights in Memphis and documenting the manner in which detainees are transported on them.
For months, they have painstakingly collected evidence of the harsh conditions in which ICE detainees are moved, bound in shackles and chains.
Wilson Air Center is a fixed-base operator or FBO, which is a company authorized to provide aviation services for certain private aircraft.
Now, she scans multiple flight tracking websites, including a real-time flight monitoring site focused on ICE flight paths.
And their pressure on private partners of ICE flights, such as Wilson Air Center, is also increasing.
text:
This story was originally published by the Institute for Public Service Reporting Memphis.

On a Saturday morning in July, Joni Laney, a 73-year-old retired English teacher, parked her car in a small lot overlooking Wilson Air Center near Memphis International Airport. She had received word from her group of fellow volunteers that a flight there was going to be used to transport several detainees held by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

Laney had shown up, as she has done numerous times over the past few months, to document what would transpire. On this occasion, Laney invited me to come along and see for myself the manner in which ICE treated its detainees in transit. Seated in her car, and attempting to be as inconspicuous as possible, we kept watch as a bus and a van — both vehicles white and unmarked — stood next to a stationary Bombardier plane registered to an ICE contractor.

“Oh gosh, can you see the shackles? Oh my God,” Laney gasped as a group of women detainees stepped out of the van, their hands and feet in shackles and chains running around their waists. “Three, four…,” she kept count of the number of detainees who got out of the van and made their way to the aircraft in front of them.

Moments earlier, a larger number of male detainees had similarly exited the bus. Laney documented the details carefully, as well as she could from the distance we were at, across a barbed wire fence bordering the air center.

“I’m a bird-watcher,” she told me. That’s what she and her group of just under ten like-minded individuals call themselves — The Bird-Watchers — as they go about tracking ICE flights in Memphis and documenting the manner in which detainees are transported on them.

Many of The Bird-Watchers, like Joni, are retired Memphians. For months, they have painstakingly collected evidence of the harsh conditions in which ICE detainees are moved, bound in shackles and chains.

“It must violate most safety regulations to have that many people shackled (on a plane)”, said Jim West, a 75-year-old retired physician and bioethicist, and another of The Bird-Watchers. “They’d never be able to evacuate if they had to.”

“(ICE) treats them as though they’re non-human at every point,” said Laney, “and every time they’re moved, the airplane gets money, ICE gets money, the prison gets money, (private prison contractor) CoreCivic gets money — I mean it’s just like a revolving door of money.”

Protesters who gathered Tuesday at a rally outside Wilson Air Center echoed those sentiments.

“And we can’t forget, too, that the reason all of this is happening is (because) someone thinks we’re less than” human, Latina activist Gisela Guerrero said.

Pressure on the Wilsons

Now, following that money trail, The Bird-Watchers are seeking to pressure the owners of the private air center where the flights are boarded, seeking to stop it from profiting from ICE operations.

At the heart of the row over ICE flights in Memphis is one of the city’s most famous business families, the Wilsons of Holiday Inn fame.

Wilson Air Center is a fixed-base operator or FBO, which is a company authorized to provide aviation services for certain private aircraft. The private enterprise was founded in 1996 by Robert Wilson, also known as Bob, son of the late Kemmons Wilson, the founder of the Holiday Inn chain of hotels. The Wilson Air Center proclaims on its website that “our Memphis location is home of one of the world’s largest aircraft canopies, and is touted by the aviation industry as among the top fixed base operations in the United States for the quality of its services and the comfort and design of its facilities.” The enterprise also has facilities in Houston and Chattanooga.

Now, as The Bird-Watchers and other advocacy groups protest Wilson Air Center’s continued operations with regard to ICE flights, the financial ties between the air center and the federal agency or its contractors have come into question.

On the day that I accompanied Laney to document the detainee transfer at the air center, the flight in question was a Bombardier registered by CSI Aviation, a private air charter company that received a $1.6 billion contract over one year from the Department of Homeland Security “for enforcement and removal operations under the ICE Air Program”. It is unclear whether the services of the Wilson Air Center were requisitioned by DHS, ICE, CSI Aviation or some other agency or contractor. Wilson Air Center did not respond to The Institute’s requests for comment.

Vecindarios 901, a grassroots rapid response group that works on immigrants’ issues in Memphis, has joined The Bird-Watchers’ call to pressure the Wilsons to drop their ICE flight operations. In a statement, the group said that Memphians are joining “a nationwide movement against ICE flights operating in our communities, and against the companies secretly servicing and profiting off the inhumane systems hurting our people.”

“People around the country are sending them emails, asking them to make the same move that other companies around the county are being asked to make,” Blake Burr, one of the co-founders of Vecindarios 901, told The Institute. Burr, who is also part of the group of Bird-Watchers, added that, as a Memphian, she felt that the Wilson family would want to be remembered in a different way, with a positive legacy.

Behind the scenes, The Bird-Watchers said they have spent weeks trying to reach out to Bob Wilson’s extended family, trying to persuade them to use their influence to get Wilson Air Center to drop its ICE flight operations. Laney, for one, said she managed to have a phone conversation with Spence Wilson Sr., son of Kemmons, brother to Robert and chairman emeritus of Kemmons Wilson Companies. Laney said that in the conversation, Spence referred to the air center’s operations as a business proposition and pushed back against her protestations.

“They’re a charitable family in lots of ways,” said another Bird-Watcher, who requested to not be identified by name due to her work on tracking ICE flights, “but then at the same time, you know, here they are profiting off human misery.”

A meticulous process

Every morning, a retired teacher in her seventies who joined The Bird-Watchers a few months ago, wakes up early and gets to work. Her tasks — detainee searches and database updates — are the start of a meticulous process that The Bird-Watchers have nearly perfected over their time working together.

The retired teacher, who requested that she not be named due to fears of retaliation over her work, logs on to an online database of detainees held at the West Tennessee Detention Facility in Mason. There, she manually searches for the names of the detainees.

“I am the one who every single morning spends up to three hours searching through Mason’s database one at a time to find out who is new there and who has left”, she told The Institute. “I don’t get everyone because they don’t make it easy. It’s a tedious process.”

“All these ways to find people was all brand new to me,” she said. But now, the searcher said that she has a long-term database of about 3,500 detainees who were there at the facility at some point since it reopened in September 2025, and over 800 names of detainees who were held there in July.

“I have a sheet for every month and so I have who at the beginning of the month started there, who comes there, and then I keep a database in the same sheet of those who are leaving. And so I can look at my sheet and I can tell you what day they came, I can tell you what day they left,” said the searcher.

When a large tranche of names that was there the previous day suddenly no longer appears the next day, she said it’s a sign that there would likely be a flight that will transfer them out of Memphis from Wilson Air Center.

“Because these planes are leaving at like nine o’clock, I get up really early to make sure we know how many people are going to be on the planes.”

As the searcher hands off this information to The Bird-Watchers, the next stage gets underway — flight tracking. On cue, a resident of Midtown Memphis who specializes in flight tracking for The Bird-Watchers, begins her part of the process.

Before she got involved with The Bird-Watchers, she had never tracked a flight before. “I didn’t know that was possible,” she told The Institute. Now, she scans multiple flight tracking websites, including a real-time flight monitoring site focused on ICE flight paths. She zeroes in on flights near Memphis International Airport, and tries to confirm whether there is a flight registered by an ICE contractor that is in the vicinity.

It’s not always easy to track the flights. “There’s like five of them (flight trackers) you have to kind of look between because they hide a lot of the flights — they have them on special lists so they don’t show up on trackers the same way.”

But when she needs help, she reaches out to a national group of ICE flight watchers who have been performing similar tasks elsewhere in the country. “The national group is helpful,” she said. “If there’s something I can’t figure out, I can ask.”

Over the past five months, The Bird-Watchers have tracked around 50 such ICE flights leaving Memphis. Most of them head toward Alexandria airport in Louisiana, she said, due to it being a hub for multiple detention centers in that Deep South state.

Once the flight details are confirmed by the tracking specialist, the details are promptly shared with the group. Finally, the last leg kicks off — Bird-Watchers must go in person to vantage points near the Wilson Air Center, and document what takes place.

West, the retired physician, and Laney, the retired teacher, are among those who are tasked with this final stretch. Both of them have been near Wilson on these observation trips on numerous occasions. Each time, it hits them just as hard.

“When you go and watch it, it just tears at your gut to see these people that have been separated from their families,” said West. He shares photos and videos from his trips documenting detainees bound in shackles. A majority have no criminal conviction yet are treated like criminals, eliciting sharp and emotional reactions.

“It’s like watching a death train,” said the flight tracking specialist, “You’re watching people get torn away from their families — some of them are going (to be sent) back to very dangerous situations. It’s not safe for them to go back.”

But for The Bird-Watchers, it reinforces the need for the work they do.

“I think it’s important to bear witness,” said the searcher, adding that they have been sharing the details on social media. “But also, we want to verify what they (ICE) are actually doing. Like I had no idea they were shackled, hands and feet.”

“It makes me want to scream because it’s not right,” she added. “They’re not getting the criminals. They’re getting somebody’s mommy and somebody’s daddy and somebody’s grandpa.”

Most Memphis detainees transferred out of state

Under the Trump administration, an overwhelming majority of immigrants listed as having been detained by ICE in Memphis end up in detention facilities in neighboring states such as Louisiana, according to The Institute’s analysis of data provided by ICE in response to a public records request by the Deportation Data Project.

Of the 2,529 ICE detainees listed as having been detained first in the Memphis Hold Room since the day President Trump took office in January 2025, over half of them — 1,291 detainees, or 51% — had their final detention stint in Louisiana. Only 15%, or 374 of the detainees, had their final detention stint within Tennessee, either at the Memphis Hold Room itself or the West Tennessee Detention Facility in Mason.

Vecindarios 901 said in a statement that these transfers of detainees are “designed to punish and wear down migrants in detention, forcing legal counsel to constantly recalibrate and families to wonder where their loved ones are being held and how they are being treated.” The statement added, “As habeas corpus petitions can only be filed in the jurisdiction of a person’s physical location, ICE can effectively prevent habeas filings with constant relocations and no transparency.”

DHS and ICE did not respond to The Institute’s request for comment.

Even as these “shuffle flights” continue, so do the efforts of those such as The Bird-Watchers of Memphis. And their pressure on private partners of ICE flights, such as Wilson Air Center, is also increasing.

“The reason I started doing this work was because I have a five-year-old grandson,” said the retired teacher who performs the early morning detainee database searches. “When he’s old and says, ‘What did you do when all this was going on?’ I want to be able to tell him, ‘I fought against this. I did something, I didn’t just sit and tsk tsk at the news.”

Erika Konig contributed to this article.
