Webworm Visits Wisconsin

by David Farrier

Getting to see Everlee in person involved a three hour flight from Los Angeles to Dallas, then another two hours from Dallas to Madison. Then it’s a two hour drive northeast, up to a small town where her mum lives, which is where Everlee Wihongi is currently staying.

I drive past cornfield after cornfield – there’s a lot of corn in this part of Wisconsin – before pulling into a little subdivision, a typical little American slice of life.

I park up, and an incredibly mellow black and white dog comes out to greet me, tail wagging. Everlee's dog, Dartangan.

It’s kind of strange, meeting this person I know so much about, but have never actually seen in person. The first thing that strikes me about Everlee is that she looks so happy: Dressed in a black tee, she’s beaming.

She passes on apologies from her dad, who just went to work. As I’d been travelling, they’d all been celebrating her nephew’s 1st birthday with the family. “A huge one-year-old, massive, typical Polynesian baby,” she laughs.

I’m mainly struck by how normal everything seems – talking about kids and dogs.

But her year has been anything but normal. Over 70 days locked up in various ICE prisons, before being suddenly spat back out into the life she was living before. Well, sort of the life she was living before.

A lot can change in three months.

The day I visit, Everlee’s been free for about six weeks. I ask her to take me through the day she got released from prison.

They woke me up at 1.30 in the morning. The guard comes and she knocks, and unlocked my door and she goes, “You're leaving”. And so I immediately shot out of the bed and I rolled up my sheets, got all packed up. I had written notes already because I knew I'd be getting out soon. And so I was running through the hallways, sliding them under people's doors. The guard came back, and I was sitting downstairs, and she goes, “What are you doing out?” And I go, “You said I was leaving!” And she goes, “You're not leaving till 3.30!” And I look at the clock and it's only 1.30.

And so I just had to sit there and tool around. They made me sit in my room. I'd given heaps of my stuff away. But at 3.30, they opened the doors to let me out, and we went down to this place called South intake. When we got in there, they took all of our things. There were two guards there: A girl and a boy. And they [had] pretty short fuses. And so when we go in there they're yelling at us, “Put your stuff down, go get changed!”

The guards were quite horrible to us. I had my backpack that got brought in from the airport, plus I had all the property I had accumulated: Books, papers, notebooks and stuff. So I had two boxes there, and he goes, “You're going to have to fit everything into this paper bag”. And then I started getting angry and I started swearing at him. I just said, “I didn't pick to come here from the airport. This is all my stuff, I'm not leaving anything here!”

I could understand why she was frustrated. Think of the one carry-on bag you take on a plane: It’s full of your most important things. There’s a reason you didn’t check it in.

Then all the stuff from her life for the last 73 days: Letters from prison mates, stories she had scrawled down, memories she needed to process once she was out. You can’t just let go of that.

Standing up for herself worked out: She got to keep her things – not just a paper bag’s worth.

Then she turned her attention to others in the room.

There was this lady that had cancer, who had been waiting to be transported. She was dressed in orange. And every time [the guards] would go out, the door would slam. And they kept doing it to her, and just looking past her, and so I said, “Stop slamming the door on that sick lady's face.”

And she says, “I didn't see her.” I was like, “You didn't see her in the bright orange with the walker, in front of the white wall? That's probably really horrible for her.”

By now it was 12.30pm, and all the prisoners began to be placed in shackles and loaded onto the bus. She was used to being moved around by this point – court dates missed because ICE would just randomly shunt her to another facility.

But right from the start, this trip felt more hopeful.

There was the bus driver. He was so cool. He was talking in Spanish. I was just standing there and I go, “Oh my God, I don't speak Spanish. I'm sorry.” And he goes, “You’re the only person in this whole facility that doesn't speak Spanish!” But then he goes, “Where are you from?” And I go, “New Zealand.” He goes, “Oh, you're a Māori. That's so cool. You're the first one I've ever met!” – and he came and shook my hand.

They’re putting on the belly belt and the shackles, and I'm just grumbling: “I don't want to wear the leg shackles. I hate wearing them.” And [the bus driver] just looks and he goes, “Dang, it looks like you need big boy ones for your big boy ankles! And I don't have any!” And I go, “Must be I don't need them then.” And he goes, “I don't have any, so you can't wear them!”

So I didn't have to have my legs shackled. He was so cool.

The bus set off from the Eloy Detention Centre, briefly stopping at another ICE facility in Florence – a place known for charming things like regular measles outbreaks. Then it was a few hours north to the city of Phoenix. She tells me most people on the bus were sleeping, after what had been a very long night.

They were woken up again as the bus pulled into a Department of Homeland Security facility.

That's when people panicked and they thought that we were just getting dropped off there and transported to a different facility. But the bus driver said, “No, everybody can relax. You're all going home today.”

Imagine hearing those words: You're all going home today.

From there, it was the final leg to the Visitor Centre. I ask – after all the ups and downs of the last three months, coming close to freedom so many times before being thwarted – when she knew this was actually it. That her ordeal was over.

It was when we were actually getting off the bus. And everybody in the bus was like, “I can't believe it.” And then we're all hugging each other, even hugging the guards.

A local church group was there waiting with boxes of food, drinks and clothing. This wasn’t some state funded group or official part of the ICE process – they were just volunteers, mutual aid at its finest.

I called my mum right away, she was the first one. And then I called the family group chat. They thought that my grandmother was calling everybody by accident again! And so they all kind of slowly hopped on there. I was just, “Hi.”

Then we have a cousins’ group chat from our holiday. I saw my aunt posted your [Webworm] thing. “Everlee has been released.” And so they had put that in the group chat. And so then the cousins started trying to call, and it was wicked. It was really cool.

She made her way from the visitors centre in Phoenix, to an Airbnb her parents had booked. She couldn’t check into a hotel, because she’d discovered ICE had kept her passport and ID.

When I got to the Airbnb, my cousin called because she was like, “Are you alright?” And I go, “Ah, a bit weird being alone, eh?” And so she talked to me for hours. Then she called her sister, and so it was probably six of us FaceTiming all at the same time, just till my parents got there.

It had been 73 days since Everlee had last seen her mum and dad.

At this point, I hear a car pull in. Betty is back from work. It’s the first time I’ve met her mum in person, too – and she’s got a grin as big as her daughters. She hands me two bottles of "Sun Drop" – a drink she swears by – before telling me what Everlee's release day was like for her.

We had rented an Airbnb for Everlee to wait at, because she didn't have any ID – so she couldn't go in a hotel. And Gordon and I scrambled and we found an AirBnB and we got it, gave her the address, she got an Uber there. And then I just said, “Wait there and go shower, swim. Wait for us. We'll be there later on, and your brothers will be there too."

So we walk in and she's there. Her two brothers and my daughter-in-law were there waiting. I went to hug Everlee and one of them had picked up her phone and I just looked at them like, “No!”

There were a lot of hugs, and I understand the temptation to take some photos.

I think I just kind of gave them the look like: “No photos right now.” Yeah. "Someone will die tonight if that happens!"

Everlee chips in.

My dad's not a hugger. Before this, he had given me two hugs in my whole life. And he gave me one right when he got there - and then when it was going, he gave me another hug. And I'm like, “Dad, you've doubled the amount of hugs I've ever gotten in my life!” He's like, “Ah, get lost!”

She says that first night out, while amazing, was also incredibly difficult.

It was so weird. There was a huge bed. I had a king-size bed, but I stayed in [the corner] like the same size as the cot. I didn't expand from there. It wasn't a good sleep. I kept hearing the keychains, you know, keychains jingling – so I would just open my eyes and then realize I wasn't in there. And then when I would fall asleep, I'd hear, “Cuenta!” and so I'd just go to stand up.

“Cuenta” is count, but as most people spoke Spanish, that's what they'd say. They'd just say “cuenta”, and then you'd have to stand up by your door. And then they would walk past the door, you know, look at the slip, make sure it matched up with your badge and your face, and then you could go back to bed. And so the first couple of days, I just kept hearing that and the keychains.

I have these little bouts when I'm by myself. Just bouts of despair. The therapist said it's like survivor's guilt. I feel happy that I'm out, but I feel sad for my mates that I just stuck in there like Lucy. She's stuck in there indefinitely and she had been there for 12 months, so she's been there for 14 months now. And she's not going to get to see an immigration judge.

Lucy was from Bulgaria, and was one of her best mates inside. She feels like she’s left her friend behind. She can’t stop thinking about her.

Her husband died two months before she got taken by ICE. They were superintendents of an apartment complex, and so her address was there because she was taking care of it. Her husband died, so there was nobody to look after the apartment. She has no address, she has no documents. She's got no family to help her at all, no way to see a judge, no lawyer, nothing. No help. I don't know what's going to happen to her.

There are others, too. She got some of them to write their stories down – Everlee has them in a notebook. Again, that’s why she fought so hard to keep all her stuff. She carries all these stories with her, on repeat, in her brain.

Just innocent people. [Another] girl in the wrong place at the wrong time: She came from Nicaragua, and she's been stuck for nine months now. No way out. And she's not a criminal, she was a medical assistant.

Mainly, Everlee realises that as bad as she had it, she had a family in the US battling for her every day. So many of her new friends didn’t have that. And so they remain in prison, no end in sight.

And Everlee, well, she’s just landed back in the life she had before. She emerged as a different person. And she’s emerged into different circumstances.

My job let me go because I was stuck in there. You know, well, I don't want to say bad things about them. They looked after my job for a bit.

She’d had a really good job as a welder – that’s gone now. She doesn’t want to sleep alone, so she’d moved back to her parents place while she tries to readjust.

In all of this, she’s still so upbeat. I have no doubt she’s putting on a brave face for me – a stranger in her house – but I have no doubt her glass half full approach has helped her through this.

I still have a place. And that money from the GoFundMe helped me keep that. And I have the most supportive friends in the world. They know that I was overwhelmed when I came out. And so they didn't jump on me. They just messaged, “When you're ready, we're here to talk, but you know I'm glad you're out.”

Two weeks ago, my best friend planned a seafood boil, and invited a bunch of our friends, and oh, it was so nice. They were so happy to see me. Everybody that was invited came. The food was really good. She knew I loved seafood, and so she went around different places to find the best seafood. Not just anything, the best.

I ask her how she kept her shit together inside. The different facilities, the transport, having court dates thwarted, the lack of control over her own life.

So there were... moments.

I didn't cry in front of anybody. I would, you know, I'd go take a shower, that would be where I would have little breakdowns. But I didn't want people to see me crying. I just wanted to keep it together too, just keep myself calm.

I feel like I learned, I practiced a lot of self-control in there. I tried to stay calm all the time. It was hard some days. If I knew that if I was having a bad day, I would just message on the tablet. I'd message [my family] and just say, “Look, can you please let everybody know I'm not going to be calling today. I don't feel like going down on the phones, and I'm having a bad day. I just want to stay in my bed.”

She says the main trick she found was just trying to make this very un-normal time feel normal. Little tricks that made her feel like she’d never been kidnapped by ICE in the first place.

I was having the worst time at Adelanto. It took me a couple of days there, but then when I realized we can go outside at 7.30am, I'm just going to get up early. I'm going to get out early, I'm gonna work-out, outside.

I started making myself a little routine. Like I did things to make myself feel normal. I love wearing makeup. So I made eyeliner there. I'd put it on every day. I'd have a shower, do my hair. And then I learned how to make these fancy ‘Starbucks’ coffees. I had a peanut butter jar. And so I was making really fancy coffee drinks for myself, little iced coffees, and I'd go outside with them too. And people are like, “Where'd you get that?” I'm like, “I made it.” I put little designs on my coffee. So I did things to make myself feel normal, as normal as I could.

But you just felt helpless often too, you know? The transport - I'd never felt so helpless before in my life. Because it was just being herded around. With the shackles, you're going where they tell you to go. And when you need to go to the bathroom, you just get one hand out of your shackles. It was the way that you were treated like farm animals: You'd try and ask questions, and they'd wave you off. I'm very particular about things, too. And so that was one of the hardest things for me was just not being able to really even advocate for myself, or advocate for others around. You just had to do what they wanted, when they wanted you to do it.

It's a humiliating experience. I think [back] to when we were transported: Like, people were crying on the plane. Lots of people. They didn't know what was happening. They were taking people from California and moving them further away from their families, people that would visit them. Things like that.

Now, she has to figure out how to live her life, with all of that still in her head.

I mean, it's left a very dirty mark on America for me. I'm so proud to be from New Zealand and I love going back there, and I love telling people I'm from New Zealand. I feel like, just the way I was treated, and the way they treated people that I've seen – I just feel like that's not part of the American dream. That's not part of the America I want to be in.

So while she’s happy to be back with her family, her friends and her dog, she also moves through the world now with a certain amount of worry. A certain amount of dread.

It's hard after something like this. I just feel I pay taxes here, I contribute to my community here, I did a lot. And just the way that I was treated was just so mind boggling. I still can't really believe it.

I think being out, I do feel anxious. I feel very anxious. You know, if I got pulled over by the police and ICE were to come, like, what would they find? I feel like anything, any excuse to fill a bed in one of the detention centers, to make the place a bit more money. I don't think anybody's really safe from them.

For all the people that I met that are stuck in there, like immigrants, innocent people. And the people that I saw weren't the criminals that Donald Trump said. They were housewives, business owners.

I keep going back to the transport, but they gave us all our regular clothes when we left. And there were people that were in their high-vis, they still had mud on their pants. There was a pregnant lady, there were children. It was just these people that they picked up on the job sites! that's not a criminal person, you picked them up from work, you know?

I ask Betty how she’s holding up.

I’m just relieved. I didn't really realize how affected I was. I thought I was doing pretty good at keeping things together, and after Everlee came home I was at work, and my boss came in and he's like, “I'm really glad Everlee’s back”, and I said, “Yeah, me too.”

And he goes, “It's just nice to have you back.” I'm like, “What?” He goes, “You've been really dark. You've really dark, and we didn’t know what to do.”

I think back to how when all this started, New Zealand’s Minister of Foreign Affairs, Winston Peters, went on the TV news and confirmed to a nation why the New Zealander had been detained at LAX.

His confirmation was false, we know that now. He said she’d failed to fill in some forms. Like she’d been hiding something. That she got what she deserved.

A narrative that a lot of people in New Zealand still believe. Look at the comments section under various news stories on social media and Winston’s narrative stuck: She wasn’t to be trusted. She brought all this upon herself.

Betty pauses.

I'm just... you know, looking back now, Winston Peters, he... he worries me for our country, he really does. He's like a mini-Trump in New Zealand for me. But just someone who can brazenly lie and tell people, “Oh, Everlee didn't fill out some forms correctly, she missed information.”

Just to blatantly lie like that was just, I couldn't believe it.

And then at first I thought, maybe he didn't know. And I'm like, “But he's the Minister of Foreign Affairs. How can he not know?” And then you come to the realisation that he just straight out lied. He's a liar. A bald-faced liar.

She had some kind things to say about the New Zealand consulate, after they finally got onboard. She also spoke favourably of Labour’s Phil Twyford, and the Maori party.

I ask if Betty plans to stay in the US herself. And, as expected, the answer isn’t straightforward.

It's a very scary time. You know, I worry for Everlee, of this happening to her again. I worry about [my other children]. You know, we've got two people that aren't citizens and it's very worrisome. And the new things that they're coming up with, like the Naturalization Bill that they tried to push through. It failed once, but it doesn't mean that they are not going to push it, try again. So it's worrisome.

We had planned on leaving when [my husband] Gordon retired, and he's looking at retiring this year. But then our kids went and had kids, kids who love us and want to be around us, and call us, and that's made it difficult for us to want to leave.

There’s been a lot of beeping while we talk, Everlee getting up and down to the kitchen. She says she saw a viral recipe for artichokes online, and she’s been making them while we talk.

We ended up eating too many of those viral artichokes, to the point that when we went out to dinner later that night we couldn’t even begin to finish what we’d ordered.

I drove back off into the corn, driving back to Madison. Betty texts me to make sure I made it back safely.

I had.

The next day, some messages from Everlee, too. She's sent me a video. It’s eight seconds long, and is soundtracked by music blasting from a speaker.

It’s a terrifically bright day, and she’s out in the middle of a lake on a paddle board, surrounded by sparking blue water and a giant sky.

It’s just her.

And while she has a long road to recovery in front of her, right now she feels about as free as any human could be.

Everlee still has a GoFundMe that anyone is welcome to contribute to, as she looks for work and gets her life back on track.

title: Legal aid for immigrant kids disrupted after Trump administration lets funding lapse - CSMonitor.com
authors: Sarah Matusek, The Christian Science Monitor
description:
The Trump administration this month has complicated – if not cut off – access to lawyers for tens of thousands of immigrant kids.
The end of the Acacia contract on July 31 threw that access further into jeopardy.
Changes in court Lawyers say the funding cliff comes as new policies in immigration court complicate and accelerate children’s cases.
Though more than 3 million cases remain, the Trump administration has whittled down the immigration court backlog.
According to her nonprofit, private funding has allowed Ayuda to continue representing around 260 unaccompanied children through September.
text:
The Trump administration this month has complicated – if not cut off – access to lawyers for tens of thousands of immigrant kids. By law, the government must try to arrange that aid for children who come to the United States alone.

At the end of July, the government let a legal-services contract for those children lapse, affecting the Acacia Center for Justice and its nearly 100 subcontractors. News this week of an upcoming federal contract with a Texas firm better known for environmental law has left immigrant advocates scrambling for answers as court dates loom.

As a result, at least one nonprofit has laid off staff. Others count the days until their funding runs out.

A federal judge in California last year ordered the Trump administration to keep funding those services. The government has since withheld funds for months and cast doubt on the legitimacy of lawyers’ work. As litigation chugs on, the White House has ramped up deportations of unaccompanied immigrant children and made it harder for them to win protections like asylum.

On Monday, a spokesperson for the Department of Health and Human Services said in a statement that its agency overseeing unaccompanied children agrees that they need legal representation, “and is actively working to resolve this matter.”

By Thursday, Acacia had proposed a new contract that would help transition cases to new providers and was waiting to hear back.

“We adamantly believe that children must continue to be represented by attorneys who specialize in immigration law,” and are trained to handle trauma, says Bettina Rodriguez Schlegel, the chief of staff at Acacia.

Access to lawyers

U.S. law says the government must ensure unaccompanied children can access legal aid “to the greatest extent practicable.” Congress has never fully funded that goal, children’s advocates say.

The end of the Acacia contract on July 31 threw that access further into jeopardy. On Monday, the spokesperson for HHS, whose Office of Refugee Resettlement takes custody of children soon after they arrive alone, said in an email that the agency is “pursuing multiple acquisition options.”

Last week, a Texas nonprofit – an Acacia subcontractor – shut down its unaccompanied children’s program and let 13 employees go. “We’re still all a little bit in shock,” says Melissa Lopez, executive director of Estrella del Paso.

Like other groups cut off from funds, Estrella del Paso has patched together philanthropy and reserves in an attempt to stay afloat.

“We have now completely used up all of our savings,” Ms. Lopez says. Her team won’t accept new cases and will discontinue know-your-rights presentations along with legal screenings.

As of Monday, the nonprofit reported 243 active cases that lawyers are trying to manage.

“We are maintaining our responsibilities to them, both ethically and morally,” Ms. Lopez says.

A Federal Register notice shows HHS plans to award a Texas firm – the Burke Law Group – a yearlong contract for legal services for unaccompanied minors. For up to $150 million, the firm would provide those services “while children remain” in HHS care, and offer referrals when they are released.

It’s unclear whether the government will announce additional contracts to cover children who have been released to sponsors.

As of Thursday, two out of around two dozen people on the Houston firm’s website listed immigration expertise. Those include an attorney who has represented employers of foreign workers – and whose name appeared on the firm’s website this week after news broke about the new contract, according to archived versions of the site.

The Burke Law Group did not respond to voicemails and written requests seeking interviews. The founder, Marcella Burke, served in the Environmental Protection Agency and the Interior Department during the first Trump administration.

Limits of law

In immigration court, people are entitled to an attorney, but not at the government’s expense.

In practice, “the government has never had enough money to provide representation for all children in their immigration proceedings,” says Mark Greenberg, a scholar in residence at the Brookings Institution and former HHS deputy general counsel during the Joe Biden presidency.

Acacia claims HHS owes it more than $65 million for months of services already completed. HHS withheld funding while requesting data on child clients that the organization refused to share.

Acacia says sharing clients’ immigration ID numbers, among other details, would violate standards of confidentiality. The Trump administration disagrees.

“As with any attorney billing, the government must know what it is funding,” especially when children appear in immigration hearings without counsel, the HHS spokesperson said in the emailed statement.

Since last November, Acacia says, more than 20,000 unaccompanied children received legal services. By comparison, since fiscal year 2021, HHS has released some half a million unaccompanied children, though not all have remained.

Before the contract ended last week, John Fabbricatore, a former Immigration and Customs Enforcement official and now an HHS adviser, linked allegations of potential fraud by Acacia to the prevalence of unaccompanied kids in court without lawyers.

Making sure federal funds are securing counsel for each child is “important for the American taxpayer, and for these children,” Mr. Fabbricatore told NewsNation.

“We have nothing to hide,” says Ms. Rodriguez Schlegel at Acacia.

“We did everything according to the way that we were asked,” she says, but later on, HHS “did an about-face and then demanded retroactive information for work already performed.” The nonprofit says the government’s underfunding explains why children still appear without lawyers in court.

Ethics also limit how many cases lawyers can take on, says Emily Brock, deputy managing attorney for the children’s program at the Rocky Mountain Immigrant Advocacy Network, an Acacia subcontractor.

“It’s a preparation and capacity issue,” she says. “Especially as the government makes it harder and harder to pursue relief.”

With the funding lapse, Ms. Brock says her organization can’t take on new cases.

“The onus shouldn’t be on us to be fundraising to provide services that the federal government is statutorily required to provide,” she says.

Changes in court

Lawyers say the funding cliff comes as new policies in immigration court complicate and accelerate children’s cases.

In past administrations, says attorney Laura Lindsay, an immigration judge would let children prepare complex applications over six to nine months. Now, she says children often face deadlines of three to four weeks.

“Which is not enough time to develop an asylum case for a traumatized 7-year-old,” says Ms. Lindsay, a staff attorney at Ayuda, another Acacia subcontractor, in Virginia.

Sometimes, “I’m the first person they’ve disclosed horrific abuse to … and it’s taken months of screening before they feel comfortable sharing,” Ms. Lindsay says.

Kathryn Mattingly, a spokesperson for the Executive Office for Immigration Review, which runs immigration courts, said the agency “prioritizes the timely completion of all cases,” including for children.

Unnecessary delays hurt immigrants with valid claims and the American public, who wish to see those without valid claims deported “as quickly as possible,” Ms. Mattingly said in an email.

Though more than 3 million cases remain, the Trump administration has whittled down the immigration court backlog. Critics say policies that have fast-tracked cases have imperiled due process rights in the court, part of the executive branch. The government counters that it’s restoring integrity to the immigration system after a Biden-era surge of illegal entries.

Ms. Lindsay reports having 11 court hearings recently in the span of three days.

According to her nonprofit, private funding has allowed Ayuda to continue representing around 260 unaccompanied children through September.

The role of Congress

For some observers, the lapsed contract underscores a flawed system set up by lawmakers – one that places children in deportation proceedings in the first place.

Minors shouldn’t face adversarial hearings, says Andrew Arthur, a resident fellow in law and policy at the Center for Immigration Studies and former immigration judge. “Congress should revisit it,” he says.

Congress hasn’t overhauled the immigration system since the 1990s.

“As an immigration judge, I would not feel comfortable going forward” with an unrepresented child, Mr. Arthur says. “You can’t take pleadings from anybody that you conclude isn’t competent.”

name: Human Rights
title: Sur Legal Collaborative stands firm to defend immigrant workers amid aggressive ICE actions
description:
The Sur Legal Collaborative has made it its mission to defend immigrant workers and ensure they know their rights.
In addition to protecting immigrant workers from the nationwide ICE crackdown, the Sur Legal Collaborative also safeguards them from employers who may take advantage of them for wage theft and labor trafficking.
Aimee Pacheco, a staff attorney and founding advocacy and communications fellow for the Sur Legal Collaborative, says they help workers file complaints.
But like many other nonprofits, the Sur Legal Collaborative is attempting to serve several people on limited funding.
Regardless of funding, this stuff is still happening.” Gambino shared the best way citizens can help immigrant workers.
text:
Of the 169 million people in the American workforce, more than 32 million are immigrants — more than 8 million of whom are undocumented. Many of those workers have become the target of the Trump Administration’s aggressive immigration enforcement.

Still, as the U.S. Constitution states, they have fundamental rights within the United States, regardless of their citizenship or immigration status. The Sur Legal Collaborative has made it its mission to defend immigrant workers and ensure they know their rights.

“We definitely hear how these immigration enforcements and workplace raids, even though they’re not happening exactly in the location that they’re in, they still hear it happening in Georgia, and that has a chilling effect on immigrants, raising panic, raising fear,” said Lucia Gambino.

“And this is why we have focused on emergency planning to try to have a plan in place instead of panicking and scrambling during a crisis.”

Gambino is the Bilingual Workers’ Rights Organizer for the Sur Legal Collaborative, a nonprofit that supports working immigrants and makes them aware of their rights, regardless of their documented status.

In addition to protecting immigrant workers from the nationwide ICE crackdown, the Sur Legal Collaborative also safeguards them from employers who may take advantage of them for wage theft and labor trafficking.

Aimee Pacheco, a staff attorney and founding advocacy and communications fellow for the Sur Legal Collaborative, says they help workers file complaints. However, the challenge they’re facing since President Trump returned to office is not knowing how much is being communicated between the Department of Labor and the Department of Homeland Security.

“So we have begun to tell workers to be a little bit more cautious and not disclose their immigration status,” said Pacheco.

“And also try to get workers to organize more and get U.S. citizens and legal permanent residents to be the ones to make some of those complaints on behalf of several workers, where workers are always more powerful together in numbers.”

Pacheco said the targeted ICE raids are affecting families and entire communities of documented and undocumented people. But like many other nonprofits, the Sur Legal Collaborative is attempting to serve several people on limited funding. Right now, they’re relying more on mutual aid and community volunteer work.

“It’s definitely been tough,” Pacheco said. “There has been a cut in funding all across the board for organizations doing this type of work. We are definitely still trying to look for sources of funding. Regardless of funding, this stuff is still happening.”

Gambino shared the best way citizens can help immigrant workers.

“For filing labor complaints, a good way is to step up for your immigrant coworkers and be the face of that complaint,” said Gambino. “Try to speak up, especially if you’re being favored because of your status.”

And the asylum petitions from immigrant children have been particularly targeted.

text:
The federal government’s decision to award a small Texas law firm run by a Trump ally a $150 million contract to represent over a thousand migrant children is nothing more than an attempt to undermine the rights and fasttrack the removal of minors who entered the country alone, including hundreds in Arizona who are seeking asylum, according to immigrant legal aid organizations

Michael Lukens, the executive director of the Amica Center for Immigrant Rights, one of a nationwide network of legal aid groups that has consistently worked with immigrant children over nearly two decades, questioned the ability of such a small law firm to take on so many cases.

Burke Law Group, which has a staff of just 26 and specializes in corporate law, will now be tasked with representing 1,800 unaccompanied children who live in federally operated shelters across the country. After news of the federal contract broke, the law firm amended its website to boast about its work in immigration law.

During a virtual news conference on Wednesday, Luken criticized the choice to hire the Burke Law Group as a “grift” and warned that immigrant children would suffer as a result. The law firm was founded by Marcella Burke, a former Trump appointee to the Environmental Protection Agency and the Department of the Interior.

“Children are going to get no meaningful due process,” Luken warned. “No meaningful day in court.”

Under a 2008 anti-human trafficking law, the federal government is obligated to ensure children who arrive in the country by themselves have access to legal counsel, but the Trump administration has repeatedly tried to erode that mandate.

Twice last year, the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, which oversees immigrant children, issued stop work orders to nonprofit organizations contracted to provide legal counsel for immigrant minors. The orders were ultimately reversed shortly after lawsuits were filed.

And since November, the Trump administration has withheld payments for the legal defense of the children, leaving law firms to expend their own resources or lay off staff to make up the difference and continue providing help.

On July 31, a contract between the federal government and the Acacia Center for Justice expired. The organization partnered with more than a hundred legal nonprofits across the country to provide legal aid for immigrant children. The federal government offered Acacia Center a new contract, but the organization rejected it, saying it would not comply with requirements that confidential information about immigrant children be shared in exchange for the funding. Among the things Acacia Center said the Trump administration demanded was detailing the legal strategies attorneys anticipated pursuing on behalf of their juvenile clients.

In Arizona, the Florence Immigrant and Refugee Rights Project is the only organization that provides free legal services for immigrant children who arrive in the country without a parent or guardian. Deputy Director Roxana Avila-Cimpeanu said she’s concerned about the quality of care children will receive if the existing legal framework is erased.

She noted that legal nonprofits that work with immigrant children do much more than attending hearings; attorneys provide individual legal consultations, set up know your rights presentations and perform wellness check ins. Just last week, Avila-Cimpeanu said, attorneys met with a young girl who is being sexually abused in a detention facility and are working to remove her from that environment.

“We, as a legal service provider, are able to go there and be the eyes and ears on the ground, talk to her, make sure that nothing else happens and get her out of that situation,” she said. “If this national network of attorneys who have experience and know what the rights of children are is dismantled — who is going to be doing that work? Who is going to ensure that children are being treated with dignity and respect, are safe and cared for and have somebody in their corner?”

Between January and June 6, according to the most recent data from U.S. Customs and Border Protection, more than 1,600 children crossed Arizona’s southern border without a parent or legal guardian.

Much of the work that the Florence Project does is in person, after a child first arrives at a detention center. Under federal law, attorneys must provide an individual legal consultation and a know-your-rights presentation to a child within ten days of their arrival at an immigration facility. And know-your-rights presentations must occur again every six months.

It’s unclear how a Texas-based law firm will fulfill those directives without immigrant children having to be moved to the Lone Star State or awarding subcontracts to local organizations.

Along with concerns about the Burke Law Group’s ability to provide adequate legal counsel, the likelihood that hundreds of cases will be moved to Texas is alarming to immigrant advocates, as the state is notorious for making deportations easier. Immigration judges in Texas deny asylum claims at higher rates than in other states. And there are no state-level protections for unaccompanied minors or independent oversight of immigration detention facilities.

Alexa Sendukas, the managing attorney for the Galveston-Houston Immigrant Representation Project, said that the outlook for unaccompanied immigrant children in the Texas judicial system has worsened under the Trump administration. She noted that children’s court proceedings have been expedited, with many cases being terminated by judges before children can be given an opportunity to tell their stories or provide evidence for why they should be granted federal protections.

And the asylum petitions from immigrant children have been particularly targeted. The Galveston-Houston Immigrant Representation Project has hundreds of asylum applications built up over five years and the courts have scheduled hearings for them in unprecedented numbers into the next few months, booking attorneys for as many as five appearances at the same time and refusing rescheduling requests.

“Protections for abused and neglected children, as well as survivors of human trafficking, are not being honored in court and these children are being deported anyway,” Sendukas said. “No one is making sure they have family available to receive them or that it would even be safe for them to return.”

In one case, an unaccompanied child who was deported was sent to a town hours away from where immigration authorities told his mother to pick him up and it was days before he was reunited with his family.

The Florence Project has 300 pending asylum cases involving unaccompanied children, according to Avila-Cimpeanu, who said she is also concerned about their legal future. Similarly to the cases in Texas, the Florence Project is also seeing an uptick in asylum cases being called up for hearings in Arizona.

And, Avila-Cimpeanu added, the possibility of the legal representation for its current clients being moved to Texas could imperil the ability of the children to be granted protection from deportation. Many children have cases that hinge on state juvenile court proceedings to apply for a humanitarian visa, and moving the children out of state or giving them Texas-based counsel could prolong or entirely scuttle that process, which is no longer available when the child turns 18.

In the end, Avila-Cimpeanu warned, the Trump administration’s move to put the legal fate of more than a thousand immigrant children, many of whom are fleeing violence or sex trafficking, in the hands of an inexperienced law firm in Texas will only result in deportations.

“Children are going to be sent back to harm, children are going to die because of this,” she said.

It is unclear who will provide legal representation to the 22,000 other unaccompanied children who live with sponsors.

One month after the United States supreme court struck down his first attempt to restrict the guarantee of birthright citizenship enshrined in the US constitution, Donald ⁠Trump signed ⁠executive orders ​on Thursday that aim to deny ⁠US citizenship to children born in the United States to so-called “birth tourists”.

That seems like a wildly inflated estimate. According to the Migration Policy Institute, the highest census-based estimate “puts birth tourism at 22,000 to 26,000 babies born annually on US soil, although government data show just 9,600 births to mothers with foreign addresses in 2024.”

For context, it seems worth keeping in mind that Trump’s own father, Fred Trump, was born a US citizen in 1905 to a non-citizen mother who arrived in New York from Germany six months pregnant. The president’s Scottish-born mother, Mary Anne Trump, later gave birth to her first two children, the current president’s older siblings, in the US before becoming a US citizen herself.

The two new executive orders on birthright citizenship signed by Donald Trump on Thursday, just five weeks ago after the US supreme court struck down his previous order denying citizenship to the children of non-citizens, attempt to limit in two ways a right that has been enshrined in the constitution since the 14th amendment was ratified in 1868.

One order bars the entry of foreigners allegedly traveling to the US “for the purpose of giving birth on American soil”, without saying how, exactly, that determination is to be made. (It might be worth noting here that such a policy, had it been in effect in 2001, might well have prevented Folarin Balogun, who was born that year to a mother visiting New York from London, from being born a US citizen and going on to represent the US in this summer’s World Cup.)

The second order seeks to deny citizenship to the children of certain categories of non-citizens.

The order excludes children born to any non-citizen parent in the following categories:

an alien enemy, “defined to include any member of a designated Foreign Terrorist Organization … or Specially Designated Global Terrorist”;

foreign government employees, including: ambassadors; other embassy or consulate employees who are nationals of that foreign country; anyone employed by a foreign government in an official capacity;

employees of international organizations that possess international-organization immunity;

people “engaged in a commercial transaction to purchase or access birthright citizenship”.

The children of foreign ambassadors have long been excluded from birthright citizenship.

Somewhat redundantly, the second order also denies citizenship to the children of non-citizens “born in a territory or territorial waters of the United States where citizenship is not conferred by Federal statute”.

Speaking in the Oval Office earlier on Thursday, Donald Trump gave a wildly inaccurate account of the nature and timing of the 14th amendment to the US constitution, which enshrined the principle of birthright citizenship, as he sought to justify two new executive orders attempting to deny citizenship to a wider pool of children born on US soil to non-citizens.

As he discussed the orders, “Continuing to Protect the Meaning and Value of American Citizenship” and “Ending Birth Tourism”, Trump called the supreme court’s decision to strike down his previous attempt to deny birthright citizenship through executive action “a very, very unfortunate decision.”

“So we’re, making adjustments because it’s very unfair,” the president said. “This was meant for the babies of slaves. It was right after – one week or two weeks after – the Civil war ended.”

In fact, General Robert E Lee surrendered the largest of the Confederate forces on 9 April 1865 at Appomattox Court House in Virginia. More than a year later, the 14th amendment was passed by Congress on 13 June 1866, and ratified on 9 July 9 1868.

Trump’s assertion that the framers of the amendment only intended it to apply to the children of former slaves was roundly rejected by the supreme court, not this year but in 1898, when the justices ruled 6-2 that Wong Kim Ark, who was born in San Francisco to parents who were both Chinese citizens, was a US citizen by birth.

Despite that well-known precedent, which was discussed at length during the recent supreme court deliberations over Trump’s first attempt to deny birthright citizenship to the children of non-citizens, the president’s adviser, Stephen Miller, insisted that Trump was right.

“As the president mentioned, the 14th amendment was passed exclusively in the aftermath of the Civil War to to ensure that the children of slaves would be citizens. It had no other meaning and purpose outside of that,” Miller said.

“They’ve taken birthright citizenship and they’ve made a joke out of it,” Trump added. “And we’re actually the only country, of size, I think just about the only country period, that does birthright citizenship.”

That too is wildly inaccurate. Thirty-two other countries, most in the western hemisphere, have birthright citizenship laws that are similar to US law, according to the Pew Research Center. About 50 more countries have more limited versions of birthright citizenship.

text:
Today, America First Legal (AFL), in partnership with co-counsel Christopher Mills, filed an amicus brief with the U.S. Supreme Court in Genalo v. Keisy G.M., urging the Court to make clear that criminal aliens must be detained until their removal proceedings are complete.

The case arises from a challenge to continued detention under 8 U.S.C. § 1226(c), the statute Congress enacted to ensure that deportable criminal aliens are held in custody pending removal rather than released into American communities. The Second Circuit held that the Due Process Clause requires a bond hearing—and places the burden on the government to justify continued detention by clear and convincing evidence—once detention has become “unreasonably prolonged,” even when the delay is caused by the alien’s own litigation choices.

AFL’s brief makes three central arguments:

First, the federal courts lack jurisdiction to hear the challenge at all: 8 U.S.C. § 1226(e) forbids courts from setting aside the Secretary’s decisions about detaining aliens.

Second, even if jurisdiction existed, the Due Process Clause does not entitle a criminal alien to escape detention that his own decision to prolong removal proceedings has extended—a criminal alien detained under § 1226(c) “has the keys in his pocket” and can end his detention at any time simply by allowing removal to proceed and leaving the country.

Third, if any bond hearing is constitutionally required, the alien—not the government—should bear the burden of proving he is not a danger or flight risk, consistent with the ordinary rule that the party seeking relief carries the burden.

AFL warns that the consequences of the Second Circuit’s rule are not abstract. Congress enacted Section 1226(c) because deportable criminal aliens who remain at large have often continued to commit crimes. In addition, historical data show that the vast majority of aliens released from custody are never removed. Rewarding delay with release, the brief argues, would give every detained criminal alien an incentive to stall his case for months in hopes of securing release into the United States.

“Criminal aliens who abuse our legal system by dragging out their own removal proceedings should not be rewarded with release into the communities they threaten,” said James Rogers, Senior Counsel at America First Legal. “The safety of the American people should always come first. The Second Circuit’s ruling would hand dangerous criminal aliens a roadmap to walk free simply by running out the clock. This is exactly the kind of judicial overreach America First Legal exists to fight. We will keep working tirelessly to defend our nation’s borders and ensure that our immigration laws are obeyed.”

Read the full amicus brief here.

text:
(NewsNation) — As federal immigration enforcement efforts ramp up at airports around the country, airlines have begun pushing back.

Immigration and Customs Enforcement officials made between 12 and 36 arrests per day at U.S. airports last month, using flight manifests to detain people accused of overstaying their visas, The Wall Street Journal reported. Some of those incidents have resulted in bystanders intervening and have elicited pushback from airlines, including Southwest.

This all comes as multiple outlets reported last month that Immigration and Customs Enforcement entered into an agreement with the Transportation Security Administration that allows the two federal agencies to share data. NewsNation reported last week that officers have been deployed to at least 25 airports amid pressure from the White House for ICE to make more arrests.

Southwest prevents ICE from boarding flight

On July 25th, a Southwest agent prevented ICE from boarding a flight from Dallas to Orlando, according to documents reviewed by the journal. The gate agent reportedly wouldn’t allow boarding access without a judicial warrant signed by a judge.

Following the incident, Southwest said in a statement that it “has longstanding policies in place to ensure appropriate legal documentation is presented by law enforcement personnel before any information about customers is shared.”

The journal also reported that an unnamed airline at a southern airport recently declined to assist ICE in accessing a jet bridge so they could arrest a man traveling with his family. Several other incidents have ended with arrests, however, including those recorded at airports in San Francisco and Las Vegas.

In one encounter last month, a passenger was heard pleading with a Southwest agent as they removed a friend from a plane headed from Denver to Oakland. Despite the intervention, ICE arrested the 27-year-old woman from Ecuador because she allegedly overstayed her visa.

DHS responds to airport enforcement efforts

Amid growing public concern, Airlines for America, a trade group representing top airlines, said its member companies “have had constructive discussions with ICE and TSA to ensure if law enforcement activity occurs at an airport, there are proper procedures and protocols in place to prioritize the safety and security of all involved.”

A Department of Homeland Security spokesperson defended the recent uptick in airport enforcement efforts, telling NewsNation, “DHS reversed the horrendous Biden-era policy that allowed aliens in our country illegally to jet around our country. Under President Trump, DHS will no longer tolerate this.”

“This administration is working diligently to ensure that aliens in our country illegally can no longer fly unless it is out of our country to self-deport,” they added.

NewsNation’s Ali Bradley and Jeff Arnold contributed to this report.

text:
Federal

July Marks New Peak in ICE Detentions Amid Expanding Crackdown and Condition Concerns

ICE arrested roughly 51,000 people in July 2026, the highest single-month total in the agency’s history and the second consecutive record-breaking month after June’s approximately 43,000 arrests, averaging about 1,645 arrests per day. The agency booked in more than 46,000 people into detention last month, averaging 1,500 new detainees daily, and by early August was holding about 68,000 people in custody, nearing the record of more than 70,000 set in January. The surge follows a significant dip earlier this year after federal agents killed two American citizens during an enforcement operation in Minneapolis, and it has been driven in part by expanded activity at airports and traffic stops, along with the deployment of newly hired agents nationwide.

The widening crackdown has coincided with mounting scrutiny of detention conditions. In New Jersey, a 41-year-old Salvadoran man, Edwin Lopez-Cornejo, died August 1 at the privately run Delaney Hall facility in Newark after what Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) described as a medical emergency. His family said he had gone without medication for chronic conditions including diabetes and epilepsy in the weeks before his death. His death is at least the 22nd fatality in ICE custody so far this year and the second confirmed death at Delaney Hall since it opened last year, and it came as a member of Congress separately disclosed a third, unreported death at the facility in late July involving a man who had a seizure shortly after being processed. To keep pace with the expanded detention population, DHS has pursued a strategy of acquiring existing private prisons rather than building new facilities, including a $1.5 billion purchase of two former contractor-run sites in California, with contract language asserting that state and local licensing, inspection, and oversight laws do not apply to facilities the government acquires.

Military Spouses Face Detention and Deportation

An investigation released on August 5 found that the Trump administration has detained more than 50 parents and spouses of active-duty U.S. troops. Notably, of those detained, six have been deported and eight remain in federal immigration custody. According to an April 2025 memorandum from the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), “U.S. military service alone does not automatically grant lawful immigration status, or exempt aliens from the consequences of violating U.S. immigration laws.” In a letter to Senator Elizabeth Warren (D-MA), DHS further confirmed that “a total of 282 aliens comprised of both former members of the U.S. Armed Forces and their immediate family members were placed in removal proceedings” between January 2025 and January 2026.

At the same time, however, the military continues to advertise its Parole in Place (PIP) benefits to attract enlistments. Under the program, DHS may grant parole on a case-by-case basis to certain military family members. However, some family members of active-duty service members have been detained despite having pending PIP applications, while others have been arrested during appointments to adjust their legal status.

Importantly, these detentions have had consequences beyond immigration enforcement. According to the investigation, some service members have been forced to delay deployments or alter military responsibilities in order to care for their children while their spouses remain in detention.

Legal

Mass Deportation Hearings Push Immigration Courts into Breakneck Pace

Immigration courts nationwide have increasingly been utilizing “mega master” calendar hearings that pack dozens or even more than 100 cases before a single judge on the same day, with more than 1,300 such hearings held in June 2026 alone. Courts have simultaneously slashed the lead time immigrants receive to prepare for hearings, from roughly six months down to about a month in many cases, contributing to a doubling of the national no-show rate, from about 20% at the start of the administration to 40% by June. The compressed schedules and shrinking notice periods have driven a sharp rise in deportation orders: monthly removal orders climbed from about 33,000 in January 2025 to roughly 79,000 in June 2026.

In Chicago, in-absentia removal orders jumped nearly fivefold in four months, from 1,267 in February to 6,012 in June, with the city’s completed cases resulting in in-absentia orders at a rate of 78.5%, among the highest in the country. Attorneys and advocates describe the practice as functioning like a “deportation machine,” warning that packed dockets, last-minute schedule changes, and judges spending an average of five minutes or less per case leave many immigrants unable to learn of hearings in time or to present their claims at all.

The Justice Department has defended the approach, saying courts are prepared to handle larger calendars and that removal orders are issued only after judges confirm proper notice was given, while the Executive Office for Immigration Review (EOIR) says it is making scheduling adjustments and hiring more judges. Even so, the national court backlog remains immense, with more than 3.4 million pending cases as of late July, underscoring the scale of the challenge the accelerated hearings are meant to address.

Federal Judge Blocks New York’s Ban on ICE Agents Wearing Masks

\A federal judge issued a preliminary injunction on August 3 blocking New York’s state law that prohibited immigration agents from wearing masks and required them to display identification while on duty, siding with the Justice Department’s argument that the state provisions unconstitutionally regulate federal officers. The judge, based in the Northern District of New York, found that the state’s face-covering and identification requirements likely violate the Constitution’s Supremacy Clause, writing that “settled law establishes that federal, not state, authorities make the policies that animate the enforcement of federal immigration laws”. The ruling acknowledged the state’s underlying concerns, noting that masked, unidentified officers “may” create dangerous situations the law sought to address, but concluded that resolving the constitutional question was the court’s task. The decision followed similar rulings against comparable mask restrictions in California, Virginia, and Pennsylvania.

In the same ruling, the judge declined to block a separate, narrower provision of New York’s law banning formal 287(g) cooperation agreements between local police departments and ICE, finding the state has legitimate authority to control how its own law enforcement resources are deployed. Governor Kathy Hochul and Attorney General Letitia James called the mixed ruling a partial win, saying they still believe masked agents do not make New York safer and are reviewing further legal options, while the broader 287(g) ban is set to take effect August 25.

State and Local

26-Employee Texas Firm Wins Major Federal Contract to Represent Migrant Children in Immigration Court

The Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) is awarding a $150 million, one-year contract to a 26-employee Houston firm to provide legal orientation, consultation, and attorney-of-record representation for unaccompanied migrant children during immigration proceedings while they remain in Office of Refugee Resettlement (ORR) custody. The firm’s stated practice areas center on administrative law, white-collar defense, commercial litigation, and securities matters, and its founder, Marcella Burke, is a former Trump appointee at the EPA and Interior Department. The agreement, set to run through August 14, 2027, replaces the prior arrangement with the Acacia Center for Justice, a network of nonprofit legal aid groups whose contract the administration allowed to expire after months of withholding funding.

The federal government has been required to help facilitate legal counsel for unaccompanied children in ORR custody since 2008. Immigrant legal aid groups have raised alarm that the new contract covers only the roughly 1,800 children currently held in government shelters, leaving no clear legal services arrangement for the nearly 22,000 unaccompanied children living with sponsors outside the shelter system. Advocates also warned that the transition creates a coverage gap, since the previous contract lapsed before the new agreement takes effect on August 15, and that children could be left without adequate representation as the administration accelerates deportation efforts.

BILLS INTRODUCED AND CONSIDERED

H.R. 10040

No TSA Data for ICE Act

The bill would amend the Homeland Security Act of 2002 to prohibit the Secretary of Homeland Security from accessing or utilizing certain information to carry out certain functions of U.S. Customs and Border Protection or U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement and from carrying out certain actions regarding Trusted Traveler programs

Sponsored by Rep. Rashida Tlaib (D-Michigan) (25 cosponsors)

08/03/2026 Introduced by Rep. Tlaib

08/03/2026 Referred to the Committee on Homeland Security, and in addition to the Committees on the Judiciary, and Ways and Means

LEGISLATIVE FLOOR CALENDAR

The U.S. House will return from recess on August 31. The U.S. Senate is scheduled to be in recess from August 7 through September 14.

text:
The new orders, titled “Continuing to Protect the Meaning and Value of American Citizenship” and “Ending Birth Tourism,” focus on birth tourism and other categories of foreign nationals that the administration argues should not confer citizenship benefits on children born in the United States.

Focus on Birth Tourism

One of the executive orders directs federal agencies to address so-called birth tourism, a practice in which foreign nationals travel to the United States primarily to give birth so their child acquires U.S. citizenship.

According to statements from the White House, the administration contends that individuals who enter the United States solely for this purpose should not be able to obtain citizenship benefits for their children through that process.

The administration has also indicated that visa-related screening and enforcement measures may be used to identify individuals suspected of traveling to the United States primarily for childbirth-related immigration benefits.

Additional Categories Targeted

The executive actions also address children born in the United States to individuals the administration characterizes as:

Foreign terrorists;

Foreign agents;

Alien enemies; or

Individuals whose presence is otherwise viewed as inconsistent with national security interests.

Administration officials argue that these categories fall outside the historical scope and intent of the Fourteenth Amendment’s Citizenship Clause.

Second Attempt Following Supreme Court Setback

The new directives follow the administration’s unsuccessful attempt earlier in President Trump’s second term to broadly restrict birthright citizenship through executive action.

That earlier initiative sought to limit automatic citizenship to children born in the United States with at least one U.S. citizen or lawful permanent resident parent. The effort became the subject of extensive litigation and ultimately faced significant legal obstacles, including a Supreme Court ruling that prevented implementation of the broader policy.

Following that decision, President Trump publicly stated that the administration would pursue alternative legal avenues to address birthright citizenship and birth tourism.

Expected Legal Challenges

The newly signed executive orders are widely expected to face immediate court challenges.

Critics argue that the measures conflict with the Fourteenth Amendment of the U.S. Constitution, which provides that virtually all persons born in the United States and subject to its jurisdiction are U.S. citizens at birth.

Supporters of the administration’s approach maintain that the Constitution was never intended to grant automatic citizenship in situations involving birth tourism or individuals lacking a sufficient connection to the United States.

Immigration attorneys and constitutional scholars expect courts to closely examine whether the executive branch has authority to alter the practical application of birthright citizenship without congressional action or constitutional amendment.

Erickson Insights and Analysis

The litigation remains ongoing, and additional rulings are expected. Erickson Immigration Group will continue monitoring developments and sharing updates as more news is available. text:
New Law Provides the Strongest Protections in the Nation Against Unlwaful Tactics of ICE

Source: mass.gov

On August 5, 2026, Governor Maura Healey stood with immigrants, advocates, community leaders, law enforcement, teachers, nurses, doctors, clergy and elected officials at La Colaborativa in Chelsea to sign the PROTECT Act, landmark legislation that provides the strongest protections in the nation against the dangerous and illegal tactics of President Donald Trump and ICE. The bill keeps ICE out of courthouses, schools, child care centers, hospitals, and health care facilities, while also providing stronger protections for parents if they are detained or deported, banning new 287(g) agreements, and allowing civil rights claims to be made against government officials, including ICE agents.

“Today, Massachusetts is standing up for what’s right and taking action to keep our people and our communities safe,” said Governor Healey. “The PROTECT Act is the strongest law in the country to protect people from ICE, because no one should be afraid to send their child to school, seek medical care or fear reporting a crime or appearing in court. It makes us all less safe. So we are getting ICE out of our courthouses, schools and hospitals. This bill is a testament to the hard work and advocacy of so many people across our state. We’re going to keep working together to make Massachusetts and this country the place we all want it to be.”

“This bill is about standing up for our immigrant communities, standing up for public safety, education and health care, and standing up for people’s rights and freedoms,” said Lieutenant Governor Kim Driscoll. “We’re grateful to our legislative partners and the many advocates who worked alongside us to strengthen public safety, protect families and reinforce trust between our communities and law enforcement.”

The PROTECT Act includes several key provisions proposed by Governor Healey earlier this year, including prohibiting warrantless immigrant arrests at courthouses, schools, child care centers, and health care facilities, including hospitals, community health centers, and nursing homes. It allows parents to pre-arrange guardianship for their children in case they are detained or deported. It also codifies the Governor’s Executive Order by limiting civil immigration enforcement in nonpublic areas of state buildings, requiring multilingual guidance on immigration enforcement procedures and individual rights, and prohibiting any new 287(g) agreements with state agencies.

This legislation is a crucial piece of the Healey-Driscoll Administration’s overall strategy to protect Massachusetts communities and stand up to the harm caused by President Trump and ICE. When Governor Healey first filed her legislation, she also signed an Executive Order prohibiting the state from entering into any new 287(g) agreements unless there is a public safety need, prohibiting ICE from making civil arrests in non-public areas of state facilities, and prohibiting the use of state property for immigration enforcement staging. She also issued statewide guidance for schools, child care providers, higher education campuses, health care facilities and places of worship regarding interactions with ICE agents.

Bill Praised by Civic Leaders Across the Commonwealth

Governor Healey also launched an online portal with Attorney General Campbell that allows Massachusetts residents to report alleged misconduct by ICE, opposed ICE flights at Hanscom Airport, called for an extension of Temporary Protected Status for Haitians and other immigrants, and opposed new ICE Detention Centers in New England. The Healey-Driscoll Administration has also connected thousands of immigrants with legal services and provided robust multilingual resources for communities and employers.

“Strong public safety requires strong partnerships with the communities we serve,” said Public Safety and Security Secretary Gina Kwon. “The PROTECT Act helps preserve the trust that law enforcement, prosecutors and community organizations rely on to protect victims, investigate crimes and keep neighborhoods safe. When people feel safe, our Commonwealth is stronger.”

“As a superintendent and teacher, I’ve seen how deeply a child’s sense of safety and belonging shapes their ability to learn,” said Education Secretary Steve Zrike. “The PROTECT Act helps ensure that early education programs and K-12 schools remain welcoming places where every child can feel safe, build confidence, and thrive. That sense of belonging is essential to educational opportunity and to the strength of our communities.”

“In my work as a clinician, I’ve seen firsthand how important it is to maintain a safe, healing environment in our hospitals,” said Health and Human Services Secretary Kiame Mahaniah, MD, MBA. “Keeping ICE out of hospitals, as well as our courthouses and schools means we also keep fear out of these places. I am grateful to Governor Healey for her continued leadership protecting our immigrant communities from the cruel acts of the Trump Administration.”

The bill also defines state and local cooperation with federal immigration enforcement while expanding legal protections and due process for immigrants. It creates a new state law civil rights claim for government officials, including ICE agents, who violate someone’s federal constitutional rights. It also establishes new oversight, reporting, and notification requirements for correctional facilities, employers, and state agencies and strengthens protections for crime victims seeking immigration relief.

“With the Governor’s signature today, Massachusetts residents will have the strongest protections from President Trump’s weaponization of federal immigration authorities in the nation,” said Senate President Karen E. Spilka (D-Ashland). “The abuses and infringements on constitutional rights we have seen in this country are reprehensible and un-American. This law is the culmination of our efforts to do everything in our state’s power to protect hardworking residents who have done nothing wrong and who contribute to the vibrancy of this state. I applaud Senator Friedman and Senator Payano for their work to reach this strong agreement, and I applaud the Governor’s signature on this bill.”

“Since the beginning of President Trump’s second term, ICE and Border Patrol agents have continued to harass and disappear innocent Americans with total impunity—a reckless approach that has led to the deaths of American citizens and legal residents, and to children being separated from their families. Those actions have immigrants in Massachusetts living in fear as they go to work or bring their children to school, and they jeopardize the trust that local law enforcement has worked hard to build,” said House Speaker Ronald J. Mariano (D-Quincy). “That’s why this legislation is so important, as it takes steps to ensure that all residents in Massachusetts are treated equally under state law, and to protect our communities through practical, thoughtful measures. I want to thank Governor Healey for signing these protections into law, as well as Chairman Cahill, Chairman Vargas, and the Black and Latino Legislative Caucus for working tirelessly to incorporate feedback from immigrant communities and law enforcement alike. Finally, I’m grateful to all my colleagues in the House, and to our partners in the Senate, for voting in favor of these critical reforms.”

“The PROTECT Act strengthens protections for our residents in the face of the aggressive tactics employed by ICE – tactics that do not enhance public safety and instead spread fear among families and our communities,” said Attorney General Andrea Joy Campbell. “I am grateful to Governor Healey and the Legislature for enacting these critical protections into law. Immigrants are an essential part of our communities, workplaces, and economy, and we will continue to use every tool available to defend their rights.”

“Today marks a historic victory for our Commonwealth. The PROTECT Act becoming law solidifies a commitment to protecting immigrant communities, ensuring due process, and upholding fundamental civil rights. The crucial safeguards the PROTECT law provides by establishing legal accountability for federal overreach and ensuring local police do not act as immigration agents will keep our neighborhoods safe. Our schools, courthouses, and hospitals will once again become places of safety and trust. We are incredibly grateful to Governor Healey, Senate President Spilka and House Speaker Mariano, as well as all legislators and the countless advocates who fought tirelessly to deliver these vital protections for all our immigrant neighbors,” said Liz Sweet, Executive Director, MIRA Coalition and Protect Massachusetts Coalition Co-Chair

Matt Bach, President, Massachusetts Teachers Association said, “The MTA proudly celebrates the signing of the PROTECT Act into law, a significant achievement made possible by the dedicated efforts of organizers, lawmakers, educators, families, and supporters across Massachusetts. While this milestone is important, our work is far from finished. We remain committed to ensuring that our immigrant students and their families feel safe and supported in our communities and public schools. Educators must have all of their students present and secure in class, ready to engage in the learning process. We look forward to collaborating with our partner organizations to continue Massachusetts’ leadership in protecting and empowering immigrant students.”

Carol Rose, Executive Director, The ACLU of Massachusetts said, “Massachusetts has sent a powerful message to the Trump administration: We will not stand idly by while ICE agents tear apart families and shatter our communities. The PROTECT Act will help to establish a firewall between Massachusetts law enforcement and federal immigration officials, ensuring that local police are not co-opted by President Trump’s cruel political agenda. Importantly, the law will also support access to courts for everyone and bolster trust in local institutions. We applaud Governor Healey, Senate President Spilka, House Speaker Mariano, and the Black and Latino Legislative Caucus, among others, for their steadfast leadership and dedication. And we are deeply grateful to the many immigrant advocates who worked for years to make this day a reality.”
