title: AP Report: Trump's immigration crackdown has detained more than 50 military spouses and parents
authors: Jack Brook, Associated Press, Safiyah Riddle, Aaron Kessler
description:
It's left military members without emotional support and caretakers for their children, delayed deployments and forced some to take leave.
"U.S. military service alone does not automatically grant lawful immigration status, or exempt aliens from the consequences of violating U.S. immigration laws."
Military members have had to take leave or delay a deployment Some service members have been left caring for children alone.
Experts in military immigration law said this marks a stark shift from previous administrations across the political spectrum, including Trump's first administration.
Benefits for service members include what's known as parole-in-place Military recruiters tout immigration benefits for troops' families as a selling point to enlist.
text:
Parents and spouses of people in the military have generally been shielded from deportation under bipartisan consensus for decades. But the AP found they're now routinely being detained for months as they try to adjust their legal status through the policies available to service members' close relatives and even as the military continues to recruit by advertising immigration benefits for enlistees' families. Experts warn that the reversal could undermine military preparedness even as the U.S. is at war in Iran. It's left military members without emotional support and caretakers for their children, delayed deployments and forced some to take leave.

"How can I even focus on my military career because I have to worry about how my wife is doing?" said Army Sgt. Hedar Leonel Turcios Juarez, who was stationed in Fort Bliss, Texas, when his wife was detained outside a Walmart in front of their 6-year-old daughter in July.

A handful of detentions of service members' spouses have prompted public backlash and led to intervention by Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin to secure their release.

READ MORE: A new ICE facility could speed up deportations for families and kids

The Department of Homeland Security has said it does not compile data on these cases. The AP obtained information by analyzing thousands of federal court records compiled by Habeas Dockets, a project run by the Immigration Justice Transparency Initiative; by reviewing existing media coverage; and by verifying information with family members and attorneys. The actual number is likely much higher than the 52 cases AP found.

The AP asked for comment from DHS on each case, including the individuals' immigration and criminal history. The agency did not provide specific information about the majority of cases but noted that at least seven people had been removed from the U.S. before, at least eight had removal orders and at least two had drunken-driving or drug-related convictions.

"DHS and ICE value the contributions of all those who have served in the U.S. military," DHS said in a statement. "U.S. military service alone does not automatically grant lawful immigration status, or exempt aliens from the consequences of violating U.S. immigration laws."

The Pentagon declined to comment on the AP's findings.

Service members are losing their safety net

Air Force Tech. Sgt. Wendy Gbeve, 30, said she hasn't had a good night's sleep since her father, Luis Alberto Ramirez Zavala, was detained by immigration officials last month. Gbeve was there when he was arrested at a routine interview with U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services in Missouri about his pending application for legal status.

She spent hours refreshing the USCIS page to track where the government was taking her father: from a county jail in Missouri to an Immigration and Customs Enforcement detention facility in Texas. Finally, roughly two weeks after he was detained, she found out he had been deported to his native Mexico.

"It's the most frustrating, helpless feeling," Gbeve said.

Gbeve said ICE still hasn't informed her family why her father was removed so quickly. Ramirez Zavala spent most of his life in the U.S. working as a ranch hand in rural Illinois.

Ramirez Zavala's wife of 30 years, a legal permanent resident, is considering returning to Mexico to be with her husband. For Gbeve, whose husband is also in the Air Force, that would leave no one to watch their children, ages 2 and 4, if both were deployed.

"That would be our entire safety net," she said.

Military members have had to take leave or delay a deployment

Some service members have been left caring for children alone.

Army Staff Sgt. Alexis Jaramillo, an aviation operations specialist who has served for more than a decade, said he would normally be involved in training soldiers at Fort Polk, Louisiana. Instead, he is on administrative leave, caring for his 5-year-old stepson, Noah, after his Brazilian wife, Maisa Lopes Eliaser, was detained in early July.

It happened during what the family thought was a routine appointment at a USCIS office in Alabama. Eliaser arrived in the U.S. on a tourist visa in 2019, and the couple was trying to change her status.

WATCH: 'Deportation trap': Immigration agents arresting migrants at mandatory court check-ins

Immigration officials asked Jaramillo and his stepson to leave the room. Minutes later, they were told that Eliaser had been detained. The next time they saw her was inside a detention facility.

"It is really overwhelming because I need to take care of my kid by myself. No one is here to help me out," Jaramillo said.

At least one active-duty soldier halted her imminent deployment after her husband was detained by immigration officers, leaving no one to care for their then-5-year-old son, court records show. A judge eventually ordered the husband released.

Trump's policy is a reversal even from his first administration

A new policy, implemented in April 2025, states that "military service alone does not exempt aliens from the consequences of violating U.S. immigration laws."

Experts in military immigration law said this marks a stark shift from previous administrations across the political spectrum, including Trump's first administration.

Dan Gividen, who served as ICE's deputy chief counsel from 2016 to 2019 under Trump, represents a soldier's father who has been in ICE custody for more than eight months. He said that during his time as an ICE prosecutor, immigration authorities rarely detained service members' immediate family members unless they had committed violent crimes.

"We would not place them into removal proceedings, period. That's insane," Gividen said. "The fact that they're doing it now is just outrageous."

ICE previously generally canceled past removal orders and allowed parents or spouses of troops to adjust their legal status, said Margaret Stock, an immigration attorney and retired lieutenant colonel in the Army Reserve. She said that's because the government wanted to ensure troops focused on their duties.

WATCH: Fired immigration judge gives inside look at Trump's deportation agenda

"It's the same thing that happens if you don't provide healthcare to the troops, or you don't provide housing to the troops," she said. If soldiers are preoccupied with detained or deported family, "they're not concentrating on their job anymore."

Even some congressional Republicans who are otherwise largely supportive of Trump's aggressive immigration crackdown have pushed for the release of service members' relatives.

"The immigration system is failing the honorable and good Americans," Florida Republican Rep. Maria Elvira Salazar said at a news conference in July advocating for the release of the wife of retired Staff Sgt. Wilmer Trujillo, who served in Iraq and Afghanistan. DHS said she illegally reentered the U.S. after being deported in 2005. Her attorney says they are seeking to rescind the removal order because she was not provided proper notice of the hearing that led to it.

Although DHS said it does not have data on active-duty troops, it has released figures for former service members, who also qualify for immigration benefits along with their immediate families. From Jan. 20, 2025, through Jan. 26, 2026, immigration authorities detained 125 military veterans — placing 34 into removal proceedings — and arrested more than 150 immediate family members, DHS said in a letter to several Democratic senators.

Anh Dung Cong Tran, known as "Tony," had both a father and son who served in the military. Tran came to the U.S. in 1990 through a program for children of American military personnel born in Vietnam. Tran, 56, was deported in July, having lived in the U.S. for decades with regular check-ins with immigration authorities after an assault conviction soon after his arrival.

His son Antonio Tran said his father persuaded him to enlist in the military in 2022. "He has a totally different view on America now," said Tran, who was discharged as an Army specialist in March after a serious injury.

"Whatever your family have done for this country, to keep this country safe, to give the people, Americans, the freedom to walk around and to sleep safe at night, well, we don't care about that," Tony Tran told the AP in a video call from Vietnam.

Benefits for service members include what's known as parole-in-place

Military recruiters tout immigration benefits for troops' families as a selling point to enlist.

One of the military's most highly advertised immigration benefits is "military parole-in-place," which allows the spouses, children and parents of active-duty service members and veterans to obtain legal immigration status from within the country. Not everyone qualifies: Those who overstayed visas or who already applied for legal status at the border, for example.

The policy was implemented under Republican President George W. Bush during the U.S. war with Iraq in 2007 and codified under Democratic President Barack Obama. DHS agencies can grant it on a case-by-case basis.

READ MORE: Federal appeals court allows Trump to resume expanded use of speedy deportations

Under Trump, the average time it takes to receive military parole-in-place has more than doubled to 12 months, according to USCIS data. That leaves military families more vulnerable to being placed in ICE custody.

Recruiters are still promoting immigration benefits

The AP found that troops' immediate family members have repeatedly been detained by ICE while applying for parole-in-place or seeking to adjust their status, including during immigration appointments.

Marine Cpl. Jose Manuel Vilchis-Valle's mother, Ursula Borja Valle, was detained at an appointment in August 2025 and deported to Mexico within a week. She had lived in the U.S. since the 1990s without a known criminal record. Her son was attempting to help her clear up a decades-old removal order through the immigration benefits that military recruiters had used to help persuade him to enlist.

"They basically told me that if you serve, and if you served honorably, you can help your parents," said Vilchis-Valle, 23, who was honorably discharged shortly after his mother was deported. "In a perfect world, I wished, because of my service, they could have pardoned her."

In other cases, ICE has detained people who had already been granted protection, with the agency later arguing in court filings that their parole status had been revoked.

In June 2025, the Marine Corps officially stopped advertising enlistment as a way to protect immigrant family members, in response to inquiries from the AP. But recruiters for the Army and the National Guard still promote it.

"For some service members, enlisting isn't just about serving their country," read an Instagram post published in late July by an official Army recruiter based in California. "It's also about doing everything they can to help protect their parents who sacrificed everything for them."

Recruiters are expected to highlight the benefits of service to attract applicants and military parole-in-place remains in effect, Army spokesperson Christopher Surridge said.

The National Guard said it does not track detentions of its troops' relatives or which recruiters advertise immigration benefits and referred additional comment to DHS.

A soldier who helped patrol the border grapples with his father's detention

For U.S. Army Specialist Romero Ralios, his father's detention has left him remorseful about his deployment last year to the Joint Task Force Southern Border, where he spent nine months supporting U.S. Customs and Border Patrol.

His father, Sebastian Ralios Tino, a Guatemalan landscaper with no known criminal record, was detained this summer. He lived in the U.S. for nearly two decades without legal status.

READ MORE: Migrants face dire conditions and prolonged waits in U.S. detention centers

Ralios' commanding officer, Capt. Mohamed Elmaola, told the AP he wanted to speak up because Ralios is a "phenomenal soldier" whose father should receive due process.

"It's very hard to communicate and to have credibility as a leader when your own subordinates are unable to get support," Elmaola said. "Considering he enlisted his time and his life into supporting and defending the United States Constitution, it is the right thing to do to support soldiers and their families."

Romero Ralios struggles to sleep at night due to the stress and wishes he had not been involved in immigration enforcement, even though he was just following orders.

"It was karma. I should've known," Ralios told the AP. "All those families I broke. I have regrets."

text:
Published on: August 5, 2026

Over 100 advocates, elected officials, and faith leaders demand the court to uphold the Dignity Not Detention Act, in place since 2022

BALTIMORE, MD – In a powerful show of unity and resistance, community leaders, immigrant rights advocates, faith leaders, and elected officials rallied this morning outside the Edward A. Garmatz United States District Courthouse for Genesis GSA Strategic One, LLC v. Howard County. The coalition, including We Are CASA, gathered to oppose the proposed ICE detention facility in Elkridge and to call on the federal court to uphold the Dignity Not Detention Act, which ends private ICE detention in Maryland. At the hearing, the County argued that the permit was invalid from the outset. The State argued that this law, regarding permits, is constitutional as it covers private actors within the state.

The proposed Elkridge center would replace ICE’s Baltimore Field Office, notorious for human rights abuses and overcrowding, with an even larger operations hub furnished with immigrant detention. The center would be further removed from public oversight, increasing enforcement activities in an area with a significant immigration population.

“I love Elkridge because it’s a very safe place. Here, I’ve experienced a beautiful sense of calm and tranquility. I go out with my friends, and we take our children to the park to play. Now that there’s been a lot of ICE activity, we’re afraid to even go out to buy groceries,” shared We Are CASA member Consuelo. “If ICE opens a detention center in Elkridge, they will never leave us alone. We won’t have any freedom left. We won’t be able to go out and play with our kids anymore. That’s why we’re fighting to preserve our beautiful community, where we work, contribute, and raise our families.”

“Since last year, ICE has taken my nephew and the father of my children. And then, in May, they took my brother. Since then, he has been moved from one detention center to another across different states. When they transfer him between detention centers, they leave in the middle of the night. They move them from plane to plane, shackled at the feet, hands, and waist,” lamented We Are CASA member Beatriz. “Sometimes they don’t reach their destination for five days. They are dropped off at places to sleep where they cover themselves with aluminum foil. They aren’t allowed to bathe or brush their teeth. Their only food is a bag with bread and a slice of yellow cheese. My brother often wakes up in the middle of the night hungry. All my brother wants is to return to Honduras. But instead of letting him leave, they are torturing him.”

Genesis GSA Strategic One, LLC, the company that owns the building and entered a contract with the federal government to build the detention center, filed this lawsuit against Howard County after the County revoked its building permit and passed emergency legislation banning privately owned detention centers. In addition to the parties in the lawsuit, the Maryland Office of the Attorney General provided arguments about why the state’s law on private detention centers should apply in this situation.

“In the last year and a half, we have seen 100,000 children separated from their parents. For the last week, we have seen about 10,000 people detained. Detentions are constantly ramping up. So we must stay vigilant and that is why we are here today at the courthouse,” said Maryland State Delegate (D-13) Gabriel Moreno. “This is not just a technical dispute or a paperwork fight. This is about transparency, accountability, and human dignity.”

The rally and hearing mark a pivotal moment in the ongoing fight against immigration detention in Maryland. Advocates argue that the Elkridge facility would exacerbate the already dire conditions faced by detainees, citing reports of overcrowding and medical neglect at the current Baltimore field office. The coalition of immigrant rights advocates called on the court to side with Howard County and reaffirm the rights of local communities to determine their own safety and well-being.

Howard County is a proudly diverse area that is committed to inclusiveness, equality, and fairness for all. Almost one in four county residents is foreign-born; students in schools come from 147 countries and speak 187 languages. Howard County passed the Liberty Act in 2020, which bans county employees from collaborating with ICE and protects immigrants from discrimination. An ICE detention center in the county would violate community members’ most deeply held principles and values.

The proposed detention center is within a one mile radius of the following community destinations: Deep Run Elementary School, Mayfield Woods Middle School, Waterloo Park, Troy Park, Timbers at Troy Golf Course, Gateway Overlook Shopping Center, Ascension Saint Agnes Primary Care Elkridge, Tarbiyah Academy, and Howard County Government Bureau of Highways’ Mayfield Shop.

Published on: August 5, 2026

Hundreds Gather at Supreme Court to Defend Temporary Protected Status and Demand Lasting Protections for Immigrant Families

WASHINGTON, D.C. — Today, over one hundred immigrant community members, a powerful coalition of national immigrant rights organizations, labor unions, faith leaders, and federal lawmakers gathered on the steps of the U.S. Supreme Court in response to the Supreme Court’s 6-3 ruling in Mullin v. Doe, which allows the Trump administration to strip Temporary Protected Status (TPS) from hundreds of thousands of Haitian and Syrian nationals fleeing war, natural disasters or other catastrophes.

Convened by We Are CASA, Haitian Bridge Alliance, the National TPS Alliance, Alianza Americas, SEIU 32BJ, Service Employees International Union (SEIU), CUSP, Popular Democracy, Fair Immigration Reform Movement (FIRM), MomsRising, FWD.us, the National Domestic Workers Alliance, and other national partners, the rally and press conference brought together directly impacted individuals, families and allies from across the country to speak out against a decision that also threatens the stability of families from other countries with TPS designations, including Cameroon, Venezuela, Sudan, Afghanistan, and El Salvador, among others.

The event featured remarks from directly impacted TPS holders that have built lives, raised families and contributed to communities nationwide for decades, community leaders, labor advocates, faith leaders, and lawmakers, including Senator Chris Van Hollen (D-Md) and Representatives Ayanna Pressley (MA-07), Pramila Jayapal (WA-07), Joaquin Castro (TX-20), and Yvette Clarke (NY-09), among others.

“If we allow this court, this country, and this government to take away the immigration status of TPS holders, then we lose everything,” said Guerline Jozef, executive director of the Haitian Bridge Alliance. “Family separation, deportation, loss of income, degrading workforce and their investment into our lives: all of this is just thrown away. This is unfair on so many different levels.”

“This is not the first time we have been here. I have been in the halls of Congress and in front of the Supreme Court before. This is not over. We are here together because we are going to fight harder than ever before to pass permanent protection,” said Claudia, member of the National TPS Alliance and TPS holder from El Salvador. A daughter of a single mother, she holds a masters in fine arts and creative writing working in the nonprofit industry.

“Today’s ruling does not erase our dignity,” said Amos, We Are CASA member and TPS holder from Cameroon. “Families who built their lives here, who work, who pay taxes, and raise children here are now being told their protection may no longer exist. But nothing about the conditions that forced people to flee has disappeared. We may have lost in the courts, but we have not lost our voice. We are not disappearing. We are not silent. And we are not giving up on each other.”

“For many of us, this ruling is not just about policy. It is about our homes, our families, and our futures,” said Solange, We Are CASA member from Cameroon. “TPS holders are nurses, workers supporting our economy, and parents raising American children. We are home, and we belong here. This is not the end. We will keep fighting.”

“We have to remind people who these members of our communities are. They are part of the fabric of their communities, contributing every day, raised in wonderful families, and they are here legally,” said Senator Chris Van Hollen. “We do need a permanent solution. That’s why I have introduced the SECURE Act, which provides TPS holders a pathway first to permanent residency and then citizenship.”

“In the midst of the World Cup, right off the Haitian team’s match, we witnessed this Supreme Court decision. Today is a devastating comma in our fight, not a finite period. But the fight to maintain the safety and integrity of the families of TPS holders in this country is not over,” said Rep. Ayana Pressley, Co-Chair of the House Haiti Caucus.

“We need to pass a permanent protection for immigrant families,” said Rep. Pramila Jayapal, Ranking Member of the Immigration Integrity, Security, and Enforcement Subcommittee. “This was an immoral and unjust decision from this MAGA-right Supreme Court. They have put at risk the 330,000 Haitians with TPS, 66000 Syrians with TPS, and 1.3 million TPS holders who are in our communities.”

text:
The federal government is interested in acquiring 249 parking spots in Boston immigration enforcement agents. Local officials are already lining up against the move.

The search for adjoining Boston spots is part of a larger "Sources Sought Notice" posted on a federal General Services Administration website. The document lists parking sought in more than a dozen cities across the country.

"The U.S. Department of Homeland Security, Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), is conducting market research to identify sources capable of providing surface and/or structured vehicle parking spaces in the vicinity of existing or planned ICE facilities in the locations identified in the Schedule below," the notice reads.

The federal interest in a big parking space was first reported by The Boston Globe.

Gov. Maura Healey issued a statement opposing the parking inquiry, saying ICE has engaged in illegal tactics.

"We see what ICE is doing to our communities every day. People are afraid to go to school, doctors' appointments, court or even church," she said. "ICE is shooting people dead, separating families, and making us all less safe. That’s why I’m about to sign the strongest protections in the country against their abuses."

The newfound federal interest in Boston parking comes as Massachusetts enacts new regulations limiting where ICE and other agencies can conduct raids and other immigration enforcement efforts in the state. Healey signed the PROTECT Act into law Wednesday morning during an event in Chelsea. The act also codified a Supreme Judicial Court ruling that limits state and local involvement in civil immigration enforcement by federal officials.

Speaking with reporters Wednesday, Boston Mayor Michelle Wu said she had not heard of any ICE expansion in Boston outside of published reports about the parking inquiry. She said she remains opposed to increased ICE presence in the city.

"We have signed executive orders at the local level, and I joined seven other mayors or city leaders in the metro area all declaring that ICE should not be able to stage on public property, on city property, or to use public buildings," she said. "When it is private property, we will have to look into our, our full legislative and legal options."

Once potential parking is identified, the feds will consider whether to continue the process of leasing the spots. The notice said leasing would be for a minimum of three years.

There are no identified ICE facilities within the city of Boston. The federal government does operate an immigration court on New Sudbury Street and a Homeland Security Investigations office on Causeway Street.

text:
In April, House Passed Pressley-Led Measure to Extend TPS for Haiti that Awaits Action in the Senate

Over 350,000 Haitian Nationals at Risk of Job Loss and Deportation

BOSTON – Today, Congresswoman Ayanna Pressley (MA-07) issued a statement in vigorous support of Temporary Protected Status (TPS) holders and the families impacted by Trump’s cruel termination of TPS for Haiti and Syria.

“The termination of Temporary Protected Status for our Haitian and Syrian neighbors will devastate our communities, bulldoze our economy, traumatize our children, and separate families who call this country home. The occupant of the Oval Office has decided he gets to act as judge, jury, and executioner to hundreds of thousands of innocent people who have done nothing but seek refuge, strengthen our communities, and bolster our economy.

“TPS is not only an essential lifeline for those who had to flee countries in crisis, but also for Americans. Businesses will be forced to close from losing their staff and our local economies will suffer. Seniors and their families will lose their caregivers as we face a caregiving crisis. Children will lose their classmates and their friends. America will lose the talent, skills, and culture that our immigrant neighbors contribute every day.

“That’s why the Senate must immediately pass our legislation to save lives and extend TPS for Haiti, which passed out of the House earlier this year.

“To our many TPS holders in the Massachusetts 7th and throughout the country from Haiti, Syria, Venezuela, Honduras, and other nations—your worth is not defined by the cruelty of this White House or Supreme Court. Your humanity, your dignity, and your lives matter. This nation is better because of you, and I will do everything in my power to support you and your families.”

Residents of the 7th Congressional District of Massachusetts can contact Congresswoman Pressley’s office for assistance. Please visit Pressley.House.Gov/TemporaryProtectedStatus for resources and more information.

text:
The Trump administration is set to award a multimillion-dollar contract to a small Texas law firm to provide legal representation for thousands of unaccompanied migrant children in government custody during immigration proceedings.

In a notice published in the Federal Register, the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) announced its intent to award the $150 million contract to Burke Law Group, a law firm headquartered in Houston, Texas.

The notice states the contract would "provide legal orientation, legal consultation, and attorney-of-record representation services for eligible unaccompanied alien children" during immigration proceedings and hearings before U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services while the children remain in government custody.

The proposed award comes after legal service providers across the country have said that the administration has withheld $65 million in overdue fees from the previous contract, alleging it is an attempt to force them to turn over confidential information about the migrant children they represent.

Burke Law Group has 26 employees across eight offices, according to its website. Their practices include administrative law, white-collar defense, commercial litigation, securities litigation and other areas.

One of the founders, Marcella Burkey, was a former Trump appointee to the Environmental Protection Agency and the Department of the Interior. Jeffrey Hall, a former employee and founding partner, was appointed and confirmed to serve in the EPA late last year.

Burke Law Group did not immediately respond to ABC News' request for comment.

In December 2023, the Acacia Center for Justice, an immigrant advocacy group, became the prime contract holder with HHS for the Unaccompanied Children Program, overseeing subcontracts with more than 100 service providers that provide legal representation to more than 20,000 unaccompanied migrant children.

A spokesperson with HHS previously told ABC News that its sub-agency, the Office of Refugee Resettlement (ORR), "offered Acacia the opportunity" to receive a new federal contract "based on requirements that include they provide the data on who they represent and that they bill [HHS] when they submit applications for immigration relief." The HHS spokesperson said Acacia refused.

Legal services providers including Acacia have said that ORR was demanding "client-level data that is confidential and legally privileged."

During the Trump administration, Acacia and many of its subcontracted groups have alleged that unaccompanied children and their sponsors are among those being targeted under the administration's immigration crackdown.

In June, DHS agents visited the offices of several Washington-area nonprofit organizations that provide legal services to unaccompanied migrant children. Last year, ABC News reported that the administration was directing immigration agents to track down unaccompanied migrant children in the United States.

text:
The Trump administration is planning on opening a new facility for migrant families and unaccompanied children next to an airport hub in Alexandria, Louisiana, a strategy intended to speed up deportations.

Unaccompanied children would be moved from foster homes and shelters across the U.S. to the Alexandria facility before they are deported. According to the Associated Press, Immigration and Customs Enforcement called the facility a “staging area” rather than a detention center and said inmates would only stay there a few days at most.

Katie Blankenship, an immigration lawyer and former legal deputy at the American Civil Liberties Union of Florida, said she does not believe in the need for more detention centers. Existing detention centers, she said, are inhumane and unlawfully detaining people.

“We’re fighting for all existing ICE detention centers to be closed,” Blankenship said. “We certainly don’t think any more should be opening up, especially not for mothers and children.”

She said the Trump administration sets up detention centers in Republican-dominated states where it doesn’t expect much pushback or disagreement. This, she said, has led to mass incarceration for people across the country, separating families and causing generational trauma.

Children in the U.S. without relatives are sent to foster care. Being sent to an ICE facility instead, Blankenship said, is “incredibly cruel.”

“Children would be placed in inhospitable conditions in these centers and treated poorly, separated from their parents,” she said. “This would be extremely traumatizing for any child.”

Blankenship said she has received countless reports of detention centers unequipped to provide detainees with dignified conditions. She has seen a denial of blankets and pillows, filthy water, reports of ice-cold food, improper clothing, freezing and boiling indoor temperatures and power cuts, as well as detainees experiencing physical and psychological abuse.

Because of this, she said she doubts another ICE facility will be able to provide children with adequate living resources and instead would cause lasting harm and trauma on detainees.

She doesn’t believe detainees would be at the Alexandria detention center for a short period of time as ICE has stated, she said, because she has seen ICE detention centers unlawfully holding people for months at a time.

“I have little reason to believe it to be a genuinely temporary facility for transitions, and it’s using taxpayer money to build inhumane detention centers that line the pockets of corrupt politicians and private prison companies,” Blankenship said.

The current administration, she said, has already shown a disregard for the well-being and human rights of adult immigrants. She said the proposed Alexandria center demonstrates a disregard for the safety of immigrant children who have no control over their immigrant status, being minors.

“Undocumented immigrant children are one of the most vulnerable demographics on earth,” she said. “This would put immigrant children and mothers in extremely vulnerable situations.”

ICE did not respond to multiple requests for comment.

Rafael Ramírez Solórzano, a UF Latin American Studies professor who researches Latino social movements, politics and immigration history, said he was not surprised by the new proposed ICE facility.

As an immigration policy historian, Solórzano said, he has seen detention centers spring up across the nation, from mega warehouses to partnerships with police departments and private businesses, all with the intention of making money.

The trend didn’t start with the Trump administration, he said; he’s observed it for the past 20 years after the Department of Homeland Security was established in 2002.

“What we’ve been seeing in the last 20-plus years is that we see evidence of inadequate care of detainees, of their healthcare,” Solórzano said. “We have seen failure of transparency, failure of public accountability of deaths.”

He’s concerned about ICE detention centers, he said, because there’s no real accountability or oversight of the centers.

“What we’re really seeing is family members, children being put not only into detentions but being in cages,” he said.

Even if ICE calls it a holding center, he said, it is still a detention center he suspects will demonstrate the same evidence of inadequate care of detainees.

“That is what’s concerning in regards to our human rights being respected within these detention centers,” Solórzano said.

The facility’s effects will start with deportations, he said, separating families from their children. Because of the fast-paced process of the staging center, he said the right to seek legal counsel will likely be violated while in detention.

Solórzano said the decision to establish the center in Louisiana was strategic. Many states in the South with historically conservative-leaning politics, like Louisiana, Texas, Georgia and Florida — some of the states with the highest numbers of detentions and deportations — don’t have protections for migrants like northern states do, he said. Florida, for example, has policies uniting local law enforcement and federal ICE enforcement.

The trend of problematic treatment toward people of color dates back to slavery in America and Jim Crow laws in the South, he said.

Wrangling children and holding them in these centers is “nothing new,” he added — people are just starting to become aware of them and their cruelty in the last few years.

“We’re just seeing history be repeated again,” he said.

When attorney Nadine Brown first heard about the Louisiana center, she said it was concerning and disturbing to see it framed as a staging area.

A staging area implies detainees’ removal is imminent, so they would not have time to present their cases for relief. She suspects the administration anticipates it will be able to hit its quotas for mass deportation without giving people an opportunity to present their cases, she said.

“I don’t know how they’re anticipating the process is supposed to work, or they’re just going to start detaining people … expediting their hearings or denying them any kind of relief without properly adjudicating each applicant,” Brown said.

In a broad sense, she said, the process isn’t legal, but every case is different, and not all immigrants are eligible to apply for relief.

“We also know that this administration is doing things based on their own perspective of how the law should work,” she said.

She said the administration has consistently tested the legal boundaries of equal protection under the law, not treating immigrants equally to U.S. citizens. For the proposed Alexandria center, Brown expects unaccompanied children who have already gone through a traumatizing journey to America may be treated as even less.

“It’s problematic that now you are re-traumatizing children and putting them in a facility where they don’t have adequate supervision or adequate services available to handle … basic hygiene to mental health,” Brown said.

text:
*Emergency protest set for Wednesday, Aug. 5, 10:30 a.m. at hospital*

Nurses at Maine Medical Center (MMC) in Portland, Maine are staging an emergency protest Wednesday, Aug. 5 to demand the immediate release of an RN colleague who is being detained by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) despite the fact that she is legally authorized to live and work in the country while she waits for her asylum case from Zambia to be processed. MMC nurses are represented by Maine State Nurses Association/National Nurses Organizing Committee, an affiliate of National Nurses United.

On July 30, ICE took into custody Debora Kapisha, a medical-surgical registered nurse at MMC while she was traveling through Logan Airport in Boston, Mass. ICE plans to transfer her Wednesday from Massachusetts to Louisiana, where she will be far from her family, legal counsel, and support systems. Her union is coordinating with her attorneys to work for her release and prevent the transfer.

Besides her release, her union nurse coworkers are demanding that their employer, Maine Medical Center, take immediate steps to formally sponsor her for permanent residency.

“Debora is an amazing nurse and takes great care of her patients,” said Abigail Nelson, an MMC RN who has worked alongside Kapisha and considers her a friend. “She is a kind and supportive coworker. We are like a family here and it feels like a piece of us is missing.”

What: Protest demanding that ICE release Debora Kapisha, RN

When: Wednesday, Aug. 5 10:30 ET

Where: Maine Medical Center, Western Promenade near 22 Bramhall St., Portland, Maine

“ICE is imprisoning a nurse who cares for and saves lives every day in our community,” said Cokie Giles, a Maine RN and vice president of NNU. “When ICE kidnaps critical, upstanding, and hardworking members of our community like this, they are broadcasting their real intentions and goal: To kick all Black and brown people out of the country and turn the United States into a fascist, white supremacist society — as well as terrorize all people who fight back. Nurses envision a just society and say, ‘Absolutely not!’”

Since ICE began kidnapping Black and brown people and terrorizing our communities, National Nurses United has called it out as an illegitimate, violent, paramilitary organization that must be promptly abolished. On top of people that immigrant enforcement officers have shot and killed in the streets, such as Johan Sebastián Guerrero, Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, VA RN Alex Pretti, and Renee Good, at least 52 people have died within the immigration detention system during Trump’s second term mainly due to withholding of adequate medical care, according to Human Rights Watch.

Nurses are outraged though not surprised that their employer, MMC, has said it will not help Kapisha. MMC’s owner, MaineHealth, is currently embroiled with its nurses in a fight to end a secretive agreement it has with Palantir, an A.I. company well known for its government contracts helping ICE target people for detention.

Maine State Nurses Association is part of National Nurses Organizing Committee, representing 4,000 nurses and other caregivers from Portland to Fort Kent. NNOC is an affiliate of National Nurses United, the largest and fastest-growing labor union of registered nurses in the United States with nearly 225,000 members nationwide.

text:
Proposed DHS rule would restrict employment authorization while adding needed safeguards

The Federation for American Immigration Reform (FAIR) has submitted a public comment in support of the Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM), Clarification of Discretionary Employment Authorization for Certain Aliens. The rule limits work permits for parolees, aliens granted deferred action, and aliens awaiting deportation on orders of supervision (OSUP) while introducing additional restrictions for criminal aliens that further the Trump administration’s immigration enforcement agenda.

Parole is a narrow legal authority that allows DHS to temporarily allow otherwise inadmissible aliens into the country for urgent humanitarian reasons or significant public benefit, such as critical medical care or serving as a witness in a trial. Yet, the Biden administration systematically abused this authority to allow millions of illegal aliens into the country. This abuse also extended to deferred action, which the Biden administration used to shield illegal aliens from removal. Outside parole and deferred action, under the Biden administration, more than 170,000 illegal aliens with criminal warrants or convictions were encountered at our borders. Of the record non-detained illegal alien population during that time, more than 425,000 had criminal convictions and another 222,000 had criminal charges pending. And there are still roughly 1.5 million aliens in the country with final orders of removal who may still be working.

By requiring aliens to show economic necessity, limiting work authorizations to one year, restricting permits for aliens with a criminal history, and conditioning renewals on employment with an E-Verify-participating employer, the rule introduces much-needed safeguards that were previously lacking. As FAIR’s comment illustrates, these measures will help protect U.S. workers from wage depression and poor working conditions by preventing mass influxes of cheap foreign labor.

“Parole and deferred action were never intended to serve as alternative pathways for economic migrants,” said Dale Wilcox, FAIR’s executive director and general counsel. “This rule is a crucial step towards protecting U.S. workers rather than rewarding illegal aliens, including violent criminals, for breaking our laws and continuing the failed policies that fueled the greatest border crisis in our nation’s history.”

text:
AURORA — Congressman Jason Crow (D-CO) and Senator John Hickenlooper (D-CO) are leading Colorado’s Democratic Congressional delegation to demand answers from the Trump Administration on a recent shooting outside a GEO-operated ICE facility in Aurora. During demonstrations outside the detention center, a GEO group employee shot a 21-year-old woman with his personally-owned firearm, striking her in the foot.

In their letter to Department of Homeland Secretary Markwayne Mullin, Crow, Hickenlooper, and their colleagues push DHS and ICE to uphold the right of lawful protestors and press the Secretary to answer how his Department will do that. They ask for clarity on how the Department is protecting peaceful protestors outside federal detention facilities; what types of de-escalation, use-of-force, and crowd management training are required for agents and contractors; what screening and vetting processes are in place for contractors before they are assigned to ICE facilities; and how the agency is cooperating with law enforcement around this incident.

“Immigration enforcement officers and the contractors supporting them have an obligation to protect public safety while exercising restraint and professionalism. Protests outside immigration detention centers are routine occurrences. An agency responsible for operating secure facilities should be equipped to maintain safe access, communicate with employees, coordinate with local law enforcement, and prevent confrontations between the community and facility personnel from escalating. Just as we believe law enforcement should never be targeted with violence, we believe lawful protesters should be protected – not attacked – by federal officials or those contracted by the government,” the group wrote.

“The incident in Aurora, and the broader pattern of shootings involving Department of Homeland Security (DHS) personnel across the country, undermine public trust and threaten community safety,” they continued. “As members of the Colorado Congressional delegation, we are responsible for defending the constitutional rights of our constituents and protecting our communities and our law enforcement. The events in Aurora raise questions about whether current DHS policies and practices keep communities, protesters, and law enforcement safe.”

Since his election to Congress, Crow has fought to promote transparency, oversight, and accountability in federal immigration detention centers. He introduced bipartisan legislation guaranteeing Members of Congress the right to conduct unannounced, in-person oversight visits of ICE detention facilities, including to check on any concerns related to public health and the humane treatment of detained individuals. He has also led the charge calling for the end to private for profit immigration detention facilities. Crow regularly conducts oversight of Aurora’s immigration detention facility. Since 2019, Crow and his staff have visited the facility to conduct oversight more than 100 times. Public reports of such visits, along with conditions at the facility, are published on Crow’s website.

A PDF of the letter can be found here, with full text appearing below:

Secretary Mullin,

We write to express our concern over the July 16, 2026 shooting of a 21-year-old woman near the Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) detention facility in Aurora, Colorado. While we are relieved that her injuries were not life-threatening, we must ensure that personnel operating at federal immigration detention facilities are adequately screened and trained to prevent incidents like this one. According to the Aurora Police Department, GEO Group employees reporting for their shifts that day were unable to enter the facility because of protest activity. Police allege that two protesters verbally confronted GEO employees and photographed their vehicles before walking away. One employee then retrieved a personally owned firearm and fired in their direction, striking one woman in the foot. He has been charged with seven offenses, including attempted second-degree murder.

Immigration enforcement officers and the contractors supporting them have an obligation to protect public safety while exercising restraint and professionalism. Protests outside immigration detention centers are routine occurrences. An agency responsible for operating secure facilities should be equipped to maintain safe access, communicate with employees, coordinate with local law enforcement, and prevent confrontations between the community and facility personnel from escalating. Just as we believe law enforcement should never be targeted with violence, we believe lawful protesters should be protected – not attacked – by federal officials or those contracted by the government.

The incident in Aurora, and the broader pattern of shootings involving Department of Homeland Security (DHS) personnel across the country, undermine public trust and threaten community safety. As members of the Colorado Congressional delegation, we are responsible for defending the constitutional rights of our constituents and protecting our communities and our law enforcement. The events in Aurora raise questions about whether current DHS policies and practices keep communities, protesters, and law enforcement safe. We believe a thorough review of the Department's policies is necessary to ensure that similar incidents do not recur.

Given this urgent need, we request written responses to the following questions by August 14, 2026:

What coordination has DHS and ICE undertaken with state and local law enforcement to manage public demonstrations while ensuring employees can safely access their places of work? What will that coordination look like moving forward?

What de-escalation, use-of-force, crisis intervention, threats against employees, and crowd-management training is required for DHS personnel and contractor employees assigned to ICE facilities? What training has been provided to the employees at the Aurora facility concerning de-escalation, use-of-force, crisis intervention, threats against employees, and crowd-management training? Which of these trainings did the employee charged in the July 16 shooting complete and on which dates did he complete them?

What screening and vetting procedures does DHS require for contractor personnel before they are assigned to ICE facilities? What screening was conducted for the individual charged in the July 16 shooting?

What policies and operational plans do DHS and ICE have in place to protect both protesters and employees outside DHS and ICE facilities, including contracted facilities? Does ICE require its detention contractors to designate alternative entrances, transportation arrangements, or other measures for employees during demonstrations or other disruptions to access?

GEO Group has placed the employee on unpaid leave and stated that it is cooperating with law enforcement. Beyond the ongoing investigation, what additional steps will DHS and ICE take to determine whether similar vulnerabilities exist at other contracted detention facilities? How will DHS and ICE strengthen oversight of its personnel and contractors and prevent similar incidents from occurring?

In addition to providing the information above, we urge the Department to conduct an independent review of its security procedures, contractor oversight, employee training, and firearms policies, especially as they relate to anticipated confrontations, and to make its findings and recommendations publicly available.

We appreciate your prompt attention to this urgent matter and look forward to your response.

description:

Body camera footage obtained through court-ordered discovery has revealed federal immigration agents calling Latinos racial slurs during Operation At Large.

text:
A federal judge in California held the Department of Homeland Security in contempt for not complying with an order to search and turn over communications in federal agents’ cellphones about immigration operations in Los Angeles, according to court documents unsealed Tuesday.

U.S. District Judge Maame Ewusi-Mensah Frimpong wrote in her order, filed July 28, that the court had provided the federal government “plenty of time” to find messages kept on agents’ personal phones relating to 15 immigration enforcement actions under Operation At Large last year.

The American Civil Liberties Union, Public Counsel and other immigration advocacy groups requested the material as part of an effort to halt federal immigration agents from using an individual’s perceived race to conduct stops.

“Given that Plaintiffs have shown by clear and convincing evidence that the Defendants

Trending

violated a specific and definite order of the court, the burden shifted to Defendants to demonstrate why they were unable to comply,” Frimpong wrote in her contempt order. “They have failed to do so.”

Frimpong ordered DHS to pay $500 every day until it complies with the order to turn over imaging of the phone messages. DHS must also reimburse the lawsuits’ plaintiffs — five Latino workers and other advocacy organizations — for the “time and costs spent by their attorneys in getting the government to comply” with the order.

Body camera footage obtained through court-ordered discovery has revealed federal immigration agents calling Latinos racial slurs during Operation At Large. Text message screenshots filed as exhibits contained conversations of agents exchanging locations of where Latino workers gather, as well as worried talks about possible violations of a temporary restraining order that prohibited indiscriminate arrests.

In December, DHS told the court that agents do not use texting functions on their mobile phones for professional duties, the court order says. Five individuals later testified that month that they, in fact, did use their personal phones for work. DHS argued again in April that agents’ personal phones were outside its possession, custody and control.

A magistrate judge rebutted DHS’ arguments in July and stated that the forensic imaging order remained in effect.

DHS submitted its first payment for violating the court on Tuesday in the amount of $3,500, according to court documents.

text:
In an order issued on August 5, 2026, Ana C. Reyes of the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia acknowledged that the Supreme Court’s judgment reversed her earlier February 2026 ruling, which had stayed the Department of Homeland Security’s termination of Haiti’s TPS designation. As a result, the court confirmed that the stay preventing implementation of the Haiti TPS termination “is no longer in effect.”

Haiti TPS Termination Moves Forward

The underlying litigation challenged DHS’s decision to terminate Haiti’s TPS designation, which provides temporary protection from removal and work authorization to eligible Haitian nationals in the United States.

The August 5 order follows the Supreme Court’s June 2026 decision in Mullin v. Doe, which limited the ability of TPS beneficiaries to challenge certain termination decisions through procedural claims. According to the court order, the D.C. Circuit remanded the case back to the district court for proceedings consistent with the Supreme Court’s ruling.

Litigation Continues Despite the End of the Injunction

Although the injunction blocking the TPS termination has been lifted, the litigation itself remains active.

Judge Reyes declined the government’s request to halt discovery and ordered the parties to submit a joint proposal outlining next steps and deadlines for the ongoing proceedings. The court also noted that the plaintiffs do not intend to file an amended complaint.

Erickson Insights and Analysis

The ruling represents another significant development in the broader legal battle over TPS terminations. With the stay no longer in place, DHS’s termination of Haiti’s TPS designation is no longer blocked by the February 2026 court order.

The case remains under review, but employers and affected individuals should closely monitor announcements from DHS, USCIS, and the courts regarding work authorization, TPS-related benefits, and compliance obligations.

Erickson Immigration Group will continue monitoring developments and sharing updates as more news is available. Please contact your employer or EIG attorney if you have questions about anything we’re reporting above or if you have case-specific questions.

text:
City and county officials in Silicon Valley are pursuing moratoriums on new federal immigration detention facilities, aiming to shield the region from President Donald Trump ’s “mass deportation” agenda.

Federal law supersedes conflicting state and local rules, leaving local officials with limited power to block such projects outright. But San Jose Mayor Matt Mahan said the group is using a new legal strategy to temporarily halt construction of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement detention centers while officials draft laws to address their potential health and environmental effects.

The push comes as ICE seeks to build a detention center on a 26-acre site it purchased near Gilroy, a Silicon Valley suburb. The Trump administration has paused the proposal as state and county officials challenge it in federal district court.

“We have zoning for a reason,” said Mahan , a moderate Democrat who mounted an unsuccessful bid for California governor earlier this year. “We should really scrutinize whether it’s a permissible use to turn a private farm into a mass deportation center.”

Mahan said Santa Clara and San Mateo counties, along with several smaller cities in Silicon Valley’s affluent suburbs, are also expected to adopt moratoriums. Rep. Sam Liccardo , who represents the region, announced the effort at a news conference Wednesday.

It’s the latest in a series of challenges to Trump ’s mass detention and deportation agenda, which has faced numerous setbacks in the courts. Cities and counties across the country have also sought to impose rules limiting ICE facilities.

Liccardo , a first-term Democrat closely aligned with the region’s powerful tech industry, said the moratoriums are meant to deter ICE from conducting more aggressive operations in Silicon Valley. The region, and the broader San Francisco Bay Area, has seen fewer large-scale ICE sweeps than other liberal-leaning metro areas, such as Minneapolis, Chicago or Boston. Last fall, Trump called off a surge of federal troops planned for San Francisco after a late-night call with the city’s mayor, Daniel Lurie , and pleas from major tech CEOs, including Nvidia’s Jensen Huang.

“What the public sees on television or social media is certainly horrific: citizens being shot, families being separated, children seeing things children should not have to see,” Liccardo said. “Of course, Lord knows what happens inside [detention centers].”

Mahan said he witnessed deplorable conditions when he visited a detention center near the Mexico border earlier this year during his campaign for governor. He said thousands of people were crammed into a facility without any natural daylight and without reliable access to health care.

“You could hear people yelling for help,” Mahan said. “It was just an incredibly unsettling experience.”

ICE and the Department of Homeland Security did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

text:
WASHINGTON — The Department of Health and Human Services plans to award a $150 million contract to a small Texas firm — with no specialty in immigration law and run by a former Trump official — to provide legal services to tens of thousands of unaccompanied immigrant children, according to a Wednesday pre-published notice in the Federal Register.

The notice, which HHS is scheduled to officially publish Thursday, comes after the department’s Office of Refugee Resettlement, which cares for unaccompanied children, let a contract with the Acacia Center for Justice for such services expire. The center has a network of roughly 100 organizations it works with that provided legal aid and representation to immigrant children across the country, including in immigration court appearances.

Lawyers from Acacia said the Trump administration did not renew the contract because attorneys refused to hand over sensitive information about their clients.

Burke Law Group, a Houston-based law firm founded in 2023, “advises companies on complex environmental, regulatory, and enforcement matters,” according to its website.

The firm will be tasked with representing as many as 24,000 unaccompanied immigrant children through their court proceedings.

The founder, Marcella Burke, during the first Donald Trump administration worked at the Environmental Protection Agency and Department of the Interior. From 2017-2018 she served as the deputy general counsel for EPA and from 2018 to 2020 worked at Interior as deputy solicitor and senior counsel, according to her LinkedIn profile.

The Burke Law Group did not immediately respond to States Newsroom’s request for comment.

Of the nearly 30 lawyers on the law firm's website, only two list experience in immigration and asylum law.

The multi-million-dollar contract is set to start Aug. 15 and run through August 14, 2027. Because it’s a “single-source cooperative agreement” contract, it gives the law firm the flexibility to subcontract work out to other firms at its discretion.

Since Monday, unaccompanied minors have lost access to their legal representation. Without it, fewer than 10% of immigrant children win the right to remain in the United States while their case goes through immigration court.

A handful of legal organizations have been able to dip into savings to continue legal coverage. But some have had to stop altogether, especially after the Trump administration since December has refused to reimburse more than $65 million in completed legal work.

A federal judge on Thursday is set to hear arguments whether to hold the Trump administration in contempt for violating an April 2025 court order that ordered the government to continue funding legal representation for unaccompanied children.

text:
Raleigh, N.C. – Today, Congresswoman Deborah Ross (NC-02) demanded that the Trump administration abandon its reported plans to open an immigration detention facility in Hertford County, North Carolina by the end of the year. In a letter to the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), Congresswoman Ross urged the agencies to abandon the proposal, citing the facility's troubling history, the burden it would place on local communities, and the administration’s documented record of mistreating detainees.

The proposed detention center would be located at the former Rivers Correctional Institution in Winton, a privately operated prison previously managed by The GEO Group. During its years of operation, the facility faced repeated complaints regarding inadequate staffing, poor medical care, unsafe conditions, and other serious deficiencies.

Congresswoman Ross warned that reopening the facility comes amid a pattern of troubling conduct by federal immigration authorities:

"Reopening the facility under The GEO Group’s ownership as an ICE detention center raises legitimate concerns that the same poor conditions could persist. I am especially concerned given your agencies’ recent practices of detaining and mistreating legal residents and even U.S. citizens,” she wrote.

In the letter Congresswoman Ross also emphasized that reopening the facility would place additional strain on local law enforcement, emergency medical services, fire departments, health care providers, utilities, and other public services in the surrounding communities, forcing local taxpayers to shoulder the costs created by the Trump administration’s decision.

title: Thomson Reuters Employees Demand That ICE “Leave Our Cities” | The Nation
authors: smccroskey, John Nichols, Carl Ginsburg, Chris Lehmann, Zephyr Teachout, Peter Kuper, The Nation, Mychal Denzel Smith, www.thenation.com
description:
The Committee to Restore Trust, representing approximately 200 Thomson Reuters employees, issued a statement today condemning their company’s deal with the US government to seek “voter fraud” and “immigration fraud” data.
Numerous sources have reported human rights abuses by ICE and DHS agents during Operation Metro Surge and around the country.
Furthermore, we encourage executive leadership to cancel existing contracts, speak out publicly against ICE’s violent campaign of terror, and use their platform to demand ICE leave our cities.
This deal represents the first time that DHS/ICE has agreed with a data broker specifically to investigate voter fraud.
This new presidential mandate and DHS/ICE ostensibly make a new case for the use of this data by immigration officials.
text:
The Committee to Restore Trust, representing approximately 200 Thomson Reuters employees, issued a statement today condemning their company’s deal with the US government to seek “voter fraud” and “immigration fraud” data. The statement reads as follows:

The Committee to Restore Trust finds this latest contract between DHS/ICE and TRSS (Thomson Reuters Special Services) to support the “presidential mandate” of the identification of Voters Fraud, Immigration Fraud and National Security” deeply troubling. Numerous sources have reported human rights abuses by ICE and DHS agents during Operation Metro Surge and around the country. We ask the company to refrain from further business with DHS and ICE until an independent board audits and reviews their usage of public records applications in 2026. For context, the only audits Thomson Reuters confirms are from 2025, prior to Operation Surge in Minneapolis. Furthermore, we encourage executive leadership to cancel existing contracts, speak out publicly against ICE’s violent campaign of terror, and use their platform to demand ICE leave our cities.

In a response to questions posed to Thomson Reuters, the company said, “As part of Thomson Reuters alignment with the United Nations Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights (UNGPs), we conduct company-wide HRSA/HRIAs every three years.” Based upon this schedule, the events of Operation Metro Surge (2026) in Minneapolis will not be assessed until December 2028. The company further responded, “As a matter of policy, we do not comment on specific customer contracts, and questions about an agency’s mission and priorities are best directed to that agency.”

The $125 million deal between the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and its enforcement arm, Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), and Thomson Reuters extends over a five-year period. This deal represents the first time that DHS/ICE has agreed with a data broker specifically to investigate voter fraud.

Thomson Reuters’ flagship investigative platform CLEAR already contains voter-registration data. Some states apparently include address, license plate and phone numbers, and even party affiliation, though data varies by state. Voter data is legally regulated, and CLEAR users are supposed to confirm a legally permissible use of the data in order to access it. This new presidential mandate and DHS/ICE ostensibly make a new case for the use of this data by immigration officials.

The company’s response: “We continue to work with our customers to provide technology and services that support investigations into areas of national security and public safety, such as child exploitation, human trafficking, narcotics and weapons trafficking, fraud and financial crime.”

Technology provided by Thomson Reuters continues to be used to round up immigrants in Minneapolis. According to a network of rapid responders made up of concerned citizens, a total of 358 individuals were detained in recent weeks, two-thirds with no criminal record. Detentions at Walmart stores and gas stations are now most common, as ICE agents pull back on controversial traffic stops. (Two US citizens were shot to death in January in the course of such stops.)

“ICE activity is ongoing and neighborhoods are continuing to organize in keeping each other safe,” says a TR employee, withholding their name for fear of retribution. That fear is real. On March 20, TR senior legal editor and Committee to Restore Trust cofounder Billie Little was fired for a so-called breach of the company code of conduct. (In response to a question about the status of the Little case, Thomson Reuters said, “We strongly dispute the allegations and will robustly defend the case. As this relates to an individual employment matter, it would be inappropriate the comment further.”)

In addition, the US Department of Justice is pursuing criminal charges, subpoenas, and conspiracy indictments against individuals, activists, and local political figures who document, track, or allegedly obstruct ICE operations. These federal enforcement and surveillance actions have escalated during high-profile crackdowns, drawing intense legal battles over First Amendment rights.

Voter-registration data may be the latest front in the White House campaign to instill distrust in the election process in the public mind leading up to the November elections, as well as to foster popular suspicion of the immigrant population.

According to the White House, “Following the 2020 presidential election, concerns about potential irregularities prompted detailed examinations of voting processes, data security, and registration practices across multiple states.” However, after extensive review by state and local elections officials, no significant irregularities have been identified.

text:
INDIANAPOLIS – A federal court today blocked Indiana Attorney General Todd Rokita from enforcing a sweeping investigative demand against Exodus Refugee Immigration. The court found that Exodus is likely to succeed in showing the investigation was retaliation for constitutionally protected speech.

The Civil Investigative Demand (CID) sought information about nearly every part of Exodus’s work, including its clients, partners, donors, advocacy and services. The ruling prevents Rokita from enforcing the demand or acting against Exodus for refusing to comply as the case continues.

Rokita issued the CID in September 2025 as part of a broader campaign targeting schools, health departments, employers and organizations connected to immigrant communities. The demand against Exodus came after the organization alerted other local service providers about a possible U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) operation in Bloomington and temporarily closed its office.

The court found that Exodus’s protected speech played a central role in Rokita’s decision to issue the demand. It also pointed to the timing, extraordinary breadth and weak connection to Rokita’s claimed labor-trafficking investigation.

“Exodus’s clients come to us after fleeing war, persecution and unimaginable hardship. They trust us to help them build safe, stable lives in Indiana,” said Cole Varga, CEO of Exodus Refugee Immigration. “This investigation undermined that trust. We hope that the Attorney General will now focus on serving Indiana residents instead of targeting our immigrant neighbors and their allies."

The preliminary injunction will remain in place while the lawsuit continues. The ACLU of Indiana will keep pursuing Exodus’s First Amendment claims and seeking a permanent end to enforcement of the CID.

“This investigation sought information about Exodus’s clients, partners and work in an effort to intimidate an organization serving immigrant communities and silence protected speech,” said Stevie Pactor, senior staff attorney at the ACLU of Indiana. “We look forward seeking final judgment against the Attorney General’s unlawful actions.”

When the enforcement of law violates human dignity, they betray the very justice they claim to defend."
text:
Catholic bishops in Texas and Michigan released new public statements this week defending the dignity of migrants and calling for comprehensive immigration reform amid recent enforcement actions by federal immigration agents.

Bishop Robert Gruss of Saginaw, Michigan, said Aug. 1 that it was "necessary" for him to respond to news reports that U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers arrested nine migrant workers while they were installing cable in Saginaw in late July. The arrests sparked local protests.

"It is understandable to remove immigrants who have caused harm to society by participating in criminal activity. But is it fair to remove those who are and have been contributing to society in a positive way, often times for many years?" Gruss said in his prepared statement.

On Aug. 3, San Antonio Archbishop Gustavo García-Siller issued a new pastoral letter, titled "We Will Come to You: United in Solidarity with Our Brothers and Sisters in Migration," offering a pastoral roadmap grounded in human dignity and the Gospel call to welcome the stranger.

"Families we know by name are now afraid to come to the sacraments. Like the Good Samaritan who drew near to the wounded, we cannot walk past them," wrote García-Siller, who released his letter on the 100th anniversary of San Antonio's elevation to a metropolitan archdiocese.

"I write to console the suffering, to awaken the indifferent, and to confront injustice with the courage the Gospel demands," García-Siller wrote in a press release.

The bishops' remarks are the latest in a series of statements that Catholic prelates across the country have released over the past year expressing solidarity with beleaguered immigrant communities that have found themselves in the crosshairs of the Trump administration's immigration crackdown.

In November 2025, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops approved a special pastoral message on immigration that condemned the indiscriminate mass deportation of people. Gruss referenced that statement in his remarks this week that called for the legal rights of migrants to be respected.

"The deportation of people without cause, the detention of immigrants without meaningful legal representation, without access to family or a supportive community, and without basic human needs being met, and the forced separation of immigrant families and incarceration of children do not represent a just and civil society," Gruss said.

Every human person, migrant or otherwise, Gruss said, must have their constitutional rights respected, including the rights to due process, protection against discrimination and protection from unreasonable search and seizure.

"Disregard for this should never be normalized in our society," said Gruss, who added that the legitimate role of civil authorities to implement the law in a humane manner, respecting the fundamental human rights, is part of a just society, "but must always include due process."

"The power of the state must always be exercised within the limits of moral law," said Gruss, who called on Congress to "remove the politics, do its work, and take the bold steps necessary to pass comprehensive immigration reform."

"Our system has been broken for more than 40 years, and our government leaders do not seem to want to try and fix the problem. Herein, lies the problem," Gruss said.

In the San Antonio Archdiocese, García-Siller said he wrote his pastoral letter, which reflects on the prevailing climate of immigration enforcement, in a spirit of love, "grounded not in ideology but in walking with you."

"Our immigration system has failed the people it was meant to serve, and a misleading public narrative has done much to sustain that failure," García-Siller wrote as he referenced statistics from the Cato Institute indicating that 73% of people in immigration detention have no prior criminal conviction.

"Research shows mass deportation would subtract more than $1 trillion from the economy, while a pathway to citizenship for these families would generate $1.7 trillion in growth. They do not weaken the nation but rather sustain it," García-Siller wrote.

The letter is organized around four pillars that emphasize the human dignity of every person, encountering Christ in welcoming the migrant, the importance of parishes and families accompanying migrants, including the detained, and appealing to civic leaders on "the non-negotiable principles" of dignity, family unity and due process.

Parishes, Catholic schools and campus ministries in the San Antonio Archdiocese will receive a reflection guide and liturgical resources, with an emphasis on World Day of Migrants and Refugees, which will be observed on Sept. 27.

García-Siller noted that immigrant detention and deportation at a large scale are not new in United States history.

"What distinguishes the present hour is not enforcement at scale alone, but a convergence of structural and legal tactics whose relative novelty calls for the careful and well-formed moral discernment of every Catholic conscience," García-Siller wrote.

The church acknowledges the legitimate authority of law enforcement to enforce immigration laws, García-Siller said, but he added that "all laws must remain at the service of human dignity. When the enforcement of law violates human dignity, they betray the very justice they claim to defend."

text:
(St. Paul, MN) – The Immigrant Law Center of Minnesota (ILCM) is appalled at the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) detention facility set to open in Appleton, Minnesota. At 1,600 beds, the CoreCivic facility would be the first private ICE detention facility in the state and among the largest carceral facilities in Minnesota.

It’s a staggering increase over the immigration detention capacity currently contracted to county jails. ILCM warns that the facility’s scale and its remoteness threaten the ability of detained people to access legal counsel. Across the country, immigrants in detention centers are denied healthcare, living in overcrowded spaces, and treated barbarically.

"At times, entering detention facilities can be a death sentence, yet not a single immigration violation is considered a capital offense,” ILCM’s Director of Public Policy and Public Affairs, Julia Decker, stated. “It starts to beg the question: what is the point of immigration detention?”

ILCM denounces privatized detention as a revenue stream. A system that pays a private company per person, per day creates an incentive to take people away and detain them for longer. As Operation Metro Surge and other actions have shown, incentivizing detentions incentivizes violence against communities, violations of civil rights and civil liberties, and further dehumanization of immigrants and refugees.

Appleton sits roughly 150 miles west of the Twin Cities, where the majority of Minnesota's immigration attorneys, accredited representatives, and interpreters are based. Detention far from counsel is a functional obstacle to due process. ILCM is also concerned that people will be transferred into Appleton from other states, separating them from their attorneys, their evidence, and their families, and compounding access to counsel problems well beyond Minnesota's borders. This announcement comes on the heels of over 3,800 ICE agents terrorizing Minnesotan communities. A new horror is at our doorstep.

During Operation Metro Surge, ILCM served 247 people detained. Appleton will operate at a far greater scale, in a community with fewer legal resources.

As the largest provider of free immigration legal services in Minnesota, with in-house language access, ILCM will work with its partners to monitor the situation, communicate clear and accurate information to community members, and continue to fight for the rights that all immigrants and refugees should have, regardless of whether they are detained or not. We will be watching this facility closely, especially as detainees are set to begin arriving in late 2026.
