text:
“I write to comfort the afflicted, to ignite the comfortable, and to confront injustice with the full conviction of the Gospel,” San Antonio Archbishop Gustavo García-Siller wrote.

In response to increased immigration enforcement measures throughout the country, two U.S. Catholic bishops have issued fresh statements affirming the human dignity of immigrants as children of God and calling for immigration reform.

Both prelates said Americans should understand why people flee their home countries in search of a better life while acknowledging the nation’s right to enforce its immigration laws. The current situation, however, is unjust, immoral, and must be fixed, both men emphasized.

On Aug. 3, the centennial anniversary of the elevation of San Antonio to a metropolitan archdiocese, Archbishop Gustavo García-Siller released a pastoral letter expressing the Church’s solidarity with migrants and calling for the “careful and well-formed moral discernment of every Catholic conscience” in response.

Meanwhile, on Aug. 1, Bishop Robert Gruss of the Diocese of Saginaw, Michigan, issued a statement in which he reminded the faithful of the “inherent human dignity” of every person.

Gruss said the current “challenge” facing the United States, which has “consistently received immigrants, refugees, exiles, and the persecuted from other lands” throughout its history, is “how to deal with a situation when one administration has allowed individuals and families to migrate … freely and the next administration wants their removal.”

The bishop wrote that the removal of “immigrants who have caused harm to society by participating in criminal activity” is understandable, but asked if it is “fair to remove those who are and have been contributing to society in a positive way, oftentimes for many years?”

He said that a “just and civil society” would not allow the deportation or detention of people “without cause” or “meaningful legal representation, without access to family or a supportive community, and without basic human needs being met.”

He urged the faithful to “push for public policy changes that secure civil rights for all immigrants” and “humane border enforcement policies” that simultaneously uphold national security while protecting the “safety and dignity” of those who come to the country to work.

‘We will come to you’

García-Siller promulgated his letter, titled “We Will Come to You: United in Solidarity with Our Brothers and Sisters in Migration,” at a Mass at San Fernando Cathedral in downtown San Antonio.

“We are living in a world of war,” the letter began. “Across continents, people are dying every day. Across borders, survivors are forced to migrate. They do not leave by choice, but because of violence, hunger, fear, and oppression.”

In the 56-page letter, composed of five sections and concluding with a prayer to Our Lady of Guadalupe, García-Siller said he prayed “for a long time” before writing, saying he wanted to write from “the right place, one of accompaniment and solidarity.”

He said the letter addresses an “unprecedented” time in the country, writing that “a convergence of structural and legal tactics … calls for the careful and well-formed moral discernment of every Catholic conscience.”

“I write to comfort the afflicted, to ignite the comfortable, and to confront injustice with the full conviction of the Gospel.”

He went on to cite his personal experience of “years walking alongside” migrants, many of whom are living in so much fear they rarely leave their homes, as well as his own story as a migrant himself.

The archbishop wrote that he has witnessed a “fear that has taken root” across the archdiocese, saying he and other pastors “pray with parents who embrace their children each morning unsure if they will be home at night,” and describing parents who avoid taking children to the doctor or to go to work “because each mile carries risk.”

“The community bears this cross, and the Church cannot be silent,” he wrote, describing declining Mass attendance and the worsening physical health of those who suffer fear related to immigration.

“The people have not lost their faith,” he wrote. “Many, however, have lost their sense of safety and belonging.”

The Church must “defend the dignity of those caught in the machinery of removal,” he emphasized.

García-Siller described visiting three detention centers in the area, including the South Texas Family Residential Center in Dilley, the largest family detention center in the nation, saying he’s witnessed “firsthand, violations of human dignity within their walls.”

He went on to quote Bishop Steven Biegler of the Diocese of Cheyenne, Wyoming, who wrote in a pastoral letter in April that “‘the current campaign of mass detention and deportations is immoral.’”

García-Siller accused private corporations of profiting from the processing and movement of large numbers of detained immigrants from one site to another.

He also cited an investigation by U.S. Sen. John Ossoff, D-Georgia, which documented more than 1,000 “credible reports of human rights abuses since January 2025, including “medical neglect, denial of food and water, overcrowding, sleep deprivation, and the separation of breastfeeding mothers from their infants,” as well as similar abuses in privately-run sites.

García-Siller called the public narrative that only criminals are being removed “misleading,” writing that “73% of those in immigration detention have no criminal conviction, and only 5% have been convicted of a violent crime.”

He described how pastors, deacons, extraordinary ministers, and trained catechists are developing “active ministries of accompaniment” in the archdiocese, visiting migrants in their homes, bringing the sacraments along with medicines and other supplies, as well as in detention centers.

“If your family has been detained, tell us. We will go to them. The Body of Christ does not abandon its members in chains,” García-Siller declared.

The archbishop went on to lament that existing legal pathways take years to navigate, years that families cannot afford to wait as they seek safety and stability. He called for more accessible legal pathways, saying migrants would take those pathways if they were available. Migrants’ “contribution to the common good of our nation” demands such, he wrote.

At the end of the letter, García-Siller entrusted the situation to Our Lady of Guadalupe, who herself crossed borders of culture and race and walked the road of exile with the Holy Family: “Long before she was Queen of Mexico … she was a mother who crossed a border. She knows this road; she walked it with her own feet.”

name: Human Rights
title: Healey will sign immigrant protections into law Wednesday - NBC Boston
description:
Maura Healey signed a new immigrant protection measure into law Wednesday morning in Chelsea, saying the compromise bill Massachusetts lawmakers sent her "provides the strongest protections in the nation against the dangerous and illegal tactics of President Donald Trump and ICE."
Healey was at La Colaborativa on 6th Street to sign the PROTECT Act -- an Act promoting rule of law, oversight, trust and equal constitutional treatment.
“Today, Massachusetts is standing up for what’s right and taking action to keep our people and our communities safe,” Healey said in a statement.
Having worked with law enforcement and standing here today with law enforcement, I want to be clear, the law I'm signing today is a public safety law," she said.
Healey went on to say we should all be proud that the PROTECT Act is the strongest law in the country to protect people from ICE and to protect public safety.
text:
Gov. Maura Healey signed a new immigrant protection measure into law Wednesday morning in Chelsea, saying the compromise bill Massachusetts lawmakers sent her "provides the strongest protections in the nation against the dangerous and illegal tactics of President Donald Trump and ICE."

Healey was at La Colaborativa on 6th Street to sign the PROTECT Act -- an Act promoting rule of law, oversight, trust and equal constitutional treatment. She was expected to be joined at the signing ceremony by Lt. Gov. Kim Driscoll, Education Secretary Steven Zrike, Office of Refugees and Immigrants Executive Director Cristina Aguilera-Sandoval, Chelsea City Manager Fidel Maltez, La Colaborativa President & CEO Gladys Vega, public safety officials, advocates and others.

The landmark legislation keeps ICE out of courthouses, schools, child care centers, hospitals and health care facilities, while also providing stronger protections for parents in case they are detained or deported, banning new 287(g) agreements and allowing civil rights claims to be made against government officials, including ICE agents.

The bill (H 5620) that cleared the House and Senate on split votes last Thursday not only expands protections against warrantless civil immigration arrests, but it also bars new agreements allowing state and local officials to perform certain federal immigration enforcement functions, preserves the Department of Correction's existing partnership with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, and codifies the Supreme Judicial Court's 2017 Lunn v. Commonwealth decision which held that there is "no authority for Massachusetts court officers to arrest and hold an individual solely on the basis of a Federal civil immigration detainer."

Lawmakers attached an emergency preamble to the bill, declaring it "an emergency law, necessary for the immediate preservation of the public safety" and arranging for it to take effect as soon as Healey signs it.

“Today, Massachusetts is standing up for what’s right and taking action to keep our people and our communities safe,” Healey said in a statement. “The PROTECT Act is the strongest law in the country to protect people from ICE, because no one should be afraid to send their child to school, seek medical care or fear reporting a crime or appearing in court. It makes us all less safe. So we are getting ICE out of our courthouses, schools and hospitals. This bill is a testament to the hard work and advocacy of so many people across our state. We’re going to keep working together to make Massachusetts and this country the place we all want it to be.”

The governor started Wednesday's press conference by saying Massachusetts is special because of its people, asking everyone to look around the room, where there were people of all races, all backgrounds, all socio-economic backgrounds, from law enforcement to organizers, teachers and clergy, parents and kids, nurses and doctors all standing together.

Local

In-depth news coverage of the Greater Boston and New England area.

"I want to be clear about something, I'm your governor, I was formerly your attorney general. For eight years I investigated, prosecuted and put away violent criminals, drug traffickers, gun traffickers, human traffickers. We all want safe communities, don't we? Having worked with law enforcement and standing here today with law enforcement, I want to be clear, the law I'm signing today is a public safety law," she said. "I don't know how anyone could look at what we see on TV and read in the news and hear from our neighbors, not just in Massachusetts, but around this country, I don't know how you can look at that and not say, this is making us less safe, ICE is making us less safe."

Healey said the ICE agents involved in these incidents are untrained, unqualified and unfit to do their jobs: "We know that what ICE is doing is wrong and it needs to stop."

The governor's remarks earned applause from the room, as she went on to add that she feels we can agree on a few things -- that we do need immigration reform in this country and we do need controls at the border, but also that "ICE is so wrong in what it's doing."

The governor said enrollment is down in schools across Massachusetts -- something she said is directly tied to Trump and ICE tactics. She also said families are skipping medical appointments and not getting the care they need.

"ICE needs to be stopped here in Massachusetts and around this country, stopped in its tracks...ICE is hurting our country. What ICE is about is Donald Trump and Stephen Miller's hateful and racist agenda, it's about threatening, antagonizing, terrorizing people simply for how they look and apparently what they represent to Trump and Miller and those who support them," she said. "Today in Massachusetts we're saying enough is enough. We're standing up for what's right and we're taking action to protect people's safety."

Healey went on to say we should all be proud that the PROTECT Act is the strongest law in the country to protect people from ICE and to protect public safety. She said last week the bill was "top of mind" for her and she expressed hope it would reach her desk.

Ahead of the PROTECT Act signing Wednesday, Healey also responded to reports that ICE is seeking 250 parking spots in downtown Boston, saying it cannot be allowed at this time.

“We see what ICE is doing to our communities every day. People are afraid to go to school, doctors' appointments, court or even church. ICE is shooting people dead, separating families, and making us all less safe. That’s why I’m about to sign the strongest protections in the country against their abuses," she said in a statement early Wednesday. "We absolutely cannot allow ICE to have 250 parking spots in downtown Boston while they are engaging in these illegal tactics. We cannot enable them to ramp up even further in Massachusetts.”

A U.S. Department of Homeland Security spokesperson released a statement to NBC10 Boston following the bill's signing Wednesday, saying, "When politicians bar local law enforcement from working with DHS, our law enforcement officers have to have a more visible presence so that we can find and apprehend the criminals let out of jails and back into communities. Seven of the top 10 safest cities in the United States cooperate with ICE. Instead of working with us, Massachusetts lawmakers are choosing to RELEASE violent criminals from their jails directly back into our communities to perpetrate more crimes and create more victims. Sanctuary politicians must stop putting politics above public safety."

State House News Service contributed to this report

name: Human Rights
title: Choosing Courage over Despair: Civil Society Is Notching Up Wins Despite Hostile Conditions
authors: Mandeep S. Tiwana, Maura Casey, Kettering Staff, Clare Byarugaba, Andrew L. Whitehead, Laura Schwartz-Henderson, Benjamin L. McKean, Se-Hyoung Yi
description:
These combined forces want civil society to believe nothing can stand in their way.
Concerted civil society campaigns have managed to achieve success even in hostile environments.
In Venezuela, scores of prisoners of conscience have been recently released following sustained civil society pressure.
These examples prove that upstanding citizens and civil society organizations throughout the world are choosing courage over despair despite adverse civic space conditions.
At the same time, it is vital for civil society to understand and critique the political economy of oppression.
text:
We live in a world where cruel and unaccountable power is on the ascendant. Powerful countries led by self-serving strongmen are wreaking havoc across borders in a neocolonial scramble for power and natural resources. Their disruption of the rules-based order through military action in breach of international law is leaving trails of death and destruction. Oligarchs powered by the entrenchment of market fundamentalism have come to monopolize large swaths of our economies. They are trying to influence how people think and act through their grip on the media, boosted by artificial intelligence (AI) and surveillance technology. These combined forces want civil society to believe nothing can stand in their way. But across the world, despite immensely challenging conditions, resistance is brewing and is notching up wins for peace, justice, equality, and environmental sustainability.

CIVICUS’s 2026 State of Civil Society Report finds that, even in the face of overwhelming odds, principled people and committed civil society organizations are putting up fierce resistance against corrupt politicians, misogynistic anti-rights groups, and extractive polluters. Street protests, legal action, community engagement, and advocacy campaigns are showing that change is still possible and hope is still an option in a world beset by crises.

Earlier this year in the United States, the Trump administration had to back down in the face of fierce resistance by people in Minneapolis who came out in large numbers to witness and protest against a racially charged immigration crackdown. In Nepal, a youthful new government comprising civil society activists and professional experts took office following an electoral revolution led by Gen Z that ousted establishment politicians following mass protests against economic exclusion and nepotism. A transnational movement urging an end to impunity for Israel’s genocide and brutal occupation of Palestinian territories continues to grow in numbers. This May, more than 400 activists from more than 50 countries belonging to the peaceful Global Sumud Flotilla were the focus of international attention and diplomatic outrage after they were abducted and ill-treated by Israeli forces for seeking to deliver life-affirming aid to besieged people in Gaza.

Visible mobilizations such as India’s Cockroach Janata Party, Kenya’s Gen-Z Uprising, and Serbia’s Anti-Corruption Youth Movement are attracting large numbers of young people hungry for political change. At the same time, civil society resistance is continuing to manifest through community action. In Afghanistan, despite Taliban diktats, underground schools continue to provide much-needed education to girls so that a generation is not deprived of this vital human right. In Greece, despite attempts to criminalize the rescue of refugees and migrants at sea, civil society groups are continuing their humanitarian missions to save people in distress and make life bearable for those incarcerated in camps. Earlier this year, courts acquitted a group of 24 activists following a long ordeal of prosecution on false charges of human trafficking.

Concerted legal action by civil society groups continues to win recognition of rights. In St. Lucia, the Eastern Caribbean Alliance for Diversity and Equality and United and Strong won a landmark court ruling in 2025 to decriminalize same-sex love. Efforts by the Pacific Islands Students Network bore fruit when the International Court of Justice (ICJ) issued a landmark advisory opinion affirming that states have an obligation to protect people from the ravages of climate change. A UN General Assembly resolution supported by more than 140 countries recently validated that ruling.

Documentation efforts by civil society groups are proving to be powerful enablers of justice for victims of serious violations. In the Philippines, painstaking evidence collection work by women’s groups proved to be crucial in the launch of International Criminal Court proceedings against former president Rodrigo Duterte, who presided over a brutal “war on drugs” that killed thousands of people. In Ukraine, civil society groups are creatively deploying AI tools to collect evidence of war crimes, while in Mexico they are using these tools to identify victims of enforced disappearances.

Concerted civil society campaigns have managed to achieve success even in hostile environments. In Venezuela, scores of prisoners of conscience have been recently released following sustained civil society pressure. In Thailand, the decade-long quest of LGBTQ+ groups led to the adoption of Southeast Asia’s first marriage equality law in 2025. Civil society efforts also led to advancement of sexual and reproductive freedoms for women in Denmark by enhancing abortion access. In Peru, Indigenous groups are putting up powerful resistance to hold extractive industries to account.

These examples prove that upstanding citizens and civil society organizations throughout the world are choosing courage over despair despite adverse civic space conditions. However, to sustain momentum in the face of severe headwinds, movements will need to embrace the intersectionality of rights to create linkages between gender, racial, social, political, environmental, and economic justice struggles. At the same time, it is vital for civil society to understand and critique the political economy of oppression. Decades of privatization of the public sphere, aggressive deregulation of markets, and tax loopholes for the extremely wealthy have created a flawed system that fails most people while enabling privileged elites to accumulate excessive wealth and bend governance structures to their will.

Most important, exercising courage and staying true to purpose is crucial in these times. Continuing the important work of truth-telling despite seemingly limited margins of maneuverability is vital. That means not abandoning transformative initiatives such as those on diversity, equity, and inclusion even when authoritarians and populists lash out. It is when times are hardest that determined resistance by civil society is most needed.

name: Human Rights
title: Governor Healey Signs PROTECT Act to Keep ICE out of Courthouses, Schools and Hospitals
description:
“The PROTECT Act helps ensure that early education programs and K-12 schools remain welcoming places where every child can feel safe, build confidence, and thrive.
The PROTECT Act affirms what should never have needed saying at all: our schools, our courthouses, and our workplaces are not hunting grounds.
The PROTECT Act ensures that the rights of all Massachusetts residents are protected under the Massachusetts Constitution and Massachusetts law.
extends our sincere gratitude to Governor Maura Healey and the Healey-Driscoll Administration for signing the Protect Act into law.
We are grateful to Governor Healey, Lieutenant Governor Driscoll, and the Legislature for their continued leadership and unwavering support of public education.
text:
CHELSEA — Governor Maura Healey today stood with immigrants, advocates, community leaders, law enforcement, teachers, nurses, doctors, clergy and elected officials at La Colaborativa in Chelsea to sign the PROTECT Act, landmark legislation that provides the strongest protections in the nation against the dangerous and illegal tactics of President Donald Trump and ICE. The bill keeps ICE out of courthouses, schools, child care centers, hospitals and health care facilities, while also providing stronger protections for parents in case they are detained or deported, banning new 287(g) agreements and allowing civil rights claims to be made against government officials, including ICE agents.

“Today, Massachusetts is standing up for what’s right and taking action to keep our people and our communities safe,” said Governor Healey. “The PROTECT Act is the strongest law in the country to protect people from ICE, because no one should be afraid to send their child to school, seek medical care or fear reporting a crime or appearing in court. It makes us all less safe. So we are getting ICE out of our courthouses, schools and hospitals. This bill is a testament to the hard work and advocacy of so many people across our state. We’re going to keep working together to make Massachusetts and this country the place we all want it to be.”

“This bill is about standing up for our immigrant communities, standing up for public safety, education and health care, and standing up for people’s rights and freedoms,” said Lieutenant Governor Kim Driscoll. “We're grateful to our legislative partners and the many advocates who worked alongside us to strengthen public safety, protect families and reinforce trust between our communities and law enforcement.”

The PROTECT Act includes several key provisions proposed by Governor Healey earlier this year, including prohibiting warrantless immigrant arrests at courthouses, schools, child care centers, and health care facilities, including hospitals, community health centers and nursing homes. It allows parents to pre-arrange guardianship for their children in case they are detained or deported. It also codifies the Governor’s Executive Order by limiting civil immigration enforcement in nonpublic areas of state buildings, requiring multilingual guidance on immigration enforcement procedures and individual rights, and prohibiting any new 287(g) agreements with state agencies.

“Strong public safety requires strong partnerships with the communities we serve,” said Public Safety and Security Secretary Gina Kwon. “The PROTECT Act helps preserve the trust that law enforcement, prosecutors and community organizations rely on to protect victims, investigate crimes and keep neighborhoods safe. When people feel safe, our Commonwealth is stronger.”

“As a superintendent and teacher, I've seen how deeply a child's sense of safety and belonging shapes their ability to learn,” said Education Secretary Steve Zrike. “The PROTECT Act helps ensure that early education programs and K-12

schools remain welcoming places where every child can feel safe, build confidence, and thrive. That sense of belonging is essential to educational opportunity and to the strength of our communities.”

“In my work as a clinician, I’ve seen firsthand how important it is to maintain a safe, healing environment in our hospitals,” said Health and Human Services Secretary Kiame Mahaniah, MD, MBA. “Keeping ICE out of hospitals, as well as our courthouses and schools means we also keep fear out of these places. I am grateful to Governor Healey for her continued leadership protecting our immigrant communities from the cruel acts of the Trump Administration.”

The bill also defines state and local cooperation with federal immigration enforcement while expanding legal protections and due process for immigrants. It creates a new state law civil rights claim for government officials, including ICE agents, who violate someone’s federal constitutional rights. It also establishes new oversight, reporting, and notification requirements for correctional facilities, employers, and state agencies and strengthens protections for crime victims seeking immigration relief.

“With the Governor's signature today, Massachusetts residents will have the strongest protections from President Trump's weaponization of federal immigration authorities in the nation,” said Senate President Karen E. Spilka (D-Ashland). “The abuses and infringements on constitutional rights we have seen in this country are reprehensible and un-American. This law is the culmination of our efforts to do everything in our state's power to protect hardworking residents who have done nothing wrong and who contribute to the vibrancy of this state. I applaud Senator Friedman and Senator Payano for their work to reach this strong agreement, and I applaud the Governor's signature on this bill.”

“Since the beginning of President Trump’s second term, ICE and Border Patrol agents have continued to harass and disappear innocent Americans with total impunity—a reckless approach that has led to the deaths of American citizens and legal residents, and to children being separated from their families. Those actions have immigrants in Massachusetts living in fear as they go to work or bring their children to school, and they jeopardize the trust that local law enforcement has worked hard to build,” said House Speaker Ronald J. Mariano (D-Quincy). “That’s why this legislation is so important, as it takes steps to ensure that all residents in Massachusetts are treated equally under state law, and to protect our communities through practical, thoughtful measures. I want to thank Governor Healey for signing these protections into law, as well as Chairman Cahill, Chairman Vargas, and the Black and Latino Legislative Caucus for working tirelessly to incorporate feedback from immigrant communities and law enforcement alike. Finally, I’m grateful to all my colleagues in the House, and to our partners in the Senate, for voting in favor of these critical reforms.”

“The PROTECT Act strengthens protections for our residents in the face of the aggressive tactics employed by ICE – tactics that do not enhance public safety and instead spread fear among families and our communities,” said Attorney General Andrea Joy Campbell. “I am grateful to Governor Healey and the Legislature for enacting these critical protections into law. Immigrants are an essential part of our communities, workplaces, and economy, and we will continue to use every tool available to defend their rights.”

This legislation is a crucial piece of the Healey-Driscoll Administration’s overall strategy to protect Massachusetts communities and stand up to the harm caused by President Trump and ICE. When Governor Healey first filed her legislation, she also signed an Executive Order prohibiting the state from entering into any new 287(g) agreements unless there is a public safety need, prohibiting ICE from making civil arrests in non-public areas of state facilities, and prohibiting the use of state property for immigration enforcement staging. She also issued statewide guidance for schools, child care providers, higher education campuses, health care facilities and places of worship regarding interactions with ICE agents.

Governor Healey also launched an online portal with Attorney General Campbell that allows Massachusetts residents to report alleged misconduct by ICE, opposed ICE flights at Hanscom Airport, called for an extension of Temporary Protected Status for Haitians and other immigrants, and opposed new ICE Detention Centers in New England. The Healey-Driscoll Administration has also connected thousands of immigrants with legal services and provided robust multilingual resources for communities and employers.

Statements of Support

District Attorney Timothy J. Shugrue:

“I fully support the PROTECT Act. Courthouses should be sanctuaries of safety for all who enter them. When ICE accesses courthouses it interferes with justice. Victims of crimes have the right to see justice on their behalf without the risk of themselves being apprehended and criminalized themselves. On the other hand, perpetrators of crime must face the consequences of their actions in a court of law. When ICE deports perpetrators before their day in court it not only absolves them of their actions without ever taking responsibility for their crimes but also allows them to exit the United States without a criminal record. Supporting the PROTECT Act not only provides protections for victims of crimes but also ensure perpetrators of crime are held responsible for their actions.”

District Attorney Kevin Hayden:

“It is fitting that Massachusetts, the state that launched the American liberty movement, is now moving forward with an act that protects the liberty of its residents, particularly those in our immigrant communities, while balancing public safety and victim rights. Our state sent a resounding message about liberty 250 years ago and we're doing it again today.”

District Attorney Marian Ryan:

“The PROTECT Act provides necessary clarity and safeguards to ensure our laws reflect our commitment to immigrant communities, protection of individual rights and the guarantee that all residents are treated equally. In addition, this measure takes important steps to reduce the risk of dangerous confrontations in public spaces, particularly in and around our courts, which serve as the foundation of public safety. Increased federal civil immigration enforcement activity in and around our courthouses has made it more difficult to ensure that victims, witnesses and defendants can safely access the justice system and has disrupted access to justice. I applaud the Governor and the Legislature for their commitment to preserving the integrity of our courts and continuing to stand in support of immigrant families.”

Senator Cindy F. Friedman, Chair, Senate Committee on Steering and Policy and Senate Committee on Health Care Financing

“With the signing of the PROTECT Act today, Massachusetts reaffirms our values of respect, dignity, and justice for ALL our residents. I am so proud of the work we have done in our capacity as a state to protect the immigrants who play such a valuable role in our communities. The federal government’s indiscriminate acts of violence against our immigrant communities do not—and never will—make us better, safer, more prosperous, or stronger. We will not let fear and hatred change who we are or what we stand for. I applaud the Administration for the swift action in signing this legislation after extensive and deliberate work between the Legislature, the Attorney General’s office, advocates, law enforcement, and immigrant community partners to create some of the strongest immigrant protections in the nation.”

Senator Pavel Payano:

“The passage of the PROTECT Act reaffirms Massachusetts' commitment to fairness, due process, and human dignity. No family should have to choose between taking a child to school, seeking medical care, or appearing in court because they are afraid. As someone who as a child immigrated from the Dominican Republic, I understand the importance of living in a state that honors the promise that hard work and contributing to your community should open doors, not close them. Today, we reaffirm that Massachusetts will continue to be a place where opportunity is built through hard work and where fear should never stand in the way of a brighter future.”

Senator Sal N. DiDomenico:

“I am a proud supporter of the PROTECT Act and it is an honor to see this landmark bill signed into law here in Chelsea, a beautiful city filled with people from all over the world, who I have the privilege of representing. This humane and righteous legislation demonstrates to every person in my district and in our state that our priority is to fight for the safety, freedoms and rights of all people, and that they will be treated with dignity and care. I want to thank Governor Healey for her leadership, as well as my colleagues and the advocates, especially my friends from the Black and Latino Caucus and La Colaborativa, who have worked tirelessly to get this essential policy over the finish line.”

Representative Andy Vargas, Chair, Black and Latino Legislative Caucus and Joint Committee on Community Development and Small Businesses:

“The PROTECT Act is the culmination of over 18 months of speaking to impacted families, advocates, and law enforcement, including Chiefs of Police and DAs. The Massachusetts Black and Latino Legislative Caucus wrote a bill that had bipartisan support and was constitutionally sound. That bill has found allies in every room across the State House. I would like to thank Speaker Mariano, Senate President Spilka and Governor Healey for their steadfast leadership in getting this done,” said Representative Andy Vargas of Haverhill. “Immigrants are the pillar of our country and Massachusetts will not allow our resources to drive them out. This law has earned praise from constituents, advocates, police chiefs and district attorneys alike. The PROTECT Act is the result of sound policymaking that is rooted in humanity, public safety, and common sense.”

Representative Judith A. Garcia:

“I am deeply grateful to Governor Healey for choosing Chelsea for the signing of the PROTECT Act. There could be no more meaningful place for this bill to become law. In Chelsea and communities across Massachusetts, immigrant families experienced the fear that brought the Massachusetts Black and Latino Legislative Caucus together to draft this legislation. Today, we affirm a simple principle: no one should have to choose between seeking justice and fearing deportation. As a House member, I am especially grateful to Speaker Mariano for the trust he placed in us to get this legislation right.”

Gladys Vega, President & CEO, La Colaborativa, Vice-chair, Governor’s Advisory Council on Latino Empowerment:

“For decades, our organization has worked to ensure that immigrant families are treated with dignity and respect. After years of witnessing workers deprived of employment, families residing in fear, and children missing school because of immigration enforcement, the passage of this historic law is a testament to our Commonwealth’s commitment to upholding human rights and dignity for all. From the very beginning, La Colaborativa proudly supported the PROTECT Act because its purpose reflects the work we do every day: protecting families and ensuring that every person can go to school, seek medical care, report a crime, access the courts, and practice their faith without fear. We are proud to stand alongside this historic law and everyone who made it possible. For communities like ours that have experienced the devastating impact of immigration enforcement, this is a powerful step toward ensuring our families are safer, protected, and heard.”

Josiane Martinez, Chair, Governor’s Advisory Council on Latino Empowerment:

“The signing of the PROTECT Act sends a clear and powerful message: everyone who calls Massachusetts home is part of the fabric of our Commonwealth and deserves dignity, safety, and equal protection under the law. By strengthening due process and protections at schools, childcare and healthcare settings, and state courts—and allowing parents to arrange guardianship in case of family separation—this law helps people safely access essential institutions while keeping local law enforcement focused on public safety. This is what happens when communities speak and government listens and delivers. On behalf of the Governor’s Advisory Council on Latino Empowerment, we thank Governor Healey, Lieutenant Governor Driscoll, the Massachusetts Black and Latino Legislative Caucus, legislative leadership, and the advocates who made this possible. Massachusetts is strongest when everyone knows they belong, their rights matter, and their family will be treated with humanity.”

Dr. Geralde V. Gabeau, Founder and CEO, Immigrant Family Services Institute:

“We are deeply grateful to Governor Healey, the Legislature, advocates, and community leaders who stood together to make this moment possible. The PROTECT Act is an important step toward restoring trust, dignity, and hope. However, it does not end the threat facing immigrant families or replace the urgent need for federal action. We must continue fighting until every immigrant family can live, work, worship, learn, and contribute to our Commonwealth without fear.”

Lenita Reason, Executive Director, Brazilian Worker Center Inc., Protect Massachusetts Coalition Co-Chair:

“The Protect Act is a crucial step forward in ensuring safety, dignity, and basic rights for all immigrant families across Massachusetts. As Executive Director of the Brazilian Worker Center and co-chair of the Protect Act Coalition, I stand proudly alongside the Black & Latino Legislative Caucus in championing legislation that uplifts our communities and protects vulnerable families. Thank you, Governor Healey, for signing this vital bill into law.”

Liz Sweet, Executive Director, MIRA Coalition and Protect Massachusetts Coalition Co-Chair:

“Today marks a historic victory for our Commonwealth. The PROTECT Act becoming law solidifies a commitment to protecting immigrant communities, ensuring due process, and upholding fundamental civil rights. The crucial safeguards the PROTECT law provides by establishing legal accountability for federal overreach and ensuring local police do not act as immigration agents will keep our neighborhoods safe. Our schools, courthouses, and hospitals will once again become places of safety and trust. We are incredibly grateful to Governor Healey, Senate President Spilka and House Speaker Mariano, as well as all legislators and the countless advocates who fought tirelessly to deliver these vital protections for all our immigrant neighbors.”

Chrissy Lynch, President, MA AFL-CIO:

“The Trump Administration is scapegoating immigrants to distract from Trump's policies that empower and enrich corporations and the ultra-wealthy while making it harder for working class people to get by. Immigrants and refugees helped to build our nation, our state and our unions, and are essential to our past, present and future. We are proud to count within our ranks thousands of immigrant workers across the Commonwealth, and we stand in unwavering solidarity with immigrant workers and their families who are scared to go to work, school, and the doctor. The PROTECT Act takes important steps towards ensuring that our Commonwealth remains a safe place for people to go to work, and we thank the Healey-Driscoll Administration as well as House and Senate leadership for their work on this critical issue.”

Matt Bach, President, Massachusetts Teachers Association:

“The MTA proudly celebrates the signing of the PROTECT Act into law, a significant achievement made possible by the dedicated efforts of organizers, lawmakers, educators, families, and supporters across Massachusetts. While this milestone is important, our work is far from finished. We remain committed to ensuring that our immigrant students and their families feel safe and supported in our communities and public schools. Educators must have all of their students present and secure in class, ready to engage in the learning process. We look forward to collaborating with our partner organizations to continue Massachusetts' leadership in protecting and empowering immigrant students.”

Jessica Tang, President, American Federation of Teachers Massachusetts:

“Immigrant families are Massachusetts families. They've raised their kids here. They've gone to our public schools. As vital members of our local economies, immigrants have given back to our neighborhoods in immeasurable ways and are an integral part of what makes Massachusetts strong. They should be allowed to live in their communities, go to school, seek medical care, and take care of their families without fear. Educators are going above and beyond to reassure students and their families that schools and their surroundings are the safe spaces they are supposed to be and the PROTECT Act provides us with the resources and protections we need to strengthen these efforts. Today, the Commonwealth is a safer, stronger place for all, and we are proud to stand with Governor Healey, Senate President Spilka, Speaker Mariano, and all the elected leaders who made this law possible. Our work is not done, we must continue to do everything in our power to support those impacted by the reckless and inhumane campaign being waged by ICE in our communities.”

Michael Curry, Esq., President and CEO of the Massachusetts League of Community Health Centers:

“Our most vulnerable patients must be certain they are safe from harm to feel comfortable seeking care and trusting their providers with sensitive medical and personal information. The PROTECT Act ensures the sacred relationship between patients and health care providers cannot be undermined by immigration enforcement activities. I am grateful to Governor Healey and the Legislature for prioritizing the integrity of our health care system, the health of patients, and the safety of our communities by enacting this pivotal bill into law.”

Elsie M. Taveras, MD, MPH, Chief Community Health & Health Equity Officer, Mass General Brigham

“Mass General Brigham is committed to providing safe, compassionate, and high-quality care when and where people need it. We are appreciative of Governor Healey’s efforts to ensure patients feel comfortable seeking care and to preserve trust in our healthcare system.”

Marty Martinez, President and Chief Executive Officer, United Way of Massachusetts Bay:

“At a time when immigrants are facing tremendous uncertainty and increased barriers to accessing basic needs, it is critical for the Commonwealth to strengthen protections, prevent family separation and keep our immigrant neighbors safe. Today's signing of the PROTECT Act by the Governor and the advocacy from all our elected officials shows our immigrant neighbors that they do not need to face these challenges alone and that their well-being and safety is inextricably linked to the health and strength of our communities.”

Anthony Benedetti, Chief Counsel, Committee for Public Counsel Services:

“CPCS is deeply grateful to the House, the Senate, and the Governor for their leadership in reaffirming a fundamental principle: constitutional rights, due process, and the rule of law do not depend on a person's immigration status.”

Doris Landaverde, Co-Coordinator, National TPS Alliance:

“We have witnessed firsthand the profound impact that the loss of Temporary Protected Status (TPS) has had on our communities. Families from Venezuela, Nepal, Honduras, Nicaragua, Haiti, Syria, and other countries are facing tremendous uncertainty, along with the heartbreaking threat of family separation. We recognize and deeply appreciate the countless individuals and organizations that have fought tirelessly to secure the passage of the Protect Act legislation. We also applaud the legislators and the Governor's leadership for signing this important measure into law, providing greater protections for communities currently facing persecution and uncertainty here in Massachusetts. This is a meaningful step toward a more just, inclusive, and compassionate Commonwealth—one that upholds the dignity, safety, and humanity of all people.”

Carol Rose, Executive Director, The ACLU of Massachusetts:

“Massachusetts has sent a powerful message to the Trump administration: We will not stand idly by while ICE agents tear apart families and shatter our communities. The PROTECT Act will help to establish a firewall between Massachusetts law enforcement and federal immigration officials, ensuring that local police are not co-opted by President Trump's cruel political agenda. Importantly, the law will also support access to courts for everyone and bolster trust in local institutions. We applaud Governor Healey, Senate President Spilka, House Speaker Mariano, and the Black and Latino Legislative Caucus, among others, for their steadfast leadership and dedication. And we are deeply grateful to the many immigrant advocates who worked for years to make this day a reality.”

Reverend Dr. Dieufort J. Fleurissaint:

“Today marks a historic moment for Massachusetts. The PROTECT Act strengthens our commitment to justice, due process, and human dignity, bringing renewed hope and stronger protections for immigrant families during a time of uncertainty. I commend Governor Maura Healey, the Legislature, and the coalition of advocates, faith leaders, and community partners whose tireless work made this possible.”

Cindy Rowe, President & CEO, Jewish Alliance for Law and Social Action:

“This is a shameful time for our country. ICE's cruelty runs directly counter to the shared values of people of faith. I'm proud that, here in Massachusetts, Governor Maura Healey and our state legislature have said clearly that we will no longer enable ICE's campaign of fear, tearing apart families and communities. Our sacred scriptures tell us that we must 'welcome the stranger.' This advice was good enough to have lasted for literally thousands of years, and it's sound advice for us to follow now. I'm grateful that our elected officials agree and have made the PROTECT ACT the law in our Commonwealth.”

Helena DaSilva Hughes, President, Immigrants' Assistance Center:

“For over 50 years, the Immigrants' Assistance Center has stood alongside immigrant families, helping them overcome barriers and build secure, productive lives in Massachusetts. Every day, we witness the fear and uncertainty many families experience. The PROTECT Act provides important safeguards that help our clients feel safer accessing schools, health care, and other essential services while strengthening trust between immigrant communities and public institutions. We thank Governor Healey for her leadership and commitment to ensuring that Massachusetts remains a welcoming Commonwealth where all families are treated with dignity, fairness, and respect.”

Jorge Rivera, Director of Organizing, International Union Painters and Allied Trades District Council 35:

“Five members of DC 35 have been taken by ICE. Five of our coworkers, our neighbors, our families. Every one of them deserved to go to work, drop their kids at school, or see a doctor without fear of being hunted to fill a federal quota. The PROTECT Act affirms what should never have needed saying at all: our schools, our courthouses, and our workplaces are not hunting grounds. We thank Governor Healey for standing with immigrant families and refusing to look away. This was never about documentation. It is about whether we still treat each other as human beings. Massachusetts just answered yes.”

Heather Yountz, Senior Immigration Attorney, Mass Law Reform institute:

“In the face of unprecedented violence and attacks on immigrants, Massachusetts legislators and Governor Healey took action. The PROTECT Act ensures that the rights of all Massachusetts residents are protected under the Massachusetts Constitution and Massachusetts law. We at MLRI are especially gratified that this bill includes the I-9 provision introduced by Senator Lewis and Representatives Philips and Cruz. This provision protects the due process rights of immigrant workers by providing them with notice before ICE reviews their private I-9 documents. ICE has recently used the I-9 inspection process to access the private files of immigrants without their knowledge or a warrant, and the data in these files is often used as a precursor for arrests and raids. Since ICE is arresting lawful immigrants without regard or understanding of their status, immigrants are being arrested erroneously and in violation of their due process rights. By providing immigrants with notice before ICE gets involved, immigrant workers are able to prepare for an ICE enforcement action by speaking with an attorney, gathering key documentation, learning their rights, and providing guardianship for their children if necessary.”

Bob Rivers, Executive Chair & Chair of the Board of Directors, Eastern Bank:

“At Eastern Bank, we focus on doing good things to help all people prosper. This includes supporting our immigrant neighbors across Massachusetts and ensuring they can get to work, their children’s school, and the doctor’s office safely. I applaud the Healey-Driscoll Administration and the Legislature for taking this important step to support our immigrant communities in today’s climate of uncertainty.”

Katie Murphy, President, Massachusetts Nurses Associations:

“As nurses and healthcare professionals, our highest duty is to care for our patients without exception, and the passage of the PROTECT Act ensures that Massachusetts healthcare facilities remain safe havens of healing for all. For too long, the fear of immigration enforcement has forced vulnerable members of our community to suffer in silence, avoiding essential medical care out of fear of deportation. By shielding sensitive public spaces like hospitals and clinics from warrantless civil arrests, this law protects patient trust, removes barriers to care, and safeguards public health. We are proud to stand with other social justice advocates and lawmakers today to celebrate legislation that allows healthcare professionals to treat every patient with the dignity, safety, and security they deserve.”

Thomas M. King, Executive Director, Massachusetts Children's Alliance:

“Every day, Children's Advocacy Centers across Massachusetts help children who have experienced abuse, violence, or exploitation receive the protection, treatment, and support they need to begin healing. For that work to succeed, families must feel safe seeking help and participating in the investigative process. Trust is essential to protecting children. The PROTECT Act strengthens that trust by helping ensure families can report abuse, work with law enforcement, and access medical care, mental health services, and victim advocacy without unnecessary barriers. Across Massachusetts, we work together, Children's Advocacy Centers, law enforcement, child protection professionals, prosecutors, medical providers, and victim advocates, to help abused children receive the best care possible. Laws that strengthen trust in these systems make that work more effective and help ensure that every child can access the services they need. Protecting children is a shared responsibility. When families are able to come forward, children are safer, multidisciplinary teams can do their work more effectively, and more children have the opportunity to heal.”

Dr. Mary M. Bourque, Executive Director, The Massachusetts Association of School Superintendents:

“M.A.S.S. extends our sincere gratitude to Governor Maura Healey and the Healey-Driscoll Administration for signing the Protect Act into law. At a time when school leaders are navigating increasingly complex challenges to ensure every student feels safe, welcomed, and able to learn, this legislation provides important clarity and reinforces the Commonwealth's longstanding commitment to protecting the rights, safety, and well-being of children and families. Massachusetts superintendents are committed to creating school environments where every student can thrive. The Protect Act supports that work by providing a clear legal framework that helps districts carry out their responsibilities with confidence while maintaining strong partnerships with students, families, and communities. We are grateful to Governor Healey, Lieutenant Governor Driscoll, and the Legislature for their continued leadership and unwavering support of public education. M.A.S.S. looks forward to working collaboratively with the Administration and state agencies to ensure thoughtful implementation that supports school districts across the Commonwealth as they continue their vital work on behalf of Massachusetts students.”

Carlos Aramayo, President, UNITE HERE Local 26:

“For the thousands of hotel, airport, and food service workers who keep Massachusetts running every single day, the passage of the PROTECT Act is a monumental victory for human dignity and workplace justice. We celebrate this milestone and thank Governor Healey, the Massachusetts Black and Latino Legislative Caucus, legislative leaders, and our dedicated coalition partners for getting this over the finish line. UNITE HERE Local 26 remains committed to ensuring that every worker can live, work, and raise their family free from fear.”

Greater Boston Legal Services:

“Greater Boston Legal Services welcomes the enactment of the PROTECT Act. Every day, we work with clients who need to be able to seek legal help, appear in court, and access essential services without fear. The PROTECT Act strengthens due process and access to counsel while helping ensure that our legal system remains fair and accessible to everyone.”

title: New USCIS Asylum Interview Rule Could Speed Up Deportations of Asylum Seekers
description:
For decades, an asylum interview has been a cornerstone of the affirmative asylum process.
The importance of an asylum interview Many asylum seekers have experienced trauma, fled under dangerous circumstances, or come from countries where documentation is difficult or impossible to obtain.
Shifting cases from USCIS to immigration courts USCIS argues that eliminating interviews in some cases will improve efficiency and reduce its own backlog.
Today, approximately 72% of all pending immigration court cases involve asylum claims.
The affirmative asylum interview has long served as a safeguard ensuring that applicants have a meaningful opportunity to explain their claims before facing removal proceedings.
text:
The Trump administration has taken another significant step toward restricting access to asylum in the United States. At the same time, it has moved to end protections such as Temporary Protected Status (TPS), increasing the risk that many will be deported to countries where they may face persecution. For many, asylum is the only remaining protection against being returned to harm. But the administration’s latest effort would make that protection harder than ever to obtain.

On July 28, U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) published an interim final rule giving its asylum officers the authority to forego providing applicants an interview before referring their application to an immigration judge, including for already pending cases. For decades, an asylum interview has been a cornerstone of the affirmative asylum process. Every person seeking asylum had the opportunity to explain their claim directly to a specially trained asylum officer in a non-adversarial setting.

Under the new rule, that presumption no longer exists. Instead, USCIS may summarily decide that an applicant is ineligible for asylum and refer the case directly to immigration court for an adversarial proceeding in the case without ever speaking to the applicant.

Although the administration frames the rule as an efficiency measure to reduce USCIS’ affirmative asylum backlog, the rule further enables the government to push asylum claims quickly through the immigration system, likely leading to increased negative outcomes. USCIS says applicants can still present their cases to immigration judges, but, over the past year, the administration has made that process faster, including by expanding the summary dismissal, or pretermission, of asylum applications before applicants can fully present their claims.

The importance of an asylum interview

Many asylum seekers have experienced trauma, fled under dangerous circumstances, or come from countries where documentation is difficult or impossible to obtain. Asylum officers receive specialized training to conduct interviews that help applicants explain inconsistencies, clarify timelines, and describe the persecution they experienced. Interviews also allow officers to assess credibility, ask follow-up questions, and identify facts that may not appear in a written application. This is important as asylum seekers may have difficulty recollecting their experiences to an officer due to their past trauma.

The interview is one of the defining characteristics of the affirmative asylum process. Unlike immigration court proceedings, it is conducted in a non-adversarial setting. Rather than arguing against the applicant, the asylum officer’s role is to gather information and determine whether the applicant qualifies for protection under U.S. law.

The new final rule falsely suggests that foregoing this requirement would have minimal impact because the asylum applicant would still have an opportunity to present their case before an immigration judge. Immigration court hearings are adversarial, where the government is represented by trained attorneys and most noncitizens go unrepresented because they are unable to afford one. Since last January, the administration has moved to rescind federal payments to nonprofits providing much of the free or low-cost legal help to immigrants that has existed in recent years, including representation to unaccompanied children.

Deciding complex cases without ever speaking to the applicant

The rule authorizes USCIS to bypass interviews for broad categories of applicants, including where the applicant is not in lawful status, has not already been scheduled or received an interview, and the asylum officer determines the person:

Is barred from applying for asylum.

Is barred from a grant of asylum.

Does not merit a grant as a matter of discretion.

Is not eligible on the merits.

Many of these determinations involve highly technical legal questions rather than straightforward factual findings. For example, one category of individuals barred from applying for asylum includes applicants who filed for asylum more than one year after their most recent arrival in the United States. At first glance, this may seem like a simple deadline. In reality, the law contains numerous statutory and regulatory exceptions.

Individuals who maintained lawful immigration status before applying, experienced changed circumstances, or faced extraordinary circumstances may still qualify despite filing after one year. USCIS estimates that 132,167 asylum applications will be referred annually in the future without an interview.

USCIS also identified as many as 444,724 pending applications that could potentially fall within this category (but, highlighting the nuance here, USCIS’ estimate also includes people who left their entry dates “blank”). That figure includes many individuals who were previously paroled into the United States, including Afghans and Ukrainians, who may have not applied for asylum within a year because they believed they would receive other protections or that circumstances in their home countries would change.

The agency states that it is reviewing which pending cases can be referred without an interview based on the current record, but that it may issue requests for evidence in certain cases or otherwise issue web-based reminder alerts. It also suggests applicants could “supplement” the record on their own if they “feel like” they need to submit more information to meet their burden.

Another change could significantly shift asylum processing by allowing USCIS to refer cases to immigration court as a matter of discretion without first determining whether the applicant qualifies as a refugee. Previous guidance required asylum officers to make that statutory determination before a discretionary referral. This change appears to conflict with a Board of Immigration Appeals’ precedential decision holding that “the danger of persecution should generally outweigh all but the most egregious of adverse factors.” Without that finding, USCIS cannot properly compare other discretionary factors.

Shifting cases from USCIS to immigration courts

USCIS argues that eliminating interviews in some cases will improve efficiency and reduce its own backlog. But efficiency for one agency does not necessarily translate into efficiency for the immigration system. Rather than resolving applications within USCIS, the rule simply shifts the workload onto an immigration court system that is already struggling under a massive backlog and has fewer due process protections.

Today, approximately 72% of all pending immigration court cases involve asylum claims. Over the past year, the administration has increased efforts to close these cases, including by increasing pressure on judges to resolve cases more quickly by dangling the threat of firing over them; rapidly rescheduling large numbers of hearings into one “mega-master” hearing aimed at catching noncitizens off-guard and ordering them removed in their absence, and increasing the number of asylum applications immigration judges are pretermitting — or dismissing — without reaching the merits.

Taken together, these changes reflect a consistent policy by this administration of reducing opportunities for individualized review while emphasizing speedy negative outcomes and ultimate removal. In fact, in January, the White House praised that its administration had achieved the lowest asylum grant rates in decades.

Efficiency should not come at the expense of fairness

Reducing backlogs is an important policy objective. But the question is not simply how quickly cases move through the system—it is whether they are decided fairly.

The affirmative asylum interview has long served as a safeguard ensuring that applicants have a meaningful opportunity to explain their claims before facing removal proceedings. Eliminating that opportunity risks sending individuals with potentially meritorious asylum claims directly into an already overburdened immigration court system, where the process is more adversarial, more complex, and often far more difficult to navigate.

Viewed in isolation, the rule may appear to be a technical procedural change. Viewed alongside the administration’s broader immigration agenda, however, it represents another step in a fundamental transformation of how the United States evaluates — and increasingly restricts — access to asylum.

name: Policy
title: This federal judge ruled against Trump. Then the threats began. - The Detroit News
description:
He called Esther Salas, a fellow federal judge in a different state.
For McConnell, the pizza delivery was part of a wave of threats unlike anything he had ever experienced and signaled a new era for federal judges.
“What’s unusual is the dehumanization, the threats, the personalization of our doing our jobs.” McConnell, an appointee of President Barack Obama, is the chief federal judge in Rhode Island.
In recent years, federal judges and Supreme Court justices have faced increasing risks to their safety.
According to the Marshals Service, there were 564 threats to federal judges in the 2025 fiscal year, up from 509 the prior year.
text:
Providence, R.I. ― The pizza delivery was strange. No one at U.S. District Judge John McConnell’s home had ordered it. But it was the name on the order that shocked him.

Daniel Anderl.

McConnell knew what he had to do. He called Esther Salas, a fellow federal judge in a different state. He told her that he had received a delivery in the name of her son, who was shot and killed in 2020 by a disgruntled lawyer targeting Salas.

Such deliveries would be made to federal judges in at least seven states, but McConnell was the first to tell Salas, and both were distraught. Who would use someone’s dead child to threaten and intimidate? “I don’t think anything disturbed me as much as that did,” McConnell recalled.

For McConnell, the pizza delivery was part of a wave of threats unlike anything he had ever experienced and signaled a new era for federal judges.

His experience is emblematic of the climate facing such jurists, whether nominated by Democratic or Republican presidents, when they make high-profile rulings that find Trump administration actions to be unlawful.

President Donald Trump and his allies have repeatedly blasted individual federal judges as rogue actors and political activists whose rulings are illegitimate, including in a post last month by the top lawyer at the Department of Homeland Security.

Some judges have found the rhetoric so troubling that they are increasingly speaking out about the danger it poses to the rule of law, an unusual move for members of the judiciary, who prefer to avoid the limelight.

“We’re just doing our job,” McConnell said. “What’s unusual is the dehumanization, the threats, the personalization of our doing our jobs.”

McConnell, an appointee of President Barack Obama, is the chief federal judge in Rhode Island. For nearly all his 15 years on the federal bench, he worked in relative obscurity. He rarely gave his personal safety a second thought.

That changed dramatically starting early last year. McConnell, 68, received credible death threats. A MAGA activist doxed his daughter. Two Republicans in Congress started impeachment proceedings against him. An insurance company even canceled McConnell’s homeowner’s policy (the insured party was too risky, the firm indicated, with an attached link to one impeachment effort).

McConnell agreed to discuss his experience in detail with The Washington Post because he’s worried about ongoing efforts to intimidate and delegitimize judges. In his relatively small federal court, all three judges have received threats in connection with rulings against the executive branch over the past 18 months, he said. This spring, one of those colleagues was lambasted by DHS in a misleading news release, a statement that “put her in personal danger,” McConnell later wrote.

A DHS spokesperson declined to respond to questions about the news release and directed The Post to a recent statement by the agency’s general counsel, the same official who last month criticized judges on social media. “Legitimate fact based critique of judges and their rulings is fair game in a free society,” James Percival wrote in a post on the social media platform X.

Tensions between the different branches of government are not new, Salas, an Obama appointee in New Jersey, said in an interview. Over the past decade, she said, members of both parties have ratcheted up their rhetoric about judges. But what is occurring under the Trump administration - where the president and other officials have called federal judges “monsters,” “lunatics” and more, and deemed rulings a form of “legal insurrection” - is something else, she said.

“This is no longer apples to apples,” Salas said, stressing that she was speaking as a mother, rather than in her official capacity. “This is apples to watermelons.”

When asked about Trump’s personalized attacks on judges, a White House spokeswoman said such opinions are a form of free expression. The implication that Trump sharing his thoughts about judges is “akin to making threats is deeply unserious and should be dismissed by anyone with half a brain,” Abigail Jackson said in a statement. “No one understands the dangers of political violence more than President Trump,” she added. “The Trump Administration cares deeply for the safety of all members of the Judicial Branch.”

‘A dagger through my heart’

McConnell, a Rhode Island native, spent most of his career as a trial lawyer. He was also active in Democratic politics, making large donations over decades, and his nomination to the federal bench cleared the Senate on party lines in 2011. When “you take that oath,” McConnell said, “your North Star changes to the rule of law.”

When McConnell first started working in the granite-faced federal courthouse in Providence, he was nonchalant about questions of safety. He remembers being chided for not telling the U.S. marshals, who protect federal judges, about an outdoor naturalization ceremony he was conducting at a minor-league baseball stadium. “I thought, ‘I’m just going to live my life,’” McConnell said.

The drastic reassessment of his own security began early last year. In late January, McConnell was randomly assigned a case, as per procedure, challenging the Trump administration’s sweeping freeze on trillions of dollars in federal funding. He granted a temporary restraining order. Ten days later, he reminded the government it was obliged to follow the order, noting that not complying would risk being held in criminal contempt.

That night, McConnell was at home alone reviewing legal papers when something startling popped up on his phone. Laura Loomer, a far-right political activist, had posted about him on the social media site X, accusing him of abusing his judicial power in the funding freeze case.

The post included a photo of McConnell’s daughter, who worked as a political appointee in the Department of Education under President Joe Biden. Elon Musk, X’s billionaire owner who was then heading the Trump administration’s Department of Government Efficiency, recirculated the post to millions of followers.

“I signed up for whatever, I’ll take the lumps,” McConnell said. But when his daughter became a target, “I felt like someone put a dagger through my heart.”

It escalated from there. Disturbing calls and emails began arriving at the federal courthouse, first by the dozens, then by the hundreds, about 400 in total. McConnell’s case manager asked not to listen to them anymore.

McConnell recently played one that is saved on his phone. In an expletive-filled rant, the caller accuses of McConnell of “stepping way over” his “boundaries.”

“You better tell little motherf---ing Judge McConnell, I don’t know who the hell he thinks he is,” the caller said. “I wish somebody would f---ing assassinate your a--.”

The U.S. Marshals Service told McConnell they had identified at least six credible death threats. One specifically menaced McConnell’s wife. Another turned up on the dark web - the swath of the internet not accessible to search engines - where someone was looking for McConnell’s home address, saying Smith & Wesson wanted “to pay him a visit.”

(McConnell won’t discuss the specific changes made to his daily routine, except to say that the cooperation with the U.S. marshals has been “exemplary.”)

McConnell’s experience is not unique. In recent years, federal judges and Supreme Court justices have faced increasing risks to their safety. In the 2025 fiscal year, security incidents of “significant concern” jumped 57 percent and are on track to rise again, the judiciary recently told Congress.

According to the Marshals Service, there were 564 threats to federal judges in the 2025 fiscal year, up from 509 the prior year. In April, the agency asked for additional funding for its judicial security division, noting that “the current and future threat environment [is] expected to intensify.”

The Trump administration has continued to launch personal attacks on judges. In April, DHS issued a news release referring to U.S. District Judge Melissa DuBose, one of McConnell’s colleagues in Rhode Island, as an “activist Biden judge” who had released an immigrant “wanted for murder” in the Dominican Republic.

The problem: When DuBose released the immigrant from custody, she was unaware of the homicide warrant against him. That information was purposely withheld by the U.S. attorney in the case, who was acting on instructions from Immigration and Customs Enforcement not to disclose it, a subsequent 80-page investigative report by a special counsel found.

The sequence of events raises the question of whether ICE “deliberately manipulated” the information it presented in the case to attack DuBose, the court said in a statement last month. “False statements by government officials … interfere with the rule of law, and as we have seen, have real world consequences,” it continued.

Last month, Percival, the top DHS lawyer, posted a list of federal judges, calling them the “Worst of the Worst” - the same language the agency uses to highlight alleged criminals it seeks to deport. McConnell reached out to one of the people named in the post. His message to that judge: Take your security seriously, know the resources available to you and be careful.

On a personal level, McConnell said, he puts his faith in the marshals when it comes to protecting him and his family. The fear that stayed with him was what the threats meant for the future of the judiciary. Attempts to intimidate judges strike “at the very heart of the constitutional role of the courts as the preserver of the rule of law in our country,” McConnell said.

McConnell said he was heartened by statements by Chief Justice John G. Roberts Jr., who has said criticism of judges as individuals - rather than of their rulings - is “not appropriate.” Roberts has also repeatedly stated that impeachment is not the correct response to a disagreement over a judicial decision. “That meant the world to me,” McConnell said.

Some of McConnell’s rulings have sparked a positive response. Last November, he issued a preliminary injunction preventing the administration from dismantling the Institute of Museum and Library Services, an agency created by Congress. Librarians across the country sent him a slew of appreciative postcards.

While the threatening calls and emails to McConnell’s office have ebbed since last year, they sometimes flare up. In June, McConnell ruled that the Trump administration’s move to freeze immigration-related applications for citizens of 39 countries was unlawful. The U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Service “violated the very immigration laws that Congress has charged it with administering, as well as the administrative laws that govern the agency’s actions,” McConnell wrote.

The same month, a Republican member of Congress moved to impeach McConnell for “high crimes and misdemeanors,” saying he had “placed the interests of noncitizens” above the “national security of the United States.”

It was the second attempt to impeach McConnell, and the administrative office of the federal judiciary reached out to see if it could assist. McConnell declined. He just wanted to get back to doing his job.
